Questions: What is Peter Lynch's view on investing without doing research?
Answers: Lynch says investing is fun, exciting, and dangerous if you don't do any work. Research is essential for investment success.

Questions: According to Lynch, where does your real investor's edge come from?
Answers: Lynch teaches that your investor's edge isn't from Wall Street experts - it's something you already have from your own knowledge and experience.

Questions: How does Lynch say amateur investors can outperform professionals?
Answers: Lynch believes you can outperform experts by using your edge - investing in companies or industries you already understand from daily life.

Questions: Why does Lynch think the market is now easier for amateur investors?
Answers: Lynch observes that professional investors now dominate the market in herds, which actually makes it easier for amateur investors who can ignore the herd.

Questions: What is Lynch's fundamental approach to stock analysis?
Answers: Lynch always reminds investors that behind every stock is a company - you must find out what the company is doing.

Questions: How does Lynch explain the relationship between company performance and stock prices?
Answers: Lynch notes there's often no correlation between company success and stock performance short-term, but 100% correlation long-term. This disparity is key to making money.

Questions: What must investors know about their holdings according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch insists you must know what you own and why you own it. Saying 'this baby is a cinch to go up!' doesn't count as analysis.

Questions: What is Lynch's view on long-shot investments?
Answers: Lynch warns that long shots almost always miss the mark - focus on solid, understandable companies instead.

Questions: How does Lynch compare owning stocks to having children?
Answers: Lynch says owning stocks is like having children - don't get involved with more than you can handle. Quality over quantity.

Questions: How many companies can a part-time investor effectively follow according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch believes part-time stockpickers can follow 8-12 companies effectively, buying and selling as conditions warrant.

Questions: What is Lynch's recommended maximum portfolio size?
Answers: Lynch suggests there don't need to be more than 5 companies in a portfolio at any one time.

Questions: What should investors do when they can't find attractive companies?
Answers: Lynch advises putting money in the bank until you discover attractive companies rather than investing in mediocre ones.

Questions: What is Lynch's most important rule about company finances?
Answers: Lynch emphasizes never investing in a company without understanding its finances - always check the balance sheet for solvency first.

Questions: Where do the biggest stock losses come from according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch warns that the biggest losses come from companies with poor balance sheets - financial strength is crucial.

Questions: What types of stocks does Lynch recommend avoiding vs. buying?
Answers: Lynch says avoid hot stocks in hot industries. Instead, buy great companies in cold, nongrowth industries - they're consistent big winners.

Questions: When should you invest in small companies according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch recommends waiting until small companies turn a profit before investing - don't speculate on pre-profit companies.

Questions: How should you approach troubled industries according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch suggests buying companies with staying power in troubled industries, but wait for signs of industry revival first.

Questions: What does Lynch say about investment risk vs. reward potential?
Answers: Lynch points out you can lose maximum $1,000 on a $1,000 investment, but stand to gain $10,000 or $50,000 over time with patience.

Questions: What advantage do individual investors have over fund managers?
Answers: Lynch explains individuals can concentrate on a few good companies, while fund managers are forced to diversify, losing the advantage of concentration.

Questions: How many big winners does Lynch say you need for investment success?
Answers: Lynch believes it only takes a handful of big winners to make a lifetime of investing worthwhile.

Questions: Where can amateur investors find undiscovered growth companies?
Answers: Lynch says in every industry and region, observant amateurs can find great growth companies long before professionals discover them.

Questions: How does Lynch want investors to view market declines?
Answers: Lynch teaches that stock market declines are as routine as January blizzards in Colorado - if prepared, they can't hurt you.

Questions: What opportunity do market declines create according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch sees declines as great opportunities to pick up bargains left behind by panicking investors.

Questions: What does Lynch say about brainpower vs. emotional control in investing?
Answers: Lynch observes everyone has the brainpower to make money in stocks, but not everyone has the stomach for volatility.

Questions: Who should avoid stock investing according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch warns that if you're susceptible to selling everything in a panic, you should avoid stocks and stock mutual funds altogether.

Questions: What should guide your selling decisions according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch advises selling because company fundamentals deteriorate, not because of scary headlines or dire predictions about the economy.

Questions: What does Lynch say about economic and market predictions?
Answers: Lynch states nobody can predict interest rates, future economic direction, or stock market movements - dismiss all such forecasts.

Questions: What should you focus on instead of forecasts according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch recommends concentrating on what's actually happening to the companies you've invested in rather than macro predictions.

Questions: What is Lynch's research success ratio?
Answers: Lynch teaches that if you study 10 companies, you'll find 1 with a better story than expected. Study 50, you'll find 5.

Questions: What happens when you don't research companies according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch warns that not studying companies gives you same success as playing poker without looking at your cards.

Questions: How does time work for investors in superior companies?
Answers: Lynch explains time is on your side with superior companies - you can afford to be patient for long-term gains.

Questions: What is Lynch's example of patience being rewarded?
Answers: Lynch notes even missing Wal-Mart in first five years, it was still great to own in the next five years.

Questions: When does time work against investors according to Lynch?
Answers: Lynch warns time is against you when you own options due to their expiration dates.

Questions: What should investors do if they lack time for stock research?
Answers: Lynch recommends investing in equity mutual funds, diversifying among different fund types with different management styles.

Questions: What is not true diversification in mutual fund investing?
Answers: Lynch clarifies that investing in six funds of the same kind is not diversification - you need different styles and approaches.

Questions: What does Lynch warn about frequent mutual fund switching?
Answers: Lynch notes the capital-gains tax penalizes investors who do too much switching between mutual funds.

Questions: What should you do with successful mutual fund investments?
Answers: Lynch advises not abandoning successful funds capriciously - stick with funds that have performed well for you.

Questions: How does Lynch rank the U.S. stock market globally?
Answers: Lynch notes the U.S. market ranks eighth among major world markets in total return over the past decade.

Questions: How can investors benefit from faster-growing global economies?
Answers: Lynch suggests investing some portion of assets in overseas funds with good records to capture faster international growth.

Questions: What does Lynch guarantee about long-term stock vs. bond performance?
Answers: Lynch states a portfolio of well-chosen stocks and/or equity mutual funds will always outperform bonds or money-market accounts long-term.

Questions: What warning does Lynch give about poorly chosen stocks?
Answers: Lynch warns that a portfolio of poorly chosen stocks won't outperform money left under the mattress - selection quality matters.

Questions: Why did Lynch get his hair cut at Supercuts?
Answers: A prospectus for the haircutting venture had found its way to his desk, leading him to cheat on his regular barber Vinnie DiVincenzo for research purposes.

Questions: Who is Lynch's regular barber and what does he charge?
Answers: Vinnie DiVincenzo offers a $10 haircut with pleasant conversation at his Marblehead, Massachusetts business.

Questions: Where was the Supercuts location Lynch visited?
Answers: 829 Boylston Street, Boston, on the second floor of a brownstone.

Questions: What were Supercuts' pricing options?
Answers: Regular Supercut: $8.95; Supercut with shampoo: $12; shampoo alone: $4.

Questions: How did Supercuts prices compare to Lynch's regular barber?
Answers: Prices were in line with Vinnie's charges and substantially less than beauty salons and unisex outlets where his family gets haircuts.

Questions: What did Lynch observe about customer demand at Supercuts?
Answers: Three customers getting haircuts, four waiting, all male, indicating people thought a Supercuts haircut was worth waiting for.

Questions: When did Supercuts make its stock market debut?
Answers: October 1991 at an initial offering price of $11 per share.

Questions: What was Supercuts' business model?
Answers: A franchise operation, the 'McTrim of barbershops,' with over 650 stores already established when it went public.

Questions: Who was brought in to oversee Supercuts expansion?
Answers: Ed Faber, former head of Computerland, an ex-marine who had done wonders for Computerland in its fast-growth phase.

Questions: What industry opportunity did Supercuts address?
Answers: Hair care is a $15-40 billion industry dominated by independent barbers and local salons, with barbers becoming a vanishing breed.

Questions: How much has the number of licensed haircutters declined?
Answers: In New York State, the number of licensed haircutters dropped in half in the last decade.

Questions: What is the basic math behind hair growth and the business opportunity?
Answers: Hair grows half an inch per month, and with independent barbers disappearing, somebody has to cut it - perfect for a nationwide franchise.

Questions: How does Lynch compare Supercuts to Service Corporation International?
Answers: Similar situation - people were dying at regular rate, somebody had to bury them, industry made up of inefficient small operators whose children wanted to go to law school.

Questions: What is Supercuts' efficiency model?
Answers: Each stylist trained for quick, efficient cutting with no dawdling, fitting the no-nonsense ethic of the 1990s.

Questions: How many heads can a Supercuts stylist cut per hour?
Answers: 2.8 heads per hour using small scissors and a 'revolutionary comb.'

Questions: What did Lynch learn about haircutter licensing requirements?
Answers: Haircutters have to be licensed (unlike fund managers), and there are no requirements for managing billions but you need to pass a test to trim sideburns.

Questions: What is the pay structure for Supercuts stylists?
Answers: $5-7 per hour base pay plus medical benefits, but can double wages with tips at 2.8 heads per hour.

Questions: What revenue does each stylist generate for the franchise?
Answers: $30 per hour in revenues for the franchise, making it very profitable to own a Supercuts.

Questions: What are the economics of owning a Supercuts franchise?
Answers: Average owner invests $100,000 upfront, expected to generate 50% pretax return on equity in just two years.

Questions: How does Supercuts benefit from franchise success?
Answers: Company receives 5% of gross revenues and 4% of Nexxus product sales, with minimal administrative costs.

Questions: What is Supercuts' training cost structure?
Answers: Hire one new trainer at $40,000/year for each 10 new shops, but those 10 shops contribute $300,000 annually in revenues.

Questions: What concerned Lynch about Supercuts' balance sheet?
Answers: Debt was 31% of total capital, a disturbing number that required further explanation.

Questions: What was Lynch's personal experience getting the Supercut?
Answers: The stylist snipped off everything including his sideburns so quickly he had no time to object, feeling like the privet hedge in Edward Scissorhands.

Questions: How did Lynch's family react to his new haircut?
Answers: 'What happened to you?' from his wife and daughters, with acquaintances saying he looked 'young' (which Lynch took as diplomatic politeness).

Questions: What is Lynch's exception to the 'like the store, buy the stock' rule?
Answers: After being sheared at Supercuts, he liked the stock prospects far more than he liked the store experience.

Questions: Who did Lynch speak with at Supercuts corporate?
Answers: Steven J. Thompson, senior vice-president and CFO, who commiserated about the lost sideburns and discussed business fundamentals.

Questions: What did Thompson say about hair growth?
Answers: 'The good news is that hair grows back at the rate of a half inch per month' - a fact Lynch had already taken hope from.

Questions: What was positive about Supercuts' employee turnover?
Answers: Thompson reported that turnover rate had been low so far, important for maintaining service quality.

Questions: How would Supercuts handle its debt situation?
Answers: $5.4 million annual free cash flow would be used to pay off debt, expecting to have no debt at all by 1993.

Questions: What advantage did Supercuts have as a franchise operation?
Answers: Money to set up new Supercuts would come from franchisees, allowing rapid expansion without using company capital or excessive borrowing.

Questions: What was the market opportunity for Supercuts?
Answers: 250 million Americans need haircuts monthly, mom-and-pop haircutters closing, no dominant chain had emerged to fill the void.

Questions: Who were Supercuts' major competitors?
Answers: Regis Corporation (Mastercuts in malls with higher rents), Fantastic Sam's (twice as many locations but half the revenue), J.C. Penney salon.

Questions: What competitive advantages did Supercuts have?
Answers: Open Sundays and evenings, working on national advertising campaign for brand recognition that competitors lacked.

Questions: What was Supercuts' growth rate and valuation when Lynch recommended it?
Answers: 20% grower selling for 16 times earnings at time of recommendation.

Questions: What did Lynch tell the Barron's panel about his Supercuts experience?
Answers: 'I got a haircut there, I tried it out.' When asked if it was his current haircut, he admitted it was.

Questions: What was Alan Abelson's reaction to Lynch's Supercuts haircut?
Answers: 'We won't advertise that' - referring to Lynch's appearance after the Supercuts experience.

Questions: What convinced Lynch to recommend Supercuts despite his bad haircut?
Answers: The excellent numbers and business fundamentals won out over the lost sideburns and poor personal experience.

Questions: What does Lynch emphasize about the haircutting industry transformation?
Answers: A perfect opportunity for a well-managed, efficient nationwide franchise to capture market from disappearing independent operators.

Questions: How does Lynch view the Supercuts business model sustainability?
Answers: Unlike aluminum industry where half earnings go to plant improvements, hair salon's biggest ongoing expenses are just scissors and combs.

Questions: What was Lynch's promise after the Supercuts experience?
Answers: Never again to stray from Vinnie DiVincenzo and his regular $10 haircut - loyalty to his regular barber was restored.

Questions: What is Lynch's preference between great industries and lousy industries?
Answers: Lynch prefers lousy industries over great industries anytime - in lousy industries, the weak drop out and survivors get bigger market share.

Questions: What does Lynch say about popular vs. unpopular industries?
Answers: A great industry that's growing fast attracts too much attention and competitors - as Yogi Berra said, 'It's so popular, nobody goes there anymore.'

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #16?
Answers: In business, competition is never as healthy as total domination.

Questions: What characteristics do great companies in lousy industries share?
Answers: Low-cost operators, penny-pinchers in executive suite, avoid debt, reject corporate caste system, well-paid workers with company stake, find niches.

Questions: What correlation does Lynch observe about corporate culture and performance?
Answers: Pompous boardrooms, overblown executive salaries, demoralized rank and file, excessive debt, and mediocre performance go hand in hand.

Questions: Who recommended Sun Television & Appliances to Lynch?
Answers: John Weiss, an analyst from Montgomery Securities in California, after Lynch asked about discount appliance store chains.

Questions: What convinced Lynch to call Sun TV directly?
Answers: Weiss's compelling story led Lynch to call corporate headquarters in Ohio to talk to the source directly.

Questions: Who did Lynch reach at Sun TV and what does this indicate?
Answers: Bob Oyster, the CEO, without delay - indicating the company doesn't suffer from excessive hierarchy.

Questions: What is Sun TV's market position?
Answers: Central Ohio's lone high-volume discount outlet for small appliances as well as major appliances, with seven stores in Columbus alone.

Questions: What demographic fact does Lynch mention about Columbus?
Answers: 50% of U.S. population lives within 500 miles of Columbus, and it's the only major city east of Mississippi, north of Mason-Dixon that grew 1950-1990.

Questions: What was Sun TV's expansion plan?
Answers: 7 new stores in 1991, 5 more in 1992, bringing total to 22 stores.

Questions: What were Sun TV's financial metrics when Lynch analyzed it?
Answers: Less than $10 million debt, stock selling for $18 with P/E ratio of 15, while growing at 25-30% rate.

Questions: How did Sun TV perform during the 1990-91 recession?
Answers: Made money when economy was terrible, home sales sluggish, and people weren't buying appliances - earnings actually increased in 1991.

Questions: What are the characteristics of Lynch's Magnificent Seven companies?
Answers: Great companies in lousy industries that have shown exceptional performance despite challenging sector conditions.

Questions: What was Southwest Airlines' stock performance in the terrible airline decade?
Answers: Rose from $2.40 to $24 during the 1980s when Eastern, Pan Am, Braniff, Continental, and Midway went bankrupt.

Questions: What is the key metric for airline cost efficiency?
Answers: Operating cost per seat mile - Southwest's ranged from 5-7 cents when industry average was 7-9 cents.

Questions: How does Lynch suggest judging a company's commitment to frugality?
Answers: Visit the headquarters - if company has a big building, it doesn't mean people are smart, but it means you helped pay for it.

Questions: What was Southwest Airlines' headquarters like?
Answers: Operated 18 years from barracks-like building at Love Field, then built modest three-story high rise, fired decorator who tried to replace employee awards with expensive art.

Questions: Who set the tone at Southwest Airlines?
Answers: CEO Herb Kelleher with wacky esprit - office decorated with turkeys, annual chili cookout, equal pay raises for all levels, executives work as counter agents monthly.

Questions: What was Southwest's employee culture?
Answers: Stewardesses in jeans and sneakers, meals limited to peanuts, safety info as rap song, prizes for biggest sock holes, no layoffs policy.

Questions: What niche did Southwest Airlines find?
Answers: 'The only high-frequency, short-distance, low-fare airline' - short hops while others flew widebodies on same routes to LA, NY, Europe.

Questions: How did Southwest benefit from competitor failures?
Answers: As others killed themselves off, Southwest grew from four-plane operation in 1978 to eighth-largest carrier, only U.S. airline profitable every year since 1973.

Questions: What was Southwest's stock performance from 1980-1990?
Answers: Shareholders saw 10-fold increase 1980-1985, then patience tested 1985-1990 when stock went sideways, but doubled again after 1990.

Questions: What does Lynch find less exciting than Bandag's business?
Answers: What could be less exciting than a company that makes retread tires in Muscatine, Iowa?

Questions: Where is Muscatine, Iowa located?
Answers: Small node on Mississippi River southwest of Davenport, southeast of Moscow, Atalissa, and West Liberty.

Questions: How many analysts have followed Bandag?
Answers: Only three analysts followed Bandag on its rise from $2 to $60 in 15 years.

Questions: What speed record does Bandag's CEO Martin Carver hold?
Answers: World speed record for a diesel truck.

Questions: What is Bandag's niche in the tire business?
Answers: The Southwest Airlines of retreads - every year 12 million worn truck/bus tires replaced with retreads, about 5 million are Bandag's.

Questions: What has been Bandag's dividend performance?
Answers: Increased dividend every year since 1975, with 17% earnings growth since 1977.

Questions: What is Cooper Tire's market strategy?
Answers: Stays out of the money-losing battle to equip new cars, instead focuses on replacement tire market for old cars.

Questions: How did Cooper Tire perform during the late 1980s tire industry struggles?
Answers: While big three (Michelin, Goodyear, Bridgestone) ruined each other's business, Cooper made money with earnings increasing every year from 1985.

Questions: What was Cooper Tire's stock performance around the Saddam Sell-off?
Answers: Tripled from 1987 low to $10, fell to $6 in Saddam Sell-off, then rose fivefold to $30 when world didn't end.

Questions: What business is Green Tree Financial in?
Answers: Mortgage loans for mobile homes - a lousy industry where sales have declined every year since 1985.

Questions: How bad was the mobile home market by 1990?
Answers: Only 200,000 new units sold, with record numbers of owners defaulting and abandoning property with notes saying 'our trailer is your trailer.'

Questions: How did Green Tree benefit from industry disaster?
Answers: Major competitors (Valley Federal, Financial Services Corp, Citicorp) gave up, leaving Green Tree to take advantage when action resumed.

Questions: What caused Green Tree's stock to fall to $8 in 1990?
Answers: Forbes published negative article 'Are the Tree's Roots Withering?' concluding even at 7x earnings, Green Tree wasn't much of a bargain.

Questions: How did Green Tree's stock perform after the negative Forbes article?
Answers: Rose from $8 to $36 in nine months as company had mobile-home loan business to itself with no competitors.

Questions: What new business lines helped Green Tree succeed?
Answers: Packaging loans for secondary market like Fannie Mae, home improvement loans, used-mobile-home loans, motorcycle financing.

Questions: What lesson does Green Tree's turnaround teach?
Answers: A survivor in a lousy industry can reverse fortunes quickly once competitors disappear.

Questions: What characterizes the Dillard family's management style?
Answers: 77-year-old William and son William II own 8% and almost all voting stock, run from Little Rock with Scroogian cost-cutting intensity.

Questions: How does Dillard treat its employees despite cost-cutting?
Answers: Employees are relatively well paid despite the family's search for cost savings.

Questions: What technology advantage does Dillard have?
Answers: Early computer adoption for inventory management - shirts selling well automatically trigger reorders from warehouse to vendor.

Questions: What markets does Dillard focus on?
Answers: Small towns and cities like Wichita and Memphis, staying away from glamour markets where larger chains stumble over each other.

Questions: How has Dillard grown through acquisitions?
Answers: Bought discarded divisions from bankrupt competitors (Joske's from Allied, J.B. Ivey from B.A.T. Industries) and connected them to Dillard computers.

Questions: What was Dillard's stock performance from 1980?
Answers: $10,000 investment in 1980 turned into $600,000 by the time Lynch wrote the book.

Questions: What does Crown Cork & Seal remind Lynch of?
Answers: New England Wire & Cable from 'Other People's Money' - messy executive suite over factory decorated with muffler-shop calendars.

Questions: What products does Crown Cork & Seal make?
Answers: Soda cans, beer cans, paint cans, pet food containers, antifreeze jugs, bottle caps, bottle washers, bottle rinsers, bottle crowners, can warmers.

Questions: What is Crown Cork & Seal's expense ratio compared to industry?
Answers: 2.5% expense-to-sales ratio vs. 15% industry average - bordering on monastic level of expenditure.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #17?
Answers: All else being equal, invest in the company with the fewest color photographs in the annual report.

Questions: How many color photographs were in Crown Cork & Seal's annual report?
Answers: Zero photographs under CEO John Connelly, who was hostile to extravagance but willing to spend on can-making technology.

Questions: What was Crown Cork & Seal's strategy under Connelly?
Answers: Profits not reinvested in operations were used to buy back shares, boosting earnings and share price for remaining shareholders.

Questions: How has Crown Cork & Seal changed since Connelly's death?
Answers: Uses cash flow to buy rivals and grow via acquisition, increased capital spending and debt, but new tactics remain profitable.

Questions: What was Crown Cork & Seal's stock performance in 1991?
Answers: Price moved from $54 to $92 during 1991.

Questions: Why does nobody want to be in the steel business?
Answers: Competition from Japanese, billions invested in equipment that may be outmoded, big producers like U.S. Steel and Bethlehem testing shareholders' patience for 12 years.

Questions: How has Bethlehem Steel performed since 1981?
Answers: Fell to $5 in 1986, recovered to current $13, but still far from 1981 high of $32.

Questions: What would Nucor investors think about the steel business?
Answers: $6 stock in 1981 worth $75 by time of writing, or $1 in 1971 now worth $75 - they'd think steel is greatest business of all time.

Questions: Who is the visionary behind Nucor's success?
Answers: F. Kenneth Iverson, who takes corporate clients to Phil's Deli across from Charlotte headquarters rather than executive dining room.

Questions: What is Nucor's egalitarian culture?
Answers: No executive dining room, limos, corporate jet, or special suit privileges - when profits decline, suits and overalls both take less pay.

Questions: What are Nucor's employee benefits?
Answers: 5,500 employees don't belong to union but fare better - profit sharing, no layoffs, children get college scholarships, shorter weeks during slowdowns.

Questions: What has been Nucor's competitive strategy evolution?
Answers: 1970s: specialized in turning scrap metal into construction-grade steel. Now: producing high-grade flat-rolled steel for auto bodies and appliances.

Questions: How much has been written about Shaw Industries?
Answers: Magazine database search produced only two listings: paragraph in Textile World and sentence in Datamation, plus two Wall Street Journal features.

Questions: What is Shaw Industries' market position?
Answers: $1 billion enterprise capturing 20% of U.S. carpet business, headquartered in Dalton, Georgia.

Questions: What is the historical significance of Dalton, Georgia?
Answers: Famous for moonshine, clog dancing, and 1895 invention of tufted bedspreads by young girl, leading to bedspread boom then carpet boom.

Questions: What is the banner behind Shaw's president's desk?
Answers: 'Maintain sufficient market share to allow full utilization of our production facilities.'

Questions: When did people stop laughing at Robert Shaw's billion-dollar company prediction?
Answers: When Shaw bought out West Point-Pepperell's carpet operations, a giant that sold twice as many carpets as Shaw.

Questions: How bad has the carpet business been historically?
Answers: In 1960s, 350 new carpet makers started with $10,000 investments, leading to price-cutting that ensured nobody made money.

Questions: What happened to the carpet industry in 1982?
Answers: Homeowners rediscovered wood floors, carpet boom ended, half of top 25 manufacturers out of business by mid-decade.

Questions: How has Shaw thrived in the nongrowth carpet industry?
Answers: As low-cost producer picking up business from every failed competitor, maintaining 20% growth rate during worst times.

Questions: What vertical integration has Shaw achieved?
Answers: Acquired yarn-making facility to eliminate middleman, has own distribution network with own truck fleet.

Questions: How does Shaw save on marketing costs?
Answers: Opted not to maintain expensive Atlanta trade showroom - sends bus to Atlanta and transports customers to Dalton.

Questions: What has been Shaw's stock performance since 1980?
Answers: Up 50-fold since 1980, lagged in 1990-91, then doubled again in 1992.

Questions: What does Shaw predict for the carpet industry's future?
Answers: By end of century, three or four huge companies will dominate carpet making worldwide, with competitors worrying Shaw will be the single dominant one.

Questions: What has made S&Ls the latest untouchables among equities?
Answers: The $500 billion S&L bailout, 675 bankrupt institutions since 1989, lavish spending by officers, 10,000 bank fraud cases pending with FBI.

Questions: How has the public perception of thrifts changed?
Answers: The word 'thrift' once reminded people of Jimmy Stewart in 'It's a Wonderful Life,' now it's Charles Keating in handcuffs.

Questions: How many S&Ls are stronger than J.P. Morgan based on equity-to-assets ratio?
Answers: More than 100 S&Ls are stronger than J.P. Morgan based on this fundamental measure of financial strength.

Questions: What is People's Savings Financial's equity-to-assets ratio compared to J.P. Morgan's?
Answers: People's Savings Financial: 12.5%, J.P. Morgan: 5.17%.

Questions: What are Lynch's three basic types of S&Ls?
Answers: The bad guys (perpetrated fraud), the greedy guys (ruined a good thing), and the Jimmy Stewarts (quietly profitable all along).

Questions: How did the 'bad guys' S&L scheme typically work?
Answers: 10 people put up $100,000 each ($1M equity), take in $19M deposits, make $20M loans, skim fees, use 'profits' to make more loans in self-feeding system.

Questions: What enabled fraudulent S&Ls to attract deposits?
Answers: Offered exceptionally high CD rates, hired brokers like Merrill Lynch, advertised government guarantees like 'In God We Trust offers 13% jumbo CD, guaranteed by FSLIC.'

Questions: How did fraudulent S&Ls create apparent profits?
Answers: Enormous up-front fees skimmed from loans were added to equity, and for every dollar equity increased, they could make another $20 in loans.

Questions: Why were most fraudulent S&Ls privately owned?
Answers: Owners and directors involved in dirty tricks couldn't tolerate the scrutiny required of publicly held companies.

Questions: How did 'greedy guys' S&Ls get into trouble?
Answers: Saw competitors getting rich on commercial loans, hired Wall Street experts, borrowed from Federal Home Loan Bank, invested in commercial real estate that went bad.

Questions: What are the characteristics of Jimmy Stewart S&Ls?
Answers: No-frills, low-cost operators taking neighborhood deposits, content making old-fashioned residential mortgage loans.

Questions: Why can Jimmy Stewart S&Ls survive on narrower spreads?
Answers: Money-center banks need 2.5-3% spread to break even due to overhead; Jimmy Stewart S&Ls can survive on 1.5% spread.

Questions: What is the inspiration for all Jimmy Stewart S&Ls?
Answers: Golden West, based in Oakland, run by Herb and Marion Sandler with 'equanimity of Ozzie and Harriet and smarts of Warren Buffett.'

Questions: What has Golden West avoided that kept it successful?
Answers: Avoided junk bonds, commercial real estate, ATMs, toaster oven promotions, misguided construction loans - stuck to residential mortgages (96% of portfolio).

Questions: How do the Sandlers economize in operations?
Answers: Corporate headquarters in lower-rent Oakland district, visitors announce themselves with black phone, no executive dining room, limos, or corporate jet.

Questions: What was the audience reaction to Marion Sandler's expense control speech?
Answers: At S&L conference, a third of attendees walked out during her talk on 'productivity and expense control' - they wanted to hear about exciting technology instead.

Questions: How many S&Ls went public after 1982 and what happened to them?
Answers: 464 S&Ls went public after 1982: 99 were acquired (usually at large profit), 65 failed (total loss), 300 still in business.

Questions: What was the Morris County Savings Bank example?
Answers: Initial offering 1983 at $10.75/share, bought out three years later for $65 - excellent return for shareholders.

Questions: How did Lynch approach S&L investing during this period?
Answers: He was so indiscriminate that he bought anything with 'first' or 'trust' in the name, investing in 135 of 145 thrifts whose prospectuses reached his desk.

Questions: What were Lynch's two explanations for his S&L attraction?
Answers: 1) Fund was so big and S&Ls so small he needed large quantities like whales surviving on plankton, 2) Unique way S&Ls came public made them automatic bargains.

Questions: What created the perfect atmosphere for S&L bargains in 1992?
Answers: S&L fraud story off front pages, replaced by housing market collapse fears, yet National Association of Home Builders showed median home prices still rising.

Questions: Why had Wall Street lost interest in S&L coverage?
Answers: Fidelity's Select S&L Fund dwindled from $66M (Feb 1987) to $3M (Oct 1990), brokerage houses reduced or stopped coverage entirely.

Questions: How many analysts track different types of companies?
Answers: Nearly 50 analysts track Wal-Mart, 46 track Philip Morris, but only a few devote themselves to publicly traded S&Ls.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #18?
Answers: When even the analysts are bored, it's time to start buying.

Questions: What publication did Lynch use for S&L research?
Answers: The Thrift Digest, published by SNL Securities, thick as Boston phone directory, costs $700/year for monthly updates.

Questions: What are the key factors in Lynch's S&L scorecard?
Answers: Current price, initial offering price, equity-to-assets ratio, dividend, book value, P/E ratio, high-risk real estate assets, 90-day nonperforming assets, real estate owned.

Questions: What is the most important number for S&L analysis?
Answers: Equity-to-Assets ratio - measures financial strength and survivability. Higher is better, with 5.5-6% average, below 5% danger zone.

Questions: What E/A ratio does Lynch prefer before investing?
Answers: At least 7.5% E/A ratio for disaster protection and because high E/A makes attractive takeover candidate.

Questions: Why are high-risk real estate assets problematic?
Answers: Commercial and construction loans have been ruination of many S&Ls. When high-risk assets exceed 5-10%, Lynch gets nervous.

Questions: What are 90-day nonperforming assets?
Answers: Loans that have already defaulted. Want very low number, preferably less than 2% of S&L's total assets, and falling not rising.

Questions: What is Real Estate Owned (REO)?
Answers: Property on which S&L has foreclosed - index of yesterday's problems since it's been written off, but worrisome when rising.

Questions: How many S&Ls did Lynch end up recommending in Barron's?
Answers: Seven S&Ls: five strong Jimmy Stewart types and two long shots (born-agains) coming back from Chapter 11 edge.

Questions: What made the five Jimmy Stewart S&Ls attractive?
Answers: Excellent marks in book value (four at discount), E/A ratio (all 6.0+), high-risk loans (under 10%), delinquencies (2% or less), REO (under 1%), P/E (below 11).

Questions: Why did Lynch pick two 'born-again' S&Ls despite poor numbers?
Answers: They maintained high E/A ratios despite problems, giving leeway to work out troubles, and stock prices had fallen so low that survival meant big gains.

Questions: What is an example of Lynch's bottom-fishing approach?
Answers: Lawrence Savings fell from $13 to 75 cents - if it survived, bottom fishers would make substantial money.

Questions: How do commercial banks benefit from acquiring strong S&Ls?
Answers: Banks can take deposits only in home states but lend anywhere, so acquiring S&L with excess equity and deposits provides valuable lending capacity.

Questions: How many banks and deposit takers does the U.S. have compared to need?
Answers: More than 7,000 banks, thrifts, and deposit takers - about 6,500 too many (Lynch's town of Marblehead has 6, half the number in all of England).

Questions: What will drive continued S&L consolidation?
Answers: Banks and thrifts will consolidate rapidly because there are far too many institutions, and strong ones with excess capacity make attractive acquisition targets.

Questions: What could casual S&L stockpickers do without detailed research?
Answers: Pick five S&Ls fitting the Jimmy Stewart profile, invest equally in each, and await favorable returns - one better than expected, three OK, one worse.

Questions: Why does Lynch usually call companies before investing?
Answers: To improve odds by finding specific information or fishing for surprises that haven't come to Wall Street analysts' attention.

Questions: What basic knowledge do you need to talk to an S&L?
Answers: How the business works: needs loyal depositors, must make money on that money by lending (but not to defaulters), needs low operating expenses.

Questions: What is the bankers' favorite saying about their business model?
Answers: Bankers like to live on threes and sixes: borrow money at 3, lend money at 6, play golf at 3.

Questions: How many S&Ls did Lynch call for his detailed research?
Answers: Six S&Ls: four strong ones plus two born-agains (he didn't call Eagle Financial because annual report arrived in time).

Questions: When did Lynch call Glacier Bancorp and what was he wearing?
Answers: Day after Christmas, wearing plaid pants and sweatshirt in the empty Fidelity building except for security guard.

Questions: Why are holidays excellent times for research calls?
Answers: Lynch is always impressed when he finds executives sitting at their desks on December 26, showing dedication.

Questions: What was Glacier Bancorp formerly called?
Answers: First Federal Savings and Loan of Kalispell - Lynch wishes they'd kept the antiquated, parochial name.

Questions: Why does Lynch prefer antiquated names over trendy ones?
Answers: He'd rather have antiquated and parochial than trendy and sophisticated, which usually means desperate to improve image.

Questions: What is Lynch's concern about 'bancorp' vs 'bank' names?
Answers: He knows what a bank is, but 'bancorp' makes him nervous - prefers companies that stick to business and let images take care of themselves.

Questions: How does Lynch establish rapport before asking serious questions?
Answers: Started with mountains, mentioned family trips to Western states and national parks, discussed timber industry, spotted owl, ski areas.

Questions: What was Glacier's impressive loan loss record?
Answers: In all of 1991, had to write off only $16,000 in bad loans - almost nonexistent nonperforming loans.

Questions: How has Glacier been growing through acquisitions?
Answers: Just bought First National Banks of Whitefish and Eureka, acquiring valuable deposits to make more loans with additional capacity.

Questions: What was Lynch's concern about Glacier's 9.2% commercial loans?
Answers: In New England that would be scary, but Montana wasn't Massachusetts - mostly multifamily housing in growing area with California escapees.

Questions: Who did Glacier's chairman recommend as other strong S&Ls?
Answers: United Savings and Security Federal, both Montana thrifts with impressive equity-to-assets ratios (20% at Security Federal).

Questions: What was Germantown Savings' key financial metrics?
Answers: $10 stock earning $2/share (P/E under 7), book value $26, equity-to-assets ratio 7.5%, less than 1% nonperforming loans.

Questions: Why was Germantown notable from a Wall Street perspective?
Answers: $1.4 billion in assets with wonderful record, yet not a single brokerage firm bothered to cover the story.

Questions: What did Lynch find in Germantown's balance sheet analysis?
Answers: Deposits up (customers keeping money there), loans down (bankers being conservative), investment securities up $50M (parking assets in bonds).

Questions: What did Germantown's CEO Martin Kleppe say about their story?
Answers: 'We have a very boring story. We also have a fortress balance sheet. When we get in trouble, other guys are walking the plank.'

Questions: How was Germantown positioned for economic improvement?
Answers: When economy improves and it's safe to lend, they'll sell investment securities and make more loans, causing surge in earnings.

Questions: What was Sovereign Bancorp's dividend strategy?
Answers: Pays 8% dividend beginning immediately, and the bell goes off in branches every time a mortgage loan is approved.

Questions: How did Lynch learn about Sovereign Bancorp?
Answers: Through November 25, 1991 Barron's article entitled 'Hometown Lender to the Well-Heeled' about serving wealthy southeastern Pennsylvania.

Questions: What was Sovereign's growth strategy according to CEO Jay Sidhu?
Answers: Determined to 'grow' business by at least 12% annually, using Golden West as model for success.

Questions: Why had Sovereign sold additional shares in 1991?
Answers: Used proceeds to buy troubled thrifts from Resolution Trust rather than squandering money, though this diluted existing shares.

Questions: What was Sovereign's loan strategy vs traditional S&Ls?
Answers: Specialized in making loans then selling them to Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac for quick money recovery and up-front fees, transferring ownership risk.

Questions: What lending standards did Sovereign maintain?
Answers: Devoted to residential mortgages, no commercial loans since 1989, average loan didn't exceed 69% of property value.

Questions: What sneaky practice did Sidhu describe for camouflaging problem loans?
Answers: Banks offer borrowers more than requested based on inflated appraisals, hold excess in reserve to cover payments if borrower defaults, keeping bad loans appearing good temporarily.

Questions: What was People's Savings Financial's competitive advantage?
Answers: Advertised security with 13% equity-to-assets ratio as weak banks failed, growing deposits from $220M (1990) to $242M (1991).

Questions: How had People's Savings enhanced shareholder value?
Answers: Bought back 16% of shares in two phases, spending $4.4M - making remaining shares scarce and valuable.

Questions: Why does Lynch prefer share buybacks over acquisitions for enhancing value?
Answers: Share buybacks are simplest, most direct way to reward shareholders, while companies often squander money on fanciful acquisitions instead.

Questions: What examples does Lynch give of successful buyback strategies?
Answers: International Dairy Queen and Crown Cork & Seal became spectacular performers because management committed to buying back shares - that's how Teledyne became 100-bagger.

Questions: When did People's Savings first go public and at what price?
Answers: 1986 at $10.25 per share, five years later selling for $11 despite being bigger, more profitable with fewer shares outstanding.

Questions: What depressed People's Savings stock price?
Answers: Operating in Connecticut, a depressed state - Lynch prefers S&Ls proven to survive in depressed states over those thriving in booming economies.

Questions: What was the source of People's Savings' nonperforming loans?
Answers: Most of 2% problem caused by single construction loan; company wasn't making new loans of this type.

Questions: How long does the foreclosure process take according to Medvec?
Answers: May take two years to oust defaulting borrower - drawn-out and expensive process.

Questions: What was First Essex's frightening financial situation?
Answers: 10% nonperforming assets, 3.5% real estate owned, 13% commercial/construction loans, lost $11M (1989) and $28M (1990).

Questions: How did First Essex CEO Leonard Wilson describe their situation?
Answers: 'Bottom fishing with a six-hundred-foot line' - facing procession of foreclosures, owning unoccupied buildings nobody wanted.

Questions: What was First Essex's equity cushion for survival?
Answers: $46M equity vs $46M commercial loans - if 50% of remaining commercial loans went bad, would lose 50% equity but still survive.

Questions: What was Lawrence Savings' riskier position compared to First Essex?
Answers: $55M commercial loans vs only $27M equity, and 21% of portfolio in commercial real estate vs First Essex's 13%.

Questions: How does Lynch analyze long-shot S&Ls?
Answers: Find equity amount, compare to commercial loans outstanding, assume the worst - if half go bad, does S&L survive?

Questions: What is the 'can't-lose proposition' Lynch describes about S&L IPOs?
Answers: Like buying a house and finding former owners left your down payment money in kitchen drawer with note 'Keep this, it belonged to you anyway.'

Questions: How do S&L public offerings differ from other IPOs?
Answers: Every dollar raised (minus fees) returns to S&L's vault as equity, unlike other companies where founders take money and buy palazzos.

Questions: What happens to book value when mutual S&L goes public?
Answers: If S&L had $10M book value, sells $10M stock (1M shares at $10), the $10M returns to vault, doubling book value to $20 while stock sells for $10.

Questions: How many mutual S&Ls have yet to go public?
Answers: 1,178 S&Ls have yet to take this step, providing many more chances for investors to be surprised.

Questions: What were the 1991 mutual thrift IPO results?
Answers: 16 came public: 2 taken over at 4x+ offering price, worst performer up 87%, all others doubled or better, including one 10-bagger.

Questions: What were the 1992 mutual thrift conversion results?
Answers: 42 came public: only 1 loser (down 7.5%), all others advanced, 38 up 50%+, 23 up 100%+ in just 20 months.

Questions: What examples does Lynch give of outstanding 1992 mutual thrift performance?
Answers: Mutual Savings Bank of Bay City, Michigan and United Postal Bancorp in St. Louis both quadrupled in value.

Questions: How did even the worst 1992 mutual thrift performers do?
Answers: Portfolio of five worst performers produced 31% return, beating S&P 500 and most equity mutual funds.

Questions: What were early 1993 mutual thrift results through nine months?
Answers: 34 came public: worst up 5%, 26 up 30%+, 20 up 40%+, 9 up 50%+ in shorter period.

Questions: What is Lynch's advice about participating in local S&L conversions?
Answers: Open savings account in any mutual savings bank in your area to get right to participate in IPO when it happens.

Questions: How many mutual savings banks haven't yet converted?
Answers: 1,372 mutual savings banks have not yet come public - check if any are in your area.

Questions: What can investors do while waiting for conversions?
Answers: Sit back and await developments after opening accounts, getting all information needed to make informed decisions when IPO happens.

Questions: What makes these local S&L investments particularly attractive?
Answers: Ultimate example of how individuals can succeed by investigating what's close to home rather than widely-held institutional stocks.

Questions: Why are Master Limited Partnerships being ignored by Wall Street?
Answers: The name 'limited partnership' brings back memories of tax-shelter boondoggles where losses far exceeded tax savings.

Questions: What types of partnerships caused the bad publicity?
Answers: Oil and gas partnerships, real-estate partnerships, movie partnerships, farming partnerships, and gravesite partnerships where investors lost money.

Questions: How do Master Limited Partnerships differ from tax shelter partnerships?
Answers: MLPs are ongoing enterprises whose purpose is to make money, not lose it to outsmart the IRS.

Questions: How many MLPs trade on stock exchanges?
Answers: More than 100 MLPs trade on various stock exchanges.

Questions: What extra requirement do MLP shareholders face?
Answers: Special tax forms have to be prepared, though the investor relations department fills in all the blanks.

Questions: Why does Lynch welcome the MLP paperwork requirement?
Answers: The nuisance dissuades many investors, particularly fund managers, keeping prices down and creating bargains.

Questions: What types of activities are MLPs typically involved in?
Answers: Down-to-earth activities like playing basketball (Boston Celtics), pumping oil and gas, janitorial services (ServiceMaster), auto parts (Sun Distributors), amusement parks (Cedar Fair).

Questions: What is appealing about MLP names according to Lynch?
Answers: Names seem antiquated and out of sync with high-tech culture - Cedar Fair could be from Thackeray, Green Acres from Jane Austen.

Questions: What type of investor is attracted to MLPs?
Answers: Takes an imaginative person attracted to romantic names, mundane activities, and complicated structure requiring extra paperwork - a small minority reaps rewards.

Questions: What is the biggest difference between MLPs and regular corporations?
Answers: MLPs distribute ALL earnings to shareholders, either as dividends or return of capital, with unusually high dividends.

Questions: What tax advantage do MLPs offer?
Answers: Return of capital feature allows certain percentage of annual distribution to be exempt from federal tax.

Questions: When did most MLPs come onto the scene?
Answers: First appeared in 1981, majority appeared in 1986 after tax law changes made this organization form more advantageous.

Questions: What happens to MLPs in 1997-98?
Answers: All except real estate and natural resource partnerships must be closed out as they lose tax benefits - earnings might drop from $1.80 to $1.20.

Questions: What brought EQK Green Acres to Lynch's attention?
Answers: The stock dropped during Saddam Sell-off from $13.75 high to $9.75, offering 13.5% yield - as good as junk bonds but more secure.

Questions: What does EQK stand for and who are the partners?
Answers: EQ comes from Equitable Life Assurance Society, K stands for Kravco - partners in this enterprise.

Questions: What is EQK Green Acres' principal asset?
Answers: Its huge enclosed mall on Long Island, situated in densely populated Nassau County.

Questions: How many people live within five miles of Green Acres mall?
Answers: 750,000 insiders on Long Island - showing how many people could have discovered this investment opportunity.

Questions: Why are enclosed malls attractive investments?
Answers: Only 450 exist in entire country, not many new ones being built, would face zoning problems and need 92 empty acres for parking.

Questions: What was Lynch's key concern about any mall investment?
Answers: Vacancies - malls averaged 4% vacancy rate while Green Acres was lower.

Questions: What positive developments were occurring at Green Acres?
Answers: Waldbaum's supermarket and Pergament Home Center moving in, one-third of stores subject to large rent increases in 1992-93.

Questions: What were the worrisome elements about Green Acres?
Answers: Highly leveraged balance sheet (company must pay back all debts in 1997), high P/E ratio, vulnerability to recession.

Questions: What warning sign did Lynch see in Green Acres' third-quarter 1991 report?
Answers: Company was debating whether to pay regular quarterly dividend increase of one cent to save $100,000 - breaking 13-quarter string for paltry savings.

Questions: What potential good news was Green Acres negotiating?
Answers: Potential agreements with Sears and J.C. Penney to lease space in second floor expansion - though not yet signed contracts.

Questions: Why didn't Lynch recommend Green Acres for a second time?
Answers: Potential agreements weren't signed contracts - he preferred waiting for proof rather than buying on rumors.

Questions: What owns and operates Cedar Fair's amusement parks?
Answers: Cedar Point on Ohio shore of Lake Erie and Valley Fair in Minnesota, open May to Labor Day plus fall weekends.

Questions: How many roller coasters does Cedar Point have?
Answers: 10 different roller coasters, including Magnum (highest drop in world) and Mean Streak (highest wooden roller coaster in world).

Questions: What historical significance does Cedar Point have?
Answers: 120th year of operation, had roller coasters for 100 years, seven U.S. presidents visited, Knute Rockne had summer jobs and invented forward pass there.

Questions: Why are amusement parks protected from competition?
Answers: Nobody will sneak up and install $500 million worth of rides on Lake Erie shores - unlike electronics where new products can destroy competitors overnight.

Questions: How many people live within three hours of Cedar Point?
Answers: About 6 million people, providing a substantial customer base for the amusement park.

Questions: What was Cedar Fair's stock performance in 1991?
Answers: Rose from $11.50 to $18, which with dividend gave shareholders over 60% one-year return.

Questions: Why might amusement parks benefit from recession?
Answers: People might forgo summer trip to France in favor of staying at Cedar Point Hotel and riding world's highest roller coaster.

Questions: What did Lynch ask about Cedar Fair's 1992 prospects?
Answers: He looks for reasons next year will be better than last - if he can't find such reason, he questions why own the stock.

Questions: What was missing from Cedar Fair's 1992 outlook?
Answers: No major new attractions like previous years' new roller coasters - attendance usually drops year after new ride introduced.

Questions: What does Sun Distributors sell?
Answers: Auto glass, sheet glass, insulated glass, cables, mirrors, windshield glass, fasteners, ball bearings, hydraulic systems to builders and auto repair shops.

Questions: Why was Sun Distributors being ignored by Wall Street?
Answers: Activities put business school graduates to sleep, financial analysts would rather count ceiling tiles than follow auto parts company.

Questions: Who was the lone analyst covering Sun Distributors?
Answers: Karen Payne of Wheat First Securities, but her April 1990 report was apparently her last.

Questions: What complicated Sun Distributors' structure?
Answers: Two classes of shares: Class A (big dividend), Class B (no dividend), both NYSE-traded, plus MLP paperwork requirements.

Questions: How did Karen Payne describe Sun Distributors?
Answers: 'A simple, well-run business hiding in a complicated financial structure.'

Questions: What was the difference between Sun's Class A and Class B shares?
Answers: Class A offered little upside (company will buy back for $10), all action was in Class B shares that fell 50% from $4 to $2.

Questions: Who owned 52% of Sun's Class B shares?
Answers: Shearson Lehman owned 52%, and management had option to buy up to half at fixed price, giving powerful incentive for success.

Questions: What evidence did Lynch see of management dedication?
Answers: President was in office taking phone calls on December 23, two days before Christmas.

Questions: How did Sun Distributors survive the recession?
Answers: Made money every year since 1986 independence, even in 1991 when glass and electrical parts businesses were terrible.

Questions: What was Sun Distributors' competitive advantage?
Answers: Low-cost operator surviving while competitors faltered - bad times worked to its benefit as rivals disappeared.

Questions: How did Lynch determine Sun was a low-cost operator?
Answers: Gross margin of 60% (dividing cost of sales by net sales) - making $40 profit on every $100 of sales, tops among distributors.

Questions: What was Sun's capital spending requirement?
Answers: Only $3-4 million annually compared to revenues - unlike steel companies that might make $1B but spend $950M.

Questions: What was Sun's growth strategy?
Answers: Buying related enterprises (36 since 1986) and folding them into operation, reducing overhead and making them more profitable.

Questions: How much goodwill did Sun have to write off?
Answers: $57 million in goodwill reduced reported earnings to $1.25/share when actual earnings were nearly twice that amount.

Questions: What are the phantom earnings called that companies have but can't claim?
Answers: Free cash flow - healthy free cash flow gives flexibility to change course in good and bad times.

Questions: How did Sun's debt situation affect Lynch's analysis?
Answers: High debt (60% of capitalization) was concerning, but cash flow sufficient to cover interest four times over.

Questions: What was Sun's recession strategy vs expansion strategy?
Answers: Expansion: used cash flow to buy $41M of businesses. Recession: curtailed acquisitions, devoted cash flow to reducing debt.

Questions: How quickly could Sun retire its debt?
Answers: The $110 million borrowed at 9.5% could be retired within two years using all excess cash flow.

Questions: What was Tenera Limited Partners' main problems?
Answers: Squabbling with federal government (major revenue source), expensive software program not paying off, forced to cut workforce drastically.

Questions: Why had Tenera's stock collapsed from $9 to $1.25?
Answers: Feds accused company of overcharging, canceled contracts, key executives including president resigned, competitors bad-mouthing to customers.

Questions: What was canceled in June 1991 at Tenera?
Answers: Dividend was canceled, company said it would 'take a long time' to restore to former 20 cents quarterly level.

Questions: Why didn't Lynch dismiss Tenera completely?
Answers: Zero debt and no large expenses meant it wasn't going out of business immediately, had well-regarded nuclear services division.

Questions: What were Tenera's positives for Lynch's analysis?
Answers: Zero debt, no capital spending needed (consultants need desk, calculator, phone), earning power of 77-81 cents/share in prior four years.

Questions: How did Lynch value Tenera as potential liquidation?
Answers: Figured auction value worth more than $1.50/share with no debts, entire amount minus legal fees would go to shareholders.

Questions: Who was brought in to oversee Tenera's recovery?
Answers: Bob Dahl, whom Lynch had met in telecommunications industry, suggested turnaround possible within 6-12 months.

Questions: What convinced Lynch that Tenera had remaining value?
Answers: Insiders were holding onto shares and new management believed turnaround was possible within reasonable timeframe.

Questions: When do professional money managers begin thinking about cyclicals?
Answers: When the economy is in the doldrums, they think about investing in aluminums, steels, paper producers, auto manufacturers, chemicals, and airlines.

Questions: What makes investing in cyclicals increasingly tricky?
Answers: Wall Street is anticipating cyclical industry revivals earlier and earlier before the fact, making timing more difficult.

Questions: How do low P/E ratios affect cyclical stock investing?
Answers: With cyclicals, low P/E ratios are usually a bad sign - they indicate companies are at the end of a prosperous interlude.

Questions: Why might a low P/E ratio be dangerous for cyclicals?
Answers: Business is still good with high earnings, but smart investors are selling. When economy falters, earnings decline at breathtaking speed.

Questions: What is the misconception about buying cyclicals with low P/E ratios?
Answers: Buying after several years of record earnings when P/E hits low point is a proven method for losing half your money quickly.

Questions: How should investors interpret high P/E ratios for cyclicals?
Answers: Often good news - may mean company is passing through worst doldrums and business will improve, earnings will exceed expectations.

Questions: What makes the cyclical game doubly hard?
Answers: It's a game of anticipation - principal danger is buying too early, getting discouraged, and selling before the turnaround.

Questions: What knowledge is essential for successful cyclical investing?
Answers: You must have working knowledge of the specific industry (copper, aluminum, steel, autos, paper) and its rhythms.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #19?
Answers: Unless you're a short seller or a poet looking for a wealthy spouse, it never pays to be pessimistic.

Questions: What led Lynch to Phelps Dodge in 1992?
Answers: He was foiled in housing rebound plays by other buyers, but they hadn't anticipated copper market rebound - his plumber confirmed copper pipe prices rising.

Questions: Why had Phelps Dodge gone nowhere in 1991?
Answers: Stock's going nowhere isn't necessarily reason to abandon it - may be reason to buy more if story improves.

Questions: What makes copper more valuable than aluminum according to Lynch?
Answers: Aluminum is 8% of earth's crust and easy to extract; copper is scarcer and vanishing asset - mines run out or flood and close.

Questions: How have environmental regulations affected the copper industry?
Answers: Forced closing of many U.S. smelters, many companies gave up smelting for good, creating smelter shortage.

Questions: What global trend supports copper demand?
Answers: All developing nations including former Soviet republics want improved phone systems, traditional systems require miles of copper wire.

Questions: Why are developing countries more important for copper than mature ones?
Answers: Developing countries are much more copper intensive than mature countries, and there are more of the former.

Questions: What was Phelps Dodge's stock pattern from 1990-1991?
Answers: 1990: earned $6.50, stock ranged $23-36 (low P/E 3.5-5.5). 1991: earnings dropped to $3.90, stock retreated from $39 to $26.

Questions: What is the most important question about any cyclical?
Answers: Whether the company's balance sheet is strong enough to survive the next downturn.

Questions: What were Phelps Dodge's balance sheet strengths?
Answers: Equity of $1.68 billion, total debt (minus cash) only $318 million - clearly no bankruptcy candidate even if copper prices fell.

Questions: How did Lynch evaluate Phelps Dodge's subsidiary businesses?
Answers: Carbon black OK, magnet wire OK, truck wheels OK, Canyon Resources gold mine could become big moneymaker.

Questions: What could Phelps Dodge's non-copper businesses be worth?
Answers: Subsidiaries earning less than $1/share in bad year, could earn $2 in decent year, worth $10-16/share at modest P/E of 5-8.

Questions: How much could the gold operations add to Phelps Dodge's value?
Answers: Gold operations could be worth $5/share to Phelps Dodge.

Questions: What technique does Lynch use for valuing diversified companies?
Answers: Thumbnail appraisal of various divisions - take earnings of each division, multiply by generic P/E ratio to get rough value.

Questions: How was Phelps Dodge's capital spending situation?
Answers: 1990: spent $290 million upgrading plants, less than half its cash flow - even in bad 1991, cash flow exceeded capital spending.

Questions: What is the basic math of copper prices and Phelps Dodge earnings?
Answers: Company produces 1.1 billion pounds copper annually, so penny increase in price creates $11 million pretax earnings, or 10 cents/share after taxes.

Questions: How much could copper price increases affect Phelps Dodge earnings?
Answers: If copper goes up 50 cents/pound, earnings improve by $5/share - dramatic leverage to commodity prices.

Questions: Why does Lynch classify autos as cyclicals rather than blue chips?
Answers: Buying auto stock for 25 years is like flying over Alps - you may get something, but not as much as the hiker experiencing ups and downs.

Questions: What convinced Lynch to look at autos again in 1991?
Answers: Auto stocks down 50% from recent highs, widespread showroom gloom, but certain that Americans will continue replacing cars.

Questions: What is Lynch's certainty about American car buying habits?
Answers: Until someone invents reliable Hovercraft for home use, cars will continue being America's most beloved personal possession.

Questions: What forces eventual car replacement according to Lynch?
Answers: Cars eventually need replacement due to being tired of old ones, brakes shot, road visible through rusted floorboards, plus mandatory inspections.

Questions: What was the car sales decline that led to Lynch's 1980s auto investment?
Answers: Annual sales declined from 15.4 million vehicles (1977) to 10.5 million (1982), but couldn't go to zero.

Questions: How have 60-month auto loans affected the replacement cycle?
Answers: Old 36-month loans meant cars were paid off when owners wanted to trade; 60-month loans mean many cars worth less than outstanding balance.

Questions: What is the key indicator Lynch uses for auto stock timing?
Answers: Used-car prices - when dealers lower prices, new car market is worse; when used prices rise, good times ahead for automakers.

Questions: What is the 'units of pent-up demand' indicator?
Answers: Chart showing actual car sales vs. trend - difference between what should have been sold vs. actual sales shows built-up demand.

Questions: What pent-up demand existed from 1980-1983?
Answers: Actual sales lagged trend by 7 million vehicles - 7 million people delayed purchases, predicting coming boom.

Questions: How long did the 1984-1989 auto boom last?
Answers: Auto sales exceeded trend by combined 7.8 million units over those years, working off the pent-up demand.

Questions: When was the right time to sell auto stocks according to the indicator?
Answers: 1988, when pent-up demand from early 1980s was exhausted after public bought 74 million vehicles in five years.

Questions: What pent-up demand has been building since 1990?
Answers: Two years under trend, building toward 5.6 million units of pent-up demand by end of 1993, suggesting 1994-96 boom.

Questions: Why did Lynch favor Chrysler, Ford, and Volvo over General Motors?
Answers: GM's reputation for excellence far exceeded desire to live up to it - company was arrogant, myopic, resting on laurels.

Questions: What was Lynch's experience with GM's investor relations?
Answers: Assigned to investor relations guy who couldn't find R&D center (size of big college campus) - took couple hours to locate it.

Questions: How did Lynch view GM in 1991 compared to earlier opinions?
Answers: Previous popular view: powerful company with profitable future. 1991 popular view: weak company with miserable future - Lynch suspected latest view equally misguided.

Questions: What parallel does Lynch draw between GM 1992 and Chrysler 1982?
Answers: Same story: powerful enterprise forgets how to make cars, loses public confidence, lays off thousands, heads for has-been scrap heap.

Questions: What gives Lynch confidence in GM's potential recovery?
Answers: Better balance sheet in 1992 than Chrysler had in 1982, plus profitable non-auto divisions.

Questions: What are GM's most profitable non-auto businesses?
Answers: European operations, financing arm (GMAC), Hughes Aircraft, Delco, Electronic Data Systems (thanks to Ross Perot).

Questions: What could GM earn if it just breaks even on U.S. auto business?
Answers: Could earn $6-8/share in 1993 with break-even autos; if auto business improves beyond break-even, could earn $10/share.

Questions: What is GM's market share situation?
Answers: Upset that share shrunk from 40% to 30%, but that's still bigger than all Japanese carmakers combined.

Questions: How could GM succeed even with declining market share?
Answers: Even with 25% of buyers, auto divisions can contribute to earnings by scaling down manufacturing and reducing expenses.

Questions: What positive developments had GM achieved by 1993?
Answers: Several cars won major awards including Cadillac, trucks looked good, mid-sized cars improved, company had plenty of cash.

Questions: What was the main attraction of utility stocks in the 1950s vs. since then?
Answers: Utility stocks were great growth stocks of the 1950s, but since then their main attraction has been yield.

Questions: What has been more profitable long-term than CDs for income investors?
Answers: Buying utility stocks has been more profitable than buying CDs - you get dividends that increase yearly plus chance at capital gain.

Questions: What examples does Lynch give of big utility winners in recent years?
Answers: Southern Company ($11 to $33 in 5 years), Oklahoma Gas and Electric ($13 to $40), Philadelphia Electric ($9 to $26).

Questions: When did Lynch have 10% of Magellan invested in utilities?
Answers: During brief periods when interest rates were declining and economy was sputtering - he treated utilities as interest-rate cyclicals.

Questions: Which utilities has Lynch done best with?
Answers: The troubled ones: General Public Utilities (Three Mile Island), Public Service of New Hampshire, Long Island Lighting, Gulf States, Middle South (now Entergy).

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #20?
Answers: Corporations, like people, change their names for one of two reasons: either they've gotten married, or they've been involved in some fiasco they hope the public will forget.

Questions: Why is Lynch's record better with troubled utilities than troubled companies generally?
Answers: Utilities are regulated by government - as long as people need electricity, a way must be found for utility to continue functioning.

Questions: What determines a utility's survival and profitability?
Answers: Regulatory system determines prices they can charge, profit allowed, and whether costs of mistakes can be passed to customers.

Questions: Who identified the 'troubled utility cycle' that Lynch references?
Answers: Three analysts at NatWest Investment Banking Group: Kathleen Lally, John Kellenyi, and Philip Smyth.

Questions: What are the four examples of companies that lived through the troubled utility cycle?
Answers: Consolidated Edison (1973 oil crisis), Entergy (lavish nuke plant), Long Island Lighting (unlicensed nuke), General Public Utilities (Three Mile Island).

Questions: What were the stock price drops during the disaster phase?
At what percentage of book value do distressed utilities trade?
Answers: 20-30% of book value during the disaster phase, as Wall Street worries damage may be fatal.

Questions: What is Stage 2 of the troubled utility cycle?
Answers: 'Crisis management' - utility responds by cutting capital spending, adopting austerity budget, dividend reduced or eliminated.

Questions: What is Stage 3 of the troubled utility cycle?
Answers: 'Financial stabilization' - management succeeds in cutting costs so utility operates on cash from bill-paying customers, survival no longer in doubt.

Questions: What characterizes Stage 4 of the utility cycle?
Answers: 'Recovery at last!' - utility capable of earning for shareholders again, Wall Street expects improved earnings and dividend reinstatement.

Questions: What determines how utilities progress after Stage 4?
Answers: 1) Reception from capital markets (need capital to expand rate base), 2) Support from regulators (how many costs passed to customers).

Questions: What is Lynch's strategy for investing in troubled utilities?
Answers: Buy on omission of dividend and wait for good news, or buy when first good news arrives in second stage.

Questions: Why shouldn't investors worry about missing the bottom in troubled utilities?
Answers: If stock falls to $4 then rises to $8, don't think you missed it - troubled nukes have long way to go, need psychological Wite-Out.

Questions: What simple strategy does Lynch suggest for troubled utilities?
Answers: Buy when dividend is omitted, hold until dividend is restored - strategy with terrific success ratio.

Questions: Which five distressed utilities did NatWest identify in summer 1991?
Answers: Gulf States, Illinois Power, Niagara Mohawk, Pinnacle West, Public Service Company of New Mexico - all in various recovery stages, selling below book values.

Questions: What was CMS Energy formerly called and why did it change?
Answers: Used to be Consumers Power of Michigan, changed name after building Midland nuclear plant - hoped shareholders would forget.

Questions: What was CMS's stock performance during the nuclear disaster?
Answers: Sailing in $20s, sank to $4.50 in less than a year, hitting bottom after dividend omitted in October 1984.

Questions: What was the regulatory pattern with nuclear plants?
Answers: Like Lucy with football - state commissions supported nuke plants throughout development until owners fully committed, then snatched projects away at last minute.

Questions: What write-off did Consumers Power have to take?
Answers: $4 billion write-off to cover costs of building nuke plant it wasn't allowed to use.

Questions: How did CMS make the best of the nuclear disaster?
Answers: Converted unusable nuclear plant to natural gas with help of Dow Chemical (biggest customer) at cost of $1,600 per kilowatt, under budget.

Questions: What was CMS's stock recovery and subsequent decline?
Answers: Came back to $36/share (ninefold gain in 5 years), then unfavorable rate decisions drove price down to $17.

Questions: Who brought CMS to Lynch's attention?
Answers: Danny Frank, manager of Fidelity's Special Situations Fund, who had investigated several troubled nukes.

Questions: What was positive about the converted Midland plant's economics?
Answers: Producing electricity at 6 cents per kilowatt vs. 9.2 cents for new coal plant and 13.3 cents for nuke - low-cost operation.

Questions: What demand trend favored CMS in Michigan?
Answers: Electricity demand grew 12 years in a row, even 1% more in recession year 1991, with only 19.6% reserve capacity on peak days.

Questions: Why was the thin reserve capacity significant?
Answers: Very thin margin in utility circles, few new Midwest plants coming online, takes 6-12 years to build from scratch.

Questions: What does Economics 101 predict when demand grows faster than supply?
Answers: Higher prices result, and higher prices produce more profits.

Questions: What was CMS's debt situation from the nuclear conversion?
Answers: Sold $1 billion bonds to finance Midland conversion plus $500 million senior notes not callable for 10 years.

Questions: How did Lynch verify CMS could handle its debt load?
Answers: Calculated cash flow of $6/share (earnings plus depreciation divided by shares), sufficient to pay interest with money left over.

Questions: What could CMS do with its excess cash according to Lynch?
Answers: Buy back stock, make acquisitions, or increase dividend - all benefiting shareholders.

Questions: What were CMS's expansion plans for the cash?
Answers: Expand gas plant and improve transmission line efficiency, both adding to generating capacity and automatically adding to earnings.

Questions: What was the Ecuador oil discovery potential for CMS?
Answers: Joint venture with Conoco scheduled to produce $25 million annual profits by 1995, adding 20 cents/share to earnings.

Questions: What was the Power Group subsidiary situation?
Answers: CMS subsidiary owning small cogeneration plants, losing money lately but could turn profit by 1993.

Questions: What disappointed CMS regarding Long Island Lighting?
Answers: Collaboration to convert LILCO's Shoreham nuke plant to natural gas fell apart in 1991.

Questions: What was CMS's greatest ongoing disappointment?
Answers: Michigan commission was uncooperative, handing down three unfavorable rate decisions in a row.

Questions: What rate commission politics affected CMS?
Answers: Recent appointee expected to be more accommodating (only mildly hostile vs. traditionally hostile), commission staff study favored concessions.

Questions: What earnings could CMS achieve with reasonable regulatory decision?
Answers: $2/share in upcoming year vs. $1.30 Wall Street expected, with steady growth thereafter.

Questions: Why did Lynch view CMS as more than just regulatory gamble?
Answers: Powerful cash flow would enable reentry to strong utility ranks regardless of commission decisions.

Questions: What were CMS's potential earnings scenarios?
Answers: Best case: $2.20/share if all resolved favorably. Worst case: $1.50/share, but either way would prosper long-run.

Questions: How could CMS grow if regulators restricted earnings?
Answers: Could plow cash back into more generating capacity and grow business internally.

Questions: At what price was CMS selling and why was it attractive?
Answers: $18/share, below book value, with lot of potential reward without much risk.

Questions: What alternatives does Lynch mention for distressed utility investing?
Answers: Public Service Company of New Mexico or 'more hapless' Tucson Electric, both with available investor relations staff.

Questions: What is Lynch's attitude toward government garage sales?
Answers: When Uncle Sam or the Queen of England is having a garage sale, Lynch always tries to attend.

Questions: Which country is ahead in privatization efforts?
Answers: Britain is way ahead, having sold everything from waterworks to airlines.

Questions: What might the U.S. have to privatize if deficit spending continues?
Answers: National parks, Kennedy Space Center, even White House Rose Garden just to pay interest on national debt.

Questions: What is the strange concept of privatization?
Answers: You take something owned by the public, sell it back to the public, and from then on it's private.

Questions: Why have privatizations usually been good deals for buyers?
Answers: In democratic countries, buyers are also voters, and governments can't afford disgruntled investors who lost money on telephone companies or gasworks.

Questions: What lesson did the British learn from early privatization mistakes?
Answers: Britoil and Amersham International came out overpriced in 1983, creating ill will, so since then British structured offers so investors unlikely to lose.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #21?
Answers: Whatever the queen is selling, buy it.

Questions: How did British Telecom perform after privatization?
Answers: Doubled in price in one day, with three million Brits snapping up shares.

Questions: What British privatization did Lynch encounter at Fidelity?
Answers: British contingent with numbered prospectus for water utilities: Northumbrian Water, Severn Trent, Yorkshire Water, Welsh Water PLC.

Questions: What advantages did British water utilities have?
Answers: Monopolies, government absorbed most prior debt, came out debt-free with extra capital (green dowry), 10-year upgrade program partially subsidized.

Questions: How low were English water bills according to the water lords?
Answers: 100 pounds per year, so low that even doubling wouldn't cause resentment, and customers couldn't stop using water anyway.
