Questions: What was the installment plan feature of British water shares?
Answers: Could buy on installment: 40% down, rest in two easy payments (12 months and 20 months), same deal offered on British Telecom.

Questions: How did the partial-paid shares feature work?
Answers: British Telecom came public at $30, buyer paid only $6 down, when price rose to $36, buyer could sell and double money on $6 investment.

Questions: What dividend advantage did water companies offer?
Answers: Paid 8% dividend immediately on full value of shares acquired at 40% down, giving 20% return on investment in first 12 months.

Questions: How did British water utilities perform after privatization?
Answers: Portfolio of all five water utilities doubled in value in three years.

Questions: What has been the pattern with privatized telephone companies worldwide?
Answers: Every telephone company privatized in any country (Philippines, Mexico, Spain) has given shareholders once-in-a-lifetime rewards.

Questions: Why are privatized telephone companies particularly attractive?
Answers: Growth rate of small growth company, size and stability of blue chip, guaranteed success of monopoly.

Questions: What was the opportunity with Mexican telephones?
Answers: Country knew it needed improved phone service before economy could expand, required well-capitalized company, had to allow decent shareholder profits.

Questions: How much had privatization sales reached worldwide by 1990?
Answers: $200 billion in sales of privatized companies worldwide, with more to come.

Questions: What countries and assets have been privatized globally?
Answers: France: electric utilities, trains; Scotland: hydroelectric plants; Spain/Argentina: oil companies; Mexico: airlines; potential: Britain's railways/ports, Japan's bullet trains.

Questions: What was the biggest recent U.S. privatization deal?
Answers: Conrail (Consolidated Rail Corporation), assembled from Penn Central and five other bankrupt Northeast lines.

Questions: How much had the government spent on Conrail before privatization?
Answers: More than $7 billion in government handouts, plus fortune gold-plating the railroad with upgraded rails and equipment.

Questions: What was Conrail's IPO performance?
Answers: March 1987: largest U.S. public offering at $1.6 billion, initial price $10/share, worth $46/share by time of Lynch's writing.

Questions: What did President Reagan joke about after Conrail deal?
Answers: 'OK, when do we sell the TVA?' referring to Tennessee Valley Authority.

Questions: What other U.S. privatization possibilities has Lynch considered?
Answers: Amtrak, naval petroleum reserves in California and Wyoming, National Gallery, Marine Band, Niagara Falls.

Questions: What is Allied Capital and its track record?
Answers: One of few publicly traded venture capital firms, lends to small companies for high interest plus equity kickers.

Questions: What was Allied Capital I's performance since 1960?
Answers: $10,000 invested when it came public in 1960 is sitting on $1.5 million nest egg by Lynch's writing.

Questions: What tangible result of Allied Capital investment does Lynch mention?
Answers: Air purifier in his bedroom that removes so much grit the room has air quality of genetic engineering lab.

Questions: What was the structure of Allied Capital II?
Answers: $92 million pool, borrows against it to raise another $92 million, total $184 million to buy loans paying 10% while borrowing costs 8%.

Questions: How does Allied Capital II's business model work?
Answers: Makes comfortable spread for shareholders plus occasional equity kickers, few employees and expenses.

Questions: What has been key to Allied's success?
Answers: Management's ability to get money back - very picky about borrowers, stringent about collateral requirements.

Questions: What was Allied Capital II's planned RTC strategy?
Answers: Buy loans from Resolution Trust Corporation - among bum loans in S&L portfolios, there are actually some good ones to reputable borrowers.

Questions: Why were small RTC loans available to Allied?
Answers: Wall Street firms and big banks bought multimillion-dollar loans, but loans of $1 million or less weren't easy for RTC to unload.

Questions: What was Allied Capital II's dividend and price when Lynch analyzed it?
Answers: Selling for $19 with 6% dividend.

Questions: How does Lynch view Allied Capital II as an investment opportunity?
Answers: Simple way to turn S&L fiasco into something advantageous - chance to make back some taxes paid for S&L bailout.

Questions: Which group on Wall Street did Lynch miss for several years?
Answers: The mutual fund industry - he missed Dreyfus, Franklin Resources, Colonial Group, T. Rowe Price, State Street Bank, Alliance Capital Management, and Eaton Vance.

Questions: How does Lynch compare himself to a mall manager regarding mutual fund stocks?
Answers: Like the mall manager who neglected to buy Gap stock despite seeing sales results daily, Lynch neglected mutual fund companies despite being in the industry.

Questions: What is the distinction between direct mutual fund plays and diversified financial companies?
Answers: Direct plays include companies solely focused on funds; diversified include Putnam (subsidiary of Marsh-McLennan) or Kemper (fund business but mostly insurance).

Questions: How did the eight mutual fund companies perform in 1988-1989?
Answers: All did well as fears of mutual fund industry collapse after 1987 correction proved exaggerated.

Questions: What what-if portfolio performance does Lynch present for mutual fund companies?
Answers: If you divided money equally among eight stocks from beginning 1988 to end 1989, you would have outperformed 99% of the funds these companies promote.

Questions: What is Lynch's observation about the Gold Rush and mutual fund investing?
Answers: In the Gold Rush, people who sold picks and shovels did better than the prospectors - during fund popularity, investing in fund companies beats their products.

Questions: When do different types of mutual fund companies prosper?
Answers: Interest rates declining: bond and equity funds attract cash (Eaton Vance, Colonial prosper). Rates rising: money markets popular (Dreyfus prospers).

Questions: What is Alliance Capital's business model?
Answers: Manages money for institutional clients and mutual funds sold through brokers, been public since 1988.

Questions: What happened during the Saddam Sell-off to mutual fund company stocks?
Answers: Eaton Vance declined 30%, Dreyfus declined 18.86%, others had smaller but significant declines.

Questions: What could investors have done to verify mutual fund industry health in 1990-1991?
Answers: Look at sales figures for mutual funds in December 1990 and January 1991 to dispel collapse fears.

Questions: How did Lynch perform with mutual fund stock recommendations in 1991?
Answers: Failed to recommend a single mutual fund company, missing Franklin (75% gain), Dreyfus (55%), T. Rowe Price (116%), UAM (80%).

Questions: Which fund-related stock did Lynch recommend in 1991 and how did it perform?
Answers: Kemper (insurance with fund business via $50 billion managed) - stock doubled in 1991.

Questions: What trend was driving mutual fund company success in 1992?
Answers: Interest rates dropping, $200 billion in CDs maturing monthly, great tide of capital emptying from banks into all manner of funds.

Questions: Why was Colonial Group undervalued compared to peers?
Answers: T. Rowe Price and Franklin selling for 20x earnings, but Colonial Group selling for only 10x earnings despite managing more assets.

Questions: What was Colonial Group's 1985 vs 1992 comparison?
Answers: 1985 IPO: $17, managed $5-6 billion, earned $1/share. 1992: same $17 price, managed $9 billion, earned $1.55/share, plus $4/share cash.

Questions: What had Colonial Group done to enhance shareholder value?
Answers: Amassed $4/share in cash, bought back 7% of stock, had no debt, yet no Wall Street analyst had mentioned it in two years.

Questions: Why was Colonial Group undervalued within the attractive mutual fund group?
Answers: Earnings stayed flat for four years while competitors thrived, wasn't household name like Dreyfus or T. Rowe Price.

Questions: Who did Lynch speak with at Colonial Group?
Answers: Corporate treasurer Davey Scoon on January 3, who reported business improvement especially in muni bond funds.

Questions: What was Colonial Group's new business development?
Answers: Chosen by State Street Bank to market new funds that State Street had created.

Questions: What is State Street Bank's role in the mutual fund industry?
Answers: Commercial bank doing paperwork ('back office' work) for most mutual fund industry - customer service, recording transactions, tracking ownership.

Questions: How profitable has State Street's back office function been?
Answers: Very lucrative - State Street stock had 81% gain in 1991.

Questions: What mistake did Lynch make with his mother-in-law regarding State Street?
Answers: Advised her to sell when money-market assets seemed declining because she'd doubled her money - stock has tripled again since then.

Questions: How do stock splits help cover up selling mistakes?
Answers: His mother-in-law thinks State Street went nowhere due to 3-for-1 split, doesn't realize Lynch sold too early - splits can camouflage timing mistakes.

Questions: Why did State Street want to start its own mutual funds?
Answers: Seeing success in back office work, wanted to get in on front end of bonanza.

Questions: Why did State Street hire Colonial Group instead of competing directly?
Answers: Didn't want to anger clients by competing against them directly, so camouflaged State Street funds by having Colonial market them.

Questions: How would the State Street relationship benefit Colonial Group?
Answers: Extra business from marketing State Street's funds would add to Colonial's revenue and growth.

Questions: What does Lynch say about restaurant stock recommendations in 1992?
Answers: He didn't recommend any restaurant stocks in 1992, but admits he should have.

Questions: When did fast food become an accessory to the automobile?
Answers: Since the 1960s, when people learned to eat lunches, then breakfasts, and finally dinners on the road.

Questions: What was Kentucky Fried Chicken's origin story?
Answers: Created out of desperation when superhighway diverted traffic from Colonel Sanders's country restaurant, facing bankruptcy, the 66-year-old took to the road offering his recipe.

Questions: What was Colonel Sanders wearing when he started franchising?
Answers: A dark suit, not the white planter's costume that later became his trademark.

Questions: When did major restaurant chains go public?
Answers: KFC: 1965, Dunkin' Donuts and Howard Johnson earlier, Bob Evans Farms: 1963, McDonald's and Shoney's: mid-1960s.

Questions: What was Shoney's stock performance as a bagger?
Answers: 168-bagger, rising from 22 cents per share (adjusted for splits) to high of $367⁄8.

Questions: What was McDonald's performance compared to other restaurant stocks?
Answers: 400-bagger, making it one of most rewarding stock market performers in modern history.

Questions: What would $10,000 invested in five early restaurant stocks have become?
Answers: By end of 1980s, would have become millionaire at least twice over, four times over if entire amount put into McDonald's alone.

Questions: What types of restaurant categories have produced big stock winners?
Answers: Hamburger joints, cafeterias (Luby's, Morrison's), family steak houses (Ponderosa, Bonanza), all-purpose eateries (Denny's, Shoney's), ice cream, yogurt, coffee bars, pizza.

Questions: What advantage do restaurant investors have?
Answers: We all know which places are popular and well-maintained, which are disheveled and passé, which have reached saturation, which have room to grow.

Questions: What 1970s restaurant opportunities could have made up for missing 1960s?
Answers: International Dairy Queen, Wendy's, Luby's, Taco Bell, Pizza Hut, Jerrico when Long John Silver appeared.

Questions: When was especially good timing for restaurant investments in the 1970s?
Answers: After bear market of 1972 when solid franchises were selling for pittance - Taco Bell dropped to $1/share despite never having disappointing quarter.

Questions: What happened to Taco Bell after Lynch discovered it?
Answers: Rebounded to $40, then acquired by PepsiCo, which likes to own food companies because they help sell Pepsi's soft drinks.

Questions: What 1980s restaurant opportunities does Lynch mention?
Answers: Cracker Barrel (popular gift shop, delicious seafood and biscuits), Chili's (public 1984), Sbarro (1985), Ryan's Family Steak Houses (1982), Uno Restaurants (1987).

Questions: How are restaurant chains protected from competition compared to other businesses?
Answers: New fish-and-chips chain in California has zero impact on better one in New York - takes long time to work across country, no foreign competition.

Questions: What separates restaurant triumphs from flops?
Answers: Capable management, adequate financing, and methodical approach to expansion - slow but steady wins this race.

Questions: What is the tale of two hamburger franchises Lynch tells?
Answers: Chili's (Dallas) vs. Fuddrucker's (San Antonio) - both featured gourmet burger and distinctive surroundings.

Questions: Why did Chili's succeed while Fuddrucker's failed?
Answers: Chili's diversified menu as hamburgers went out of style, Fuddrucker's stuck with burgers; Chili's expanded methodically, Fuddrucker's expanded too rapidly.

Questions: What is the danger of expanding more than 100 new units per year?
Answers: Company likely to run into problems - can pick wrong sites or managers, pay too much for real estate, fail to train employees properly.

Questions: What other restaurant chains fell into the rapid expansion trap?
Answers: Fuddrucker's, Flakey Jake's, Winners, TGI Friday's all moved too fast and suffered.

Questions: What is Chili's sensible expansion pace?
Answers: 30-35 new units per year under experienced Norman Brinker (founder of Chili's, Steak & Ale, and Bennigan's).

Questions: What is Chili's expansion goal?
Answers: Reach ceiling of 400-450 restaurants in 1996-98, hoping to produce $1 billion in sales.

Questions: What are the different ways restaurant chains can increase earnings?
Answers: Add more restaurants, improve existing operations, high turnover with low prices, low turnover with high prices, food vs. gift shop profits, cheap ingredients.

Questions: What are the key elements to follow in restaurant stories?
Answers: Growth rate, debt, and same-store sales - want same-store sales increasing every quarter.

Questions: What is the danger zone for restaurant expansion?
Answers: Above 100 new outlets per year puts company in potential danger zone.

Questions: What should restaurant debt levels be?
Answers: Debt should be low to nonexistent if possible.

Questions: Who provides excellent restaurant industry analysis?
Answers: Montgomery Securities in California keeps regular tabs and produces excellent reports on entire restaurant group.

Questions: What is Montgomery Securities' analysis of current restaurant trends?
Answers: Hamburger joints suffering from overexposure (top 5 chains have 24,000 U.S. locations), baby boomers turning away from fast food.

Questions: Where has restaurant momentum shifted according to Montgomery?
Answers: To niche restaurants like Au Bon Pain and Spaghetti Warehouse, and medium-priced family restaurants with varied menus.

Questions: What was the performance of Montgomery's top 8 restaurant recommendations in 1991?
Answers: Would have doubled your money by December: Bertucci's, Cracker Barrel, Brinker International (Chili's), Spaghetti Warehouse, Shoney's, Rally's, Applebee's, Outback Steakhouse.

Questions: What is the overall growth rate of the restaurant group?
Answers: Only 4% per year - soon this will be another nongrowth industry.

Questions: Who will prosper in the mature restaurant industry?
Answers: Superior operators with strong balance sheets will prosper as they always have, as industry consolidates.

Questions: What percentage of meals do Americans eat outside the home?
Answers: 50% of meals eaten outside home, ensuring continued opportunities for new 20-baggers in food courts and neighborhoods.

Questions: Where did Lynch spot Au Bon Pain?
Answers: In the Burlington Mall - started in Boston in 1977, went public in 1991 at $10/share.

Questions: What is Au Bon Pain's concept?
Answers: Croissant and coffee shop combining French sensibility with U.S. efficiency - plain croissant for breakfast, filled for lunch, chocolate for dessert in under 3 minutes.

Questions: How does Au Bon Pain ensure fresh bread?
Answers: Made at central location, sent uncooked to outlets where it rises and is baked fresh on-site.

Questions: What new products has Au Bon Pain introduced?
Answers: Fresh orange juice, fruit salad, and about to launch the state-of-the-art bagel.

Questions: What is Lynch's preference between high-tech investments and food?
Answers: If choice between state-of-the-art computer chip and state-of-the-art bagel, he'll take the bagel any time.

Questions: Why didn't Lynch recommend Au Bon Pain initially?
Answers: Stock had doubled to carry P/E ratio of 40 based on expected 1992 earnings.

Questions: At what point would Lynch back up the truck on Au Bon Pain?
Answers: When price fell to $14 (less than 20x 1993 earnings) - any 25% grower selling for 20x earnings is a buy.

Questions: What global potential does Au Bon Pain have?
Answers: Company is doing well in recession and can grow long time without running into itself, has lot of potential overseas.

Questions: Why does a healthy portfolio require regular checkups?
Answers: Even with blue chips and top Fortune 500 companies, the buy-and-forget strategy can be unproductive and downright dangerous.

Questions: What examples does Lynch give of buy-and-forget dangers?
Answers: Investors who bought and forgot IBM, Sears, and Eastman Kodak are sorry they did - these stocks declined significantly over time.

Questions: What is the six-month checkup according to Lynch?
Answers: Not simply looking up stock price in newspaper, but following the stories to get answers to two basic questions.

Questions: What are the two basic questions for the six-month checkup?
Answers: 1) Is the stock still attractively priced relative to earnings? 2) What is happening in the company to make earnings go up?

Questions: What are the three possible conclusions from a six-month checkup?
Answers: 1) Story has gotten better (increase investment), 2) Story has gotten worse (decrease investment), 3) Story unchanged (stick with it or find more exciting prospects).

Questions: How did Lynch's 21 Barron's selections perform in the first six months?
Answers: The portfolio increased 19.2% while the S&P 500 returned only 1.64% - extremely well in a so-so market.

Questions: What happened to the Body Shop stock price by July 1992?
Answers: Fallen 12.3% from 325 pence to 263 pence, now selling for 20 times estimated 1993 earnings.

Questions: What is Lynch's view on paying 20 times earnings for a 25% grower?
Answers: He doesn't mind it, especially when entire NYSE was selling at 20x earnings for companies growing at only 8-10% rate.

Questions: What bad publicity hurt the Body Shop?
Answers: Chieftain from Kayapó Indian tribe (hired to produce Brazil nut hair conditioner) was arrested in London for raping Portuguese nanny.

Questions: How often has the Body Shop suffered major setbacks?
Answers: Two major setbacks: 1987 and 1990, both despite company perking along with no letup - Lynch attributes to British unfamiliarity with small growth companies.

Questions: What did Monica Kalmanson at Body Shop report about 1991 performance?
Answers: Same-store sales and earnings both increased in 1991, considerable achievement given four major markets (England, Australia, Canada, U.S.) all in recession.

Questions: What strategic move was Body Shop making to improve margins?
Answers: Using cash to buy up suppliers of potions and lotions to cut merchandise costs and improve profit margin.

Questions: What did Cathy Stephenson report about her Body Shop franchises?
Answers: 6% sales gain over previous year at Burlington, Harvard Square too early to tell, customers flocking to new products like Complete Color and mango body butter.

Questions: What was Body Shop's expansion plan?
Answers: 40 new U.S. outlets in 1993, 50 more in 1994, 50/year in Europe, equal number in Far East.

Questions: How does Lynch categorize Body Shop's growth phase?
Answers: Attractive mid-life phase - second decade of 30 years of growth.

Questions: Why was Pier 1 stock punished despite meeting expectations?
Answers: Analysts expected 18-20 cents first quarter earnings, Pier 1 earned 17 cents, stock got clobbered - Wall Street deaf to good news.

Questions: How had Pier 1 strengthened its financial position?
Answers: Sold $75 million convertible debentures, used proceeds to retire debt, further reducing already-reduced long-term debt.

Questions: What competitive advantage was Pier 1 gaining during the recession?
Answers: Major competitors (department stores) getting out of home furnishings business, longer recession lasted, more competitors would drop out.

Questions: What was Lynch's earnings projection for Pier 1?
Answers: 80 cents from own stores plus 10-15 cents from revived Sunbelt Nursery = $1/share, making it $14 stock at reasonable 14x P/E.

Questions: What disappointing development occurred with General Host?
Answers: Issued $65 million convertible preferred stock with 8% yield, creating more shares that would dilute existing shareholders.

Questions: How did General Host's use of proceeds differ from Pier 1's?
Answers: Pier 1 used proceeds to pay off debt (reducing interest expense), General Host used proceeds for further Frank's Nursery renovation (chancier proposition).

Questions: What was General Host's earnings revision?
Answers: Expected to earn 60 cents when stock was $7.75, now $8 stock expected to earn only 45 cents.

Questions: What positives kept General Host as a hold for Lynch?
Answers: Strong cash flow, dividend raised 14th year in a row, stock selling below book value, expansion proceeding as planned.

Questions: Who had bought General Host stock according to Lynch's research?
Answers: Mario Gabelli had bought million shares for his value-oriented fund.

Questions: What happened to Sunbelt Nursery after Lynch's recommendation?
Answers: Lost money since January due to more rain in Southwest dampening gardening enthusiasm.

Questions: How cheap had Sunbelt become by the six-month checkup?
Answers: $4.50 stock with $1.50/share in cash, so buying all garden outlets for only $3.

Questions: Why did Lynch prefer Calloway's over Sunbelt by the checkup?
Answers: Calloway's also fell in half due to rain, but was best company in industry with better fundamentals.

Questions: What did Dan Reynolds report about Calloway's operations?
Answers: 20 employees sharing 3,000 square feet - no communications gap, management attention available by standing up and yelling.

Questions: What were Calloway's financial metrics?
Answers: 13 nurseries plus 50 cents/share cash, expected to earn 50 cents in 1993, giving P/E ratio of 10.

Questions: What was positive about Calloway's Wall Street coverage?
Answers: No followers on Wall Street, and company was buying back its own shares.

Questions: What is Lynch's principle about investing within attractive groups?
Answers: Find the undervalued stock within attractive group - technique he's often employed with good results.

Questions: What happened to Ed Faber at Supercuts?
Answers: Left the company, with explanation he wanted to devote himself to managing his own Supercuts salon - explanation not entirely convincing.

Questions: What overhang problem did Lynch discover with Supercuts?
Answers: Carlton Investments (part of bankrupt Drexel Burnham Lambert) owns 2.2 million shares that creditors will demand be sold.

Questions: What positive developments were happening at Supercuts despite problems?
Answers: Named 'Official Hair Salon Services Supplier for Olympics,' same-store sales up 6.9% in first quarter, expanding into upstate New York.

Questions: What was Lynch's concern about Supercuts expansion?
Answers: 80-100 new franchises planned for 1993 - he's seen promising franchises ruined by overeager expansion.

Questions: What advice did Lynch give to Supercuts CEO?
Answers: 'If you have choice between reaching your goal in fifteen years or five years, fifteen is better.'

Questions: How did the seven S&Ls perform in the first six months?
Answers: They were the best performers of Lynch's 21 picks - not an accident since he took industry surrounded by most doom and gloom.

Questions: Why have S&Ls been the best performers?
Answers: Interest rates falling created happy year for financial institutions making huge earnings on spreads between loan rates and deposit rates.

Questions: What were the specific S&L performance numbers?
Answers: Germantown up 59%, Sovereign up 64.5% (plus two 10% stock dividends), Eagle Financial up from $11 to $16, Glacier up 40%+, People's up 26%.

Questions: How did the long-shot S&Ls perform?
Answers: Lawrence up 37%, First Essex up 70% - proving riskiest stocks often carry greatest rewards.

Questions: What did Leonard Wilson report about First Essex's improvement?
Answers: Reduced 'bottom fishing' line from 600 feet to 60 feet - foreclosed properties selling, nonperforming loans down, mortgage market picking up.

Questions: What sign of optimism did Wilson show at First Essex?
Answers: Actually dared to make a new construction loan after being driven close to poorhouse - somebody thinks region has future.

Questions: What was First Essex's potential if real estate market continued improving?
Answers: Could eventually earn $1/share, making stock worth $7-10 vs. current $35⁄8.

Questions: What mixed signals came from Lawrence Savings?
Answers: April: CEO Paul Miller optimistic, seven pages of nonperformers reduced to one. June: sounded discouraged.

Questions: What was Lawrence Savings' precarious position?
Answers: $55 million commercial real estate loans outstanding vs. only $21 million net worth - if half go sour, Lawrence wiped out.

Questions: What better S&L opportunity had emerged by the checkup?
Answers: First Federal of Michigan (FFOM) - hadn't budged while other S&Ls increased in value.

Questions: What was FFOM's problem despite being a strong Jimmy Stewart thrift?
Answers: Money borrowed from Federal Home Loan Bank at 8-10% fixed rates through 1994, while borrowers refinancing at lower rates.

Questions: When will FFOM's problems resolve?
Answers: Once FHLB debt retired and interest rate futures contracts expire, earnings will explode - resolution could add $2+/share to earnings in 1994-96.

Questions: What is FFOM's book value and current earnings situation?
Answers: Book value over $26/share, current earnings $2/share making it $12 stock, could earn $4 when problems resolve.

Questions: How did Colonial Group benefit from bond fund popularity?
Answers: Specializes in bond funds, particularly tax-exempt and limited maturity government funds enjoying widespread popularity.

Questions: What did Davey Scoon report about Colonial Group's recent performance?
Answers: Sales up 58% in recent quarter, now manages $9.5 billion vs. $8.1 billion year earlier.

Questions: What additional positive news did Colonial Group announce?
Answers: $10 million stock buyback program, plus $4/share in cash with stock selling around $20.

Questions: What is the key to making money in stocks according to Lynch?
Answers: The key to making money in stocks is not to get scared out of them. This point cannot be overemphasized.

Questions: What determines success in both dieting and stocks?
Answers: In dieting and in stocks, it is the gut and not the head that determines the results.

Questions: Who is better off - the person who studies the market or the person who ignores it?
Answers: The person who never bothers to think about the economy, blithely ignores market conditions, and invests on a regular schedule is better off than the person who tries to time investments.

Questions: What is the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: An annual gathering where supposed experts meet for eight hours to trade quips and tips, published in three weekly issues of Barron's magazine.

Questions: How long has Lynch participated in the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: Lynch has participated in the Barron's Roundtable every year since 1986.

Questions: Who is Alan Abelson and what is his role?
Answers: Alan Abelson is Barron's editor and the resident wit who directs the friendly inquisition at the Roundtable, having done for finance what Dorothy Parker did for romance.

Questions: What are the regular panelists on the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: Mario Gabelli, Michael Price, John Neff, Paul Tudor Jones, Felix Zulauf, Marc Perkins, Oscar Schafer, Ron Baron, and Archie MacAllaster.

Questions: What happened to Jimmy Rogers from the panel?
Answers: Jimmy Rogers gave up Wall Street to follow the old silk trade route across China on a motorcycle, later shipping it to Peru to ride around the Andes.

Questions: What is the format of the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: It starts at noon with two parts: first an overview of financial markets and economy, then individual stock recommendations. The overview discussions get them into trouble.

Questions: What does Lynch say about weekend worrying?
Answers: Weekend worrying is dangerous for investors because they have extra time to ponder distressing news, leading to emotional decisions that spoil nest eggs.

Questions: What types of scary news do people encounter on weekends?
Answers: Global warming, Soviet empire collapse, recession, inflation, health care costs, budget deficits, tribal warfare, organized crime, sex and money scandals.

Questions: Why are Mondays historically the biggest down days in stocks?
Answers: Because weekend logic leads to sell orders pouring in on Mondays after people have had time to worry about world events over the weekend.

Questions: What were the panel's worries in 1986?
Answers: M-1 versus M-3, Gramm-Rudman deficit reduction, what the Group of Seven would do, and whether the J Curve effect would reduce the trade deficit.

Questions: What were the main concerns in 1987?
Answers: Dollar collapsing, foreign dumping, Iran-Iraq War causing oil shortage, foreigners stopping bond purchases, over-indebted consumers, and Reagan term limits.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #4?
Answers: You can't see the future through a rearview mirror.

Questions: What was Felix Zulauf's pessimistic 1988 statement?
Answers: 'The honeymoon, from 1982 to 1987, is over' - which was the most optimistic thing said all day.

Questions: What were the two types of bear markets the panel debated in 1988?
Answers: A standard bear market taking the Dow to 1500 or lower, versus a killer bear market that would 'wipe out most people in the financial community.'

Questions: What Chinese cosmological concern did Zulauf raise in 1989?
Answers: He noted that 1989 was the Year of the Snake, which was a bad sign in Chinese cosmology.

Questions: What was the panel's concern in 1990 despite the Dow reaching 2500?
Answers: They worried about real estate collapse and that after seven straight up years, a down market was inevitable - worrying that things had been going too well.

Questions: What extreme behavior did Lynch observe in 1990?
Answers: He heard cabdrivers recommending bonds and barbers bragging about buying 'puts' (options that increase in value as stocks decline).

Questions: What does Bernard Baruch's saying about shoeshine boys suggest?
Answers: If Baruch was right about selling when shoeshine boys are buying stocks, then the right time to buy is when barbers discover put options.

Questions: What were some of the pessimistic headlines Lynch collected from fall 1990?
Answers: 'Layoffs Hit Professional Ranks,' 'How Safe Is Your Job?,' 'The Real Estate Bust,' 'Housing Slump Hammering Remodelers,' 'Can Your Bank Stay Afloat?'

Questions: What was the Mother of All Worries in 1991?
Answers: The Gulf War, with fears about chemical and biological weapons, body bags, and the well-trained Iraqi army in reinforced bunkers.

Questions: What were the Roundtable's dire predictions for 1991?
Answers: Zulauf saw Dow falling to 2000-2700, Michael Price saw 500-point downside, Marc Perkins predicted 1600-1700, Lynch feared 33% drop if war was terrible.

Questions: Despite the dire predictions, what actually happened in 1991?
Answers: Instead of a 33% drop, there was a 30% gain in S&P 500, 25% gain in Dow, and 60% gain in smaller stocks - making 1991 the best year in two decades.

Questions: What was Lynch doing personally during the pessimistic predictions?
Answers: Lynch was actually buying stocks, adding to holdings in his personal account and for charitable trusts, increasing stakes in W.R. Grace and Morrison-Knudsen.

Questions: What does Lynch say about preparing for total disaster?
Answers: It's beyond him why investors bail out of best investments to prepare for total disaster - if disaster strikes, cash will be as useless as stock certificates.

Questions: What is the Even Bigger Picture according to Lynch?
Answers: Over 70 years, stocks have provided 11% annual gains while Treasury bills, bonds, and CDs returned less than half that amount.

Questions: How many scary market declines have occurred in 70 years?
Answers: There have been 40 scary declines of 10% or more, including 13 terrifying declines of 33% or more, including the 1929-33 sell-off.

Questions: What does Lynch identify as the main factor keeping people away from stocks?
Answers: The cultural memory of the 1929 Crash, which continues to scare people 60 years later, including people who weren't even born in 1929.

Questions: How costly has the post-Crash trauma syndrome been?
Answers: People avoiding stocks for 60 years have missed stock market gains and suffered inflation damage that exceeded what another crash would have done.

Questions: What misconception persists about market crashes and economic collapses?
Answers: People believe stock market collapses lead to economic collapses, even though crashes in 1972 and 1987 didn't cause economic disasters.

Questions: How does Lynch compare market declines to Minnesota weather?
Answers: A decline in stocks is as normal as frigid air in Minnesota - you expect it, prepare for it, and know that warmer weather will return.

Questions: What should a successful stockpicker do during market drops?
Answers: Like a Minnesotan with freezing weather, you know it's coming, you're ready to ride it out, and when favorites go down, you buy more.

Questions: How severe was the Great Correction of 1987?
Answers: 508 points were shaved from the Dow in a single day, representing a 1000-point decline (33% from August high).

Questions: Was the 1987 crash as apocalyptic as predicted?
Answers: No, it was a normal, albeit severe, correction - the 13th such 33% drop in the century, not the end of civilization many expected.

Questions: What will be the significance of the next 10% market decline?
Answers: It will be the 41st in recent history, or if it's 33%, the 14th - just another in a long string of chances to buy great companies at bargain prices.

Questions: How did Lynch prepare Magellan shareholders for inevitable setbacks?
Answers: In annual reports, he often reminded shareholders that such setbacks were inevitable and normal parts of market cycles.

Questions: What comfort does Lynch find in the story of 40 market declines?
Answers: The story continues to comfort him during gloomy periods when there's another chance to buy great companies at bargain prices.

Questions: What mistake do investors make regarding market timing?
Answers: They feel better after the market gains 600 points (when stocks are overvalued) and worse after it drops 600 points (when bargains abound).

Questions: What type of faith does Lynch say stockpickers need?
Answers: Faith that America will survive, people will keep getting up and putting on pants, and corporations making pants will profit for shareholders.

Questions: What faith should investors have about American business?
Answers: Faith that as old enterprises lose momentum, exciting new ones like Wal-Mart, Federal Express, and Apple Computer will emerge to replace them.

Questions: What is Lynch's view on American workers and entrepreneurs?
Answers: Lynch has faith that America is a nation of hardworking and inventive people, and that even yuppies have gotten a bad rap for being lazy.

Questions: How should investors think about the Even Bigger Picture during doubt?
Answers: Focus on 70 years of stocks providing 11% annual returns versus bonds and CDs providing less than half that, despite all the calamities.

Questions: What will be more lucrative than following 200 commentators predicting depression?
Answers: Acting on the information that stocks have outperformed other investments for 70 years will be far more lucrative long-term.

Questions: How many times has the market declined 33% or more in this century?
Answers: The market has had 13 terrifying declines of 33% or more, including the Mother of All Terrifying Declines from 1929-33.

Questions: What would have happened in 39 out of 40 market corrections if you sold everything?
Answers: You would have sold all your stocks and been sorry, since stocks eventually came back even from the Big One.

Questions: How should investors view market corrections?
Answers: As recurring events, not surprising events - as normal as frigid air in Minnesota, requiring preparation but not panic.

Questions: How many mutual funds existed when Lynch wrote this book?
Answers: There were 3,565 mutual funds: 1,266 equity funds, 1,457 bond and income funds, 566 taxable money-market funds, and 276 short-term municipal bond funds.

Questions: How does the number of funds in 1992 compare to 1976?
Answers: In 1976 there were only 452 funds (278 equity), compared to 3,565 in 1992 - nearly an 8-fold increase.

Questions: What milestone has been reached in fund-making history?
Answers: The number of funds now exceeds the number of individual stocks traded on the New York and American stock exchanges combined.

Questions: What is the first decision investors must make when structuring a portfolio?
Answers: Whether the mix of stocks and bonds should be changed - the initial growth-versus-income decision, which has the greatest consequence for future net worth.

Questions: What percentage of mutual fund money went into stock funds in 1980 vs 1990?
Answers: In 1980, 69% went into stock funds. By 1990, only 43% of mutual-fund assets were invested in stocks.

Questions: What percentage of mutual fund dollars was parked in bond and money-market funds?
Answers: Approximately 75% of all mutual-fund dollars was parked in bond and money-market funds.

Questions: Why do stocks do better than bonds over time?
Answers: As companies grow larger and more profitable, stockholders share in increased profits through raised dividends, while no company has ever rewarded bondholders by raising interest rates.

Questions: How many companies have raised dividends for 20 years in a row?
Answers: 134 companies have an unbroken 20-year record of dividend increases, and 362 have a 10-year record.

Questions: What is Lynch's simple strategy for Wall Street success?
Answers: Buy stocks from Moody's Dividend Achievers list and stick with them as long as they stay on the list.

Questions: Why is the stocks-for-young, bonds-for-old prescription becoming obsolete?
Answers: People aren't dying as readily - a healthy 62-year-old faces 20 more years of spending and inflation, requiring growth to maintain living standards.

Questions: What problem do senior citizens face with low interest rates?
Answers: With CDs paying 3.5%, even people with huge portfolios have trouble living off interest alone.

Questions: What happens to a retired couple with $500,000 in bonds paying 7% with 5% inflation?
Answers: Their $35,000 annual income will be cut in half in 10 years and cut by two-thirds in 15 years due to inflation.

Questions: What advice does Lynch give about stock allocation?
Answers: Increase the stock part of the mix to the limit of your tolerance for the best long-term results.

Questions: What was the bond/stock mix Lynch's nonprofit organization had before restructuring?
Answers: 50% stocks and 50% bonds, yielding about 6% return with 4% growth rate - barely enough to keep up with inflation.

Questions: What are the historical returns from stocks vs other investments?
Answers: Stocks return nearly 11% (3% dividends, 8% price appreciation), while bonds don't appreciate at all over time.

Questions: What would happen to portfolio growth by adjusting stock/bond percentages?
Answers: Table 3-1 shows that increasing stock allocation sacrifices short-term income but provides much better long-term growth and eventually higher income.

Questions: In Case C (100% stocks), what were the 20-year results vs Case A (100% bonds)?
Answers: Case C: $13,729 dividend income, portfolio worth $46,610. Case A: $14,000 interest income, original $10,000 returned.

Questions: What does Lynch's radical conclusion suggest about bonds for income?
Answers: Theoretically, it makes no sense to put any money into bonds, even if you need income - you're better off with stocks even when dipping into capital.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #5?
Answers: There's no point paying Yo-Yo Ma to play a radio (referring to paying loads for government bond funds).

Questions: What does Lynch say about government bond funds?
Answers: He can't figure out why anyone would invest in intermediate or long-term government bond funds when they could buy Treasury bonds directly with no fees.

Questions: How can you buy Treasury bonds without fees?
Answers: Treasury bonds and bills can be purchased through a broker or directly from a Federal Reserve bank, which charges no commission.

Questions: What study shows bond funds underperforming individual bonds?
Answers: Gabriele, Hueglin & Cashman found that from 1980-1986, bond funds were consistently outperformed by individual bonds, sometimes by 2% annually.

Questions: What is Warren Buffett's advice about stock volatility?
Answers: People who can't tolerate seeing their stocks lose 50% of their value shouldn't own stocks (this also applies to stock funds).

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #6?
Answers: As long as you're picking a fund, you might as well pick a good one.

Questions: What percentage of equity funds failed to outperform market indexes in the 1980s?
Answers: Up to 75% of equity funds have been worse than mediocre, failing to outgain random baskets of stocks in market indexes.

Questions: What is the modern paradox of fund management?
Answers: Most fund managers investing in stocks that make up the averages somehow manage to do worse than the averages themselves.

Questions: What are the theories for why funds underperform indexes?
Answers: Fund managers are lousy stockpickers, herd instinct creates closet indexers, large company stocks had a great run, or popularity of index funds creates self-fulfilling prophecy.

Questions: What would $100,000 in Vanguard 500 index fund be worth from 1983-1991?
Answers: $308,450, compared to only $236,367 in the average managed equity fund over the same 8-year period.

Questions: What does the Investment Vision study show about chasing past performance?
Answers: Investing in prior 3-year best performers lagged S&P by 2.05%. Even 5- and 10-year best performers only beat S&P by 0.88% and 1.02% respectively.

Questions: What is Lynch's advice about past performance charts?
Answers: Don't spend a lot of time poring over past performance charts - it's better to stick with steady, consistent performers than move in and out trying to catch waves.

Questions: How many funds have shown gains in every calendar year since 1978?
Answers: Only 9 out of 264 funds that go back to 1978 have shown gains every calendar year since then.

Questions: What is the best performer among funds with gains every year since 1977?
Answers: Phoenix Growth, with a compound annual gain of 20.2% since 1977.

Questions: Does paying a load mean you get a better fund?
Answers: Not necessarily. Some successful funds charge loads while others don't. If you plan to stick with a fund for several years, the 2-5% load becomes insignificant.

Questions: What was the 'too big to succeed' criticism of Magellan?
Answers: Beginning in 1983 at $1 billion, critics said Magellan was too big to succeed at $2B, $4B, $10B, and $14B, but it continued to outperform.

Questions: What are the drawbacks of running a big fund?
Answers: Like a linebacker on petits fours - you need considerable quantities to get nourishment. Can't buy enough small company shares to matter, takes months to build positions.

Questions: What are sector funds designed for?
Answers: For investors with special knowledge about a commodity or business prospects, not for whimsical speculation.

Questions: Who are the best candidates for sector fund investing?
Answers: Jewelry store owners (gold), builders (lumber), insurance adjusters (rates), gas station managers (oil), doctors (drug approvals), scientists (biotech products).

Questions: What was Fidelity Biotechnology's performance in 1991 and 1992?
Answers: 99.05% gain in 1991, but down 21.5% through first nine months of 1992, showing the volatility of sector investing.

Questions: What have been the most and least profitable sectors over the past decade?
Answers: Most profitable: health care, financial services, utilities. Least profitable: precious metals.

Questions: Why is Lynch getting interested in gold sector again?
Answers: Gold supply from new mines running out, decade of low prices discouraged exploration, demand increasing (especially China factor), potential inflation hedge.

Questions: What are convertible funds and their advantage?
Answers: Funds investing in convertible bonds that combine high performance of small-cap stocks with stability of bonds, offering best of both worlds.

Questions: How do convertible bonds work?
Answers: They pay lower interest than regular bonds but allow conversion to common stock at a specific price, usually 20-25% above current stock price.

Questions: What was the performance comparison in 1990 between convertible bonds and common stocks?
Answers: Common stocks connected to convertibles were down 27.3%, while convertible bonds themselves lost only 13% of value.

Questions: What is the key difference between closed-end and open-ended funds?
Answers: Closed-end funds have static share counts and trade like stocks; open-ended funds create/retire shares as investors buy/sell.

Questions: What advantage do closed-end fund managers have?
Answers: Job security - the fund can't shrink due to customer exodus, so they can only fail by generating portfolio losses.

Questions: What opportunity exists with closed-end funds during market sell-offs?
Answers: Bargain hunters can buy closed-end funds at substantial discounts to their net asset value.

Questions: What are country funds and how many exist?
Answers: Funds that invest in specific countries, with at least 75 country and/or region funds in existence, growing with communist bloc breakup.

Questions: What is the best argument for country funds as long-term investments?
Answers: Foreign economies are growing faster than the U.S., causing their stock markets to advance faster than ours.

Questions: What example does Lynch give of country fund overenthusiasm?
Answers: Germany Fund was bid up 25% above underlying stock values as Berlin Wall fell, then sold at 20-25% discount when reality set in.

Questions: When is the best time to buy a country fund?
Answers: When it's unpopular and you can get it for a 20-25% discount to underlying asset value.

Questions: What are the drawbacks of country funds?
Answers: High fees, currency risk, government policy risk, and need for knowledgeable managers who understand the local market.

Questions: What is Lynch's view on U.S. vs foreign companies?
Answers: The U.S. still has the best companies and system for investing - Europe lacks growth companies, information is sketchy, earnings estimates are unreliable.

Questions: What does Lynch say about Japanese superiority claims?
Answers: It's malarkey - Japan is the richest country where people have trouble making ends meet, with $5 apples, $100 dinners, and $1 million, 1000-square-foot homes.

Questions: What was the problem with the Japanese market according to Lynch?
Answers: It was subject to behind-the-scenes manipulation unknown since the 1920s, with money-back guarantees from brokers and controlled stock prices.

Questions: What does Lynch recommend for mutual fund strategies?
Answers: Put as much money into stock funds as possible, know what kinds you own, divide among 3-4 types, add money to lagging sectors, stick with solid performers.

Questions: When did the Magellan Fund originally start and what was it called?
Answers: The fund started in 1963 as the Fidelity International Fund, founded by Ned Johnson.

Questions: Why did the International Fund become a domestic fund?
Answers: A tax on foreign investments promoted by President Kennedy forced international fund managers to sell foreign stocks and buy domestic stocks.

Questions: When did the fund officially become Magellan?
Answers: It became Magellan on March 31, 1965, after two years as a domestic fund in disguise.

Questions: What was Magellan's biggest position when it launched in 1965?
Answers: Chrysler was the biggest position, which came back from bankruptcy 20 years later to become Lynch's biggest position.

Questions: What was Lynch doing when Magellan was launched in 1965?
Answers: Lynch was a student at Boston College, caddying golf games on weekends.

Questions: How did Lynch's mother get involved in mutual funds?
Answers: A schoolteacher moonlighting as a fund salesman convinced her to buy Fidelity Capital because 'a Chinese guy' (Gerry Tsai) was running it.

Questions: What happened to Magellan's assets from 1966 to 1976?
Answers: The fund declined from $20 million in 1966 to only $6 million by 1976 due to steady outflow from customer redemptions.

Questions: Why was the Essex Fund merged with Magellan in 1976?
Answers: Essex had shrunk from $100 million to $12 million but had a valuable $50 million tax-loss carryforward that could benefit Magellan.

Questions: What was Lynch's situation when he took over Magellan in 1977?
Answers: $18 million in assets, $50 million tax-loss carryforward, terrible stock market, declining customers, and the fund was closed to new buyers.

Questions: Why was Magellan closed to new investors for four years?
Answers: Not by design - there was simply no interest. The fund business was so dismal that brokerage houses had disbanded sales departments.

Questions: What does Lynch say about being brought along slowly as a fund manager?
Answers: The obscurity for the first four years was a blessing, enabling him to learn and make mistakes without being in a spotlight.

Questions: What was Lynch's background before managing Magellan?
Answers: He was director of research at Fidelity from 1974-1977, served on the investment committee, and had begun helping a Boston charity manage its portfolio in 1975.

Questions: What was Lynch's first stock pick that he missed as a 30-bagger?
Answers: General Cinema, which was selling for less than $1 when he visited on October 12, 1977, and went to over $30.

Questions: What were Lynch's biggest positions by December 1977?
Answers: Congoleum (51,000 shares worth $833,000), Transamerica, Union Oil, and Aetna Life and Casualty.

Questions: How did Lynch discover Hanes stock?
Answers: Through his wife Carolyn, who was crazy about their L'eggs pantyhose product.

Questions: What was Lynch's reaction when he first ordered Taco Bell stock?
Answers: His trader Charlie Maxfield asked 'What's that, the Mexican telephone company?' showing how unknown the company was.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #7?
Answers: The extravagance of any corporate office is directly proportional to management's reluctance to reward the shareholders.

Questions: What attracted Lynch to Congoleum?
Answers: It had invented seamless vinyl flooring that could be rolled out like carpet, and was building naval frigates using modular prefab techniques.

Questions: Why did Lynch like Taco Bell initially?
Answers: Tasty tacos, 90% of country not yet exposed to them, good record, strong balance sheet, and home office that resembled a neighborhood garage.

Questions: What was Magellan's performance in Lynch's first 12 months?
Answers: The fund was up 20% while the Dow Jones average lost 17.6% and S&P 500 lost 9.4% in the same period.

Questions: How did Lynch describe his early strategy in 1978?
Answers: 'Reduced holdings in autos, aerospace, railroads, pollution, utilities, chemicals, electronics, energy; added to financial institutions, broadcasting, entertainment, insurance, banking, consumer products, lodging, leasing.'

Questions: Did Lynch have an overall strategy when he started?
Answers: No, Lynch never had an overall strategy. His stockpicking was entirely empirical, going from case to case like a bloodhound following a scent.

Questions: How did Lynch's approach differ from growth fund managers?
Answers: As a capital appreciation fund manager, he could buy anything when growth sectors were overvalued, while growth fund managers were forced into overpriced inventory.

Questions: What five categories did Magellan define for its investments in 1979?
Answers: Small and medium-sized growth companies, companies with improving prospects, depressed cyclicals, high-yielding dividend payers, and undervalued asset companies.

Questions: What was Lynch's turnover rate in the early years?
Answers: 343% in the first year with 41 stocks, and 300% in each of the three years thereafter - a very high trading pace.

Questions: Why was Lynch trading so frequently in the early years?
Answers: He was constantly selling to raise cash for redemptions while discovering new prospects, and had to sell something to buy something new in the small fund.

Questions: What does Lynch mean by 'pulling out the flowers and watering the weeds'?
Answers: Selling winning stocks too early while holding onto losing stocks - a common and expensive mistake he made early on.

Questions: Which great stocks did Lynch sell too early?
Answers: Albertson's (300-bagger), Toys 'R' Us, Pic 'N' Save, Warner Communications, Federal Express ($5 to $70 in two years), and Home Depot.

Questions: How did Lynch learn about companies in his early years?
Answers: He visited dozens at headquarters, attended regional investment conferences, and companies came to Fidelity for lunches, breakfasts, and dinners.

Questions: What was Fidelity's policy of 'taking a corporation to lunch'?
Answers: This replaced lunches with cronies - every week they had printed menus of corporate guests, enabling access to hundreds of companies annually.

Questions: Why was Boston advantageous for seeing companies?
Answers: As the mutual fund capital, executives could make rounds of multiple firms in one trip, and both sides initiated these educational exchanges.

Questions: What was Lynch's monthly rule for industry contact?
Answers: Once a month he tried to have at least one conversation with a representative of each major industry group as an early-warning system.

Questions: What question did Lynch always ask at the end of company meetings?
Answers: Which of your competitors do you respect the most? When a CEO admits a rival is doing better, it's a powerful endorsement.

Questions: What does Lynch say about being lied to in corporate meetings?
Answers: In thousands of encounters, he was lied to only a handful of times - there may be fewer liars on Wall Street than Main Street.

Questions: Why are there fewer liars on Wall Street according to Lynch?
Answers: Financial types are so widely distrusted that every claim is reviewed by the SEC, so they aren't allowed to lie, and lies can't survive quarterly earnings reports.

Questions: How did Lynch learn about the insurance industry?
Answers: Through crash courses from executives at Aetna, Travelers, and Connecticut General in Hartford over a couple of days.

Questions: What was Lynch's insurance allocation in March 1980?
Answers: 25.4% of the fund was in property or casualty underwriters, making him insurance's best friend.

Questions: How did Lynch discover the potential in bank stocks?
Answers: At a Robinson-Humphrey conference in Atlanta, he took a side trip to visit First Atlanta, which had 12 years of continuously higher earnings.

Questions: What impressed Lynch about regional banks?
Answers: First Atlanta had earnings greater than the sales of many flashy companies, yet solid banks were selling for half the P/E ratio of the market.

Questions: Which banks does Lynch show as examples of great performance?
Answers: Wachovia (10-fold increase in 10 years), Norwest of Minneapolis, and NBD Bancorp of Detroit - all looking like fast-growth company charts.

Questions: Why are regional banks mispriced according to Lynch?
Answers: Banks growing at 15% like Pep Boys or Dunkin' Donuts get low P/E multiples, treated like mature utilities instead of growth companies.

Questions: What was Magellan's bank allocation strategy?
Answers: Lynch consistently had four or five times the market weighting in bank stocks due to these mispricings.

Questions: What was Lynch's bond strategy in early 1982?
Answers: With Treasury bonds paying 13-14%, Lynch made them his biggest position because yields exceeded normal stock returns.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #8?
Answers: When yields on long-term government bonds exceed the dividend yield of the S&P 500 by 6% or more, sell your stocks and buy bonds.

Questions: Why doesn't Lynch recommend preparing for total disaster?
Answers: If total disaster strikes, cash will be as useless as stock certificates, but if it doesn't (more likely), the 'cautious' become reckless by selling valuable assets.

Questions: How did Lynch approach the 1982 recession fears?
Answers: He focused on the Even Bigger Picture, assumed the worst wouldn't happen, and asked what would happen if it didn't - leading him to both stocks and bonds.

Questions: What led Lynch to Chrysler in March 1982?
Answers: He got interested in Ford as an auto rebound play, and talking to Ford convinced him Chrysler would benefit even more.

Questions: Why was Chrysler selling for only $2 in 1982?
Answers: Wall Street expected the number-three automaker to go bankrupt like Penn Central, but Lynch found over $1 billion in cash on the balance sheet.

Questions: What convinced Lynch that Chrysler could survive?
Answers: The company had capacity to survive at least a couple of years, the government had guaranteed loans, and the entire industry was due for a rebound.

Questions: What new products excited Lynch about Chrysler's future?
Answers: The Dodge Daytona, Chrysler Laser, G-124 Turbo Car, convertibles, sportier New Yorker, and especially the T-115 minivan.

Questions: What did Iacocca call 'the first new thing in the auto industry in twenty years'?
Answers: The T-115, which became the Chrysler minivan and sold over 3 million copies in nine years, saving the company.

Questions: What time did Lynch's working day begin?
Answers: Lynch's working day began at 6:05 A.M. when he met his carpool ride with radiologists Jeff and Bobbie Moore.

Questions: What was Lynch doing during his carpool ride?
Answers: Lynch sat in the back with a small light, perusing annual reports and chart books, while Bobbie held X-rays up to a light in the front seat.

Questions: What time did Lynch arrive at the office?
Answers: By 6:45 A.M., but he wasn't alone - Fidelity was full of analysts and fund managers who arrived before dawn.

Questions: What were Lynch's 'sophisticated tools of the trade'?
Answers: The S&P stock guide (free from brokers), antique Rolodex, empty yellow legal pads, 21⁄2 pencils, and clunky Sharp calculator with oversize buttons.

Questions: Why did Lynch prefer the old Quotron system?
Answers: The blank screen was better because you couldn't stare at it all day watching stocks go up and down - he had to turn off the newer versions.

Questions: What did Lynch do in the precious morning hours before market opened?
Answers: Reviewed buy/sell summaries from the day before, read in-house analyst reports, read Wall Street Journal, and wrote out new buy/sell lists.

Questions: Who were Lynch's head traders?
Answers: Barry Lyden handled buys, and later Carlene DeLuca was assigned to handle sells, both very patient with Lynch's extensive trading lists.

Questions: How much time did Lynch spend on trading?
Answers: About an hour a day instead of 10 minutes - he admits he should have used the extra 50 minutes to call two more companies.

Questions: What is Lynch's key insight about successful investing?
Answers: Focus on the companies, not on the stocks - this is one of the keys to successful investing.

Questions: How did Lynch keep track of his company contacts?
Answers: He wrote down the name of everyone he met and kept detailed notes in loose-leaf binders with company names, stock prices, and story summaries.

Questions: Why did Lynch avoid the lobby when going to the bathroom?
Answers: Corporate guests and analysts waited there, and he'd have to waste time on small talk or snub friends, so he snuck down a back stairway.

Questions: Who was Lynch's first assistant and what happened to him?
Answers: Rich Fentin set the standard for quality and went on to run the Fidelity Growth and Fidelity Puritan funds.

Questions: What other successful fund managers came from Lynch's assistant program?
Answers: Danny Frank (Special Situations), George Noble (Overseas Fund), Bob Stansky (Growth), Will Danoff (Contrafund), and Jeff Vinik (later ran Magellan).

Questions: What was revolutionary about Fidelity's research approach?
Answers: Fund managers were required to do their own research rather than relying on analysts' recommendations, making them accountable for results.

Questions: How did Fidelity's system differ from traditional fund management?
Answers: Traditional managers choose stocks from analyst recommendations and blame analysts when stocks fail; Fidelity managers did independent research.

Questions: What advantage did Lynch have as a capital appreciation fund manager?
Answers: He had the widest latitude to buy stocks recommended by special situations, small-stock, growth, value, and over-the-counter specialists.

Questions: How did Fidelity formalize information sharing?
Answers: Random hallway powwows were replaced by scheduled conference room meetings where all analysts and fund managers presented weekly picks.

Questions: What was Lynch's innovation with the kitchen timer?
Answers: He pretended to set it at three minutes for presentations but actually shortened it to 90 seconds to keep discussions focused.

Questions: Why were the presentations non-combative?
Answers: Combat isn't the best way to arrive at truth about stocks; hostile receptions might undermine confidence in future recommendations.

Questions: What was Lynch's approach to feedback at presentations?
Answers: No feedback was allowed - listeners could follow up on leads or ignore them, focusing on idea quality rather than speaker quality.

Questions: How did fund managers share information with competitors?
Answers: They eagerly shared buy lists with each other after acquiring their planned positions, with competitors returning the favor.

Questions: How did Lynch evaluate outside analysts?
Answers: He was selective, noting great variation in quality and preferring analysts who called companies regularly and visited them in person.

Questions: Who were some of Lynch's trusted outside analysts?
Answers: Maggie Gilliam at First Boston (Home Depot, Limited), John Kellenyi at NatWest (utilities), Elliot Schneider at Gruntal (financial services).

Questions: What made certain analysts valuable to Lynch?
Answers: Analysts who reinforced opinions with multiple reports as stocks rose, not just initial buy signals that were quickly forgotten.

Questions: How did Lynch's patience change by 1981?
Answers: He became more patient, redemptions were down so he wasn't forced to sell for cash, and turnover dropped from 300% to 110%.

Questions: What was Magellan's size and ranking in 1981?
Answers: $100 million in assets, putting it in the bottom fifth of all general equity funds, with 200 different stocks.

Questions: What types of companies did Lynch favor in 1981?
Answers: John Blair (broadcaster), Tandy (Radio Shack), Quixote (plastic barriers), Telecredit, ChemLawn, Seven Oaks (coupon processor), various restaurant chains.

Questions: Why was Lynch impressed with restaurant chains and retailers?
Answers: By expanding across the country, these companies could maintain 20% growth rates for 10-15 years with favorable math.

Questions: What is the Rule of 72?
Answers: Divide 72 by the annual return percentage to get the number of years it takes to double your money.

Questions: Why did Lynch prefer retailers and restaurants over high-tech companies?
Answers: They were less risky - a computer company can lose half its value overnight, but a donut chain won't lose business when a competitor opens in another state.

Questions: What was Lynch's biggest holding at the end of 1981?
Answers: Mattel, the toy maker, which was 3% of the fund.

Questions: What characterized Lynch's top 10 holdings in early 1982?
Answers: Companies like Chemical Bank, Pic 'N' Save, Verbatim, Horn & Hardart, and Pep Boys - strong balance sheets with favorable prospects.

Questions: Why could Lynch buy offbeat companies like Seven Oaks?
Answers: In a wide-open fund like Magellan, nobody was looking over his shoulder, unlike managers subject to hierarchical second-guessing.

Questions: What does Lynch say about professional responsibility and monitoring?
Answers: When you have to worry about what someone behind you thinks, you cease to be professional and doubt your ability to succeed.

Questions: What luxury did Lynch have by 1982?
Answers: Instead of selling one stock to buy another, new money was pouring in at $40-71 million per month, allowing him to maintain old positions while initiating new ones.

Questions: How did Lynch's stock focus change as Magellan grew?
Answers: Ironically, when Magellan was small he concentrated on bigger stocks, and when it became bigger he found himself concentrating on smaller stocks.

Questions: What happened to Magellan's popularity in 1983?
Answers: Another $76 million in February, $100 million in March had to be invested, making fund growth and stock selection increasingly challenging.

Questions: Why was Lynch depressed by the early 1983 market?
Answers: The Dow had advanced 300 points from 1982 lows, technology issues reached giddy heights - he preferred corrections that created bargains.

Questions: What does Lynch say about bargains and market sell-offs?
Answers: Bargains are the holy grail of the true stockpicker; corrections are opportunities to acquire more shares at low prices, not disasters.

Questions: What remained Lynch's biggest holding through 1983?
Answers: Chrysler remained at 5% of the fund (SEC maximum) and stayed his biggest holding for most of the year.

Questions: When did Magellan hit the $1 billion milestone?
Answers: April 1983, which elicited a 'great ho-hum' at the office, soon followed by criticism that it was too big to succeed.

Questions: What was the structure of Lynch's day by the mid-1980s?
Answers: 6:05 AM carpool, 6:45 arrival, morning preparation, trading orders by 8 AM, then constant phone calls and company research until late.

Questions: How many companies did Lynch visit annually?
Answers: His visits escalated from 214 in 1980 to 330 in 1982, 489 in 1983, 411 in 1984, 463 in 1985, and 570 in 1986.

Questions: What was Lynch's approach to corporate lunches as Magellan grew?
Answers: He cut back on lunches in favor of more efficient phone calls while eating sandwiches, having developed enough sources from earlier lunches.

Questions: How did Lynch's office setup facilitate his work style?
Answers: Four secretaries led by Paula Sullivan routed calls, chairs had become file cabinets so visitors couldn't sit, forcing brief interactions.

Questions: What was Lynch's rule about keeping up with companies?
Answers: He kept detailed notebooks of every contact with companies, including stock prices and story summaries, essential for tracking hundreds of investments.

Questions: How did Lynch use his Saturday work time?
Answers: Devoted to cleaning his desk, reviewing three-foot-high stacks of mail, perusing annual reports in February/March, and reviewing company notebooks.

Questions: What was Lynch's Saturday goal?
Answers: To see some wood (desktop) at the end of the afternoon, though he didn't always achieve it.

Questions: How did Lynch handle the terrible first half of 1982?
Answers: Prime rate hit double digits along with inflation and unemployment; he bought Treasury bonds paying 13-14% as his biggest position.

Questions: Why did Lynch buy bonds in 1982?
Answers: Not for defensive purposes due to fear of stocks, but because bond yields exceeded normal expected returns from stocks.

Questions: What convinced Lynch not to prepare for total economic collapse?
Answers: If the economy collapsed, he'd be fishing with everyone else and portfolio strategy would be irrelevant; if not, he wanted to be in stocks and bonds.

Questions: How did Lynch approach the 1982 recession?
Answers: He assumed the worst wouldn't happen and asked 'what then?' - figuring interest rates had to come down and both stocks and bonds would profit.

Questions: How does Lynch describe the relationship between research time and number of stocks owned?
Answers: How much time you spend researching stocks is directly proportional to how many stocks you own. It takes a few hours a year to keep up with each one.

Questions: How many stocks did Magellan have by mid-1983 and fall 1983?
Answers: By mid-1983 there were 450 stocks, and by fall the number had doubled to 900 stocks in the portfolio.

Questions: What was Magellan's size ranking by end of 1983?
Answers: Magellan was running a close second to John Neff's Vanguard Windsor as the largest mutual fund, with $1.6 billion in assets.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #9?
Answers: Not all common stocks are equally common.

Questions: How does Lynch defend having 900 stocks in the portfolio?
Answers: An imaginative fund manager can pick 1,000+ stocks in unusual companies that will never appear in standard Wall Street portfolios, 'flying off the radar scope.'

Questions: What percentage of Magellan's 900 stocks in 1983 were tiny positions?
Answers: 700 of the 900 stocks accounted for less than 10% of the fund's total assets.

Questions: What were Lynch's two reasons for taking tiny positions?
Answers: 1) Companies were quite small, so even owning 10% didn't amount to much, or 2) He wasn't convinced they deserved substantial commitment.

Questions: How did the Jan Bell Marketing meeting lead to a major opportunity?
Answers: Jan Bell executives mentioned their best customers were discount clubs ordering tremendous jewelry, leading Lynch to invest in Costco, Wholesale Club, and Pace.

Questions: What was Will Danoff's role in the discount club discovery?
Answers: Lynch asked Danoff, the retail analyst who later took over Contrafund, to research the discount clubs after the Jan Bell tip.

Questions: Why were discount club stocks available at bargain prices?
Answers: After IPO euphoria faded, expectations were too lofty, stocks sold off, and Wall Street lost interest with no analysts following them.

Questions: What were the results from Lynch's discount club investments?
Answers: All three made money - Costco was a triple, proving the value of following up on unexpected leads.

Questions: How many S&Ls did Lynch buy in April 1983?
Answers: 39 of his 83 new acquisitions in April 1983 were banks or S&Ls, eventually totaling 100 S&Ls making 3% of the fund.

Questions: What was Lynch's approach to building positions in auto stocks?
Answers: He made what's known as an 'industry bet' by analyzing each company case-by-case rather than arbitrarily deciding on 8% auto allocation.

Questions: Which auto companies did Lynch favor over General Motors and why?
Answers: Ford, Chrysler, and Volvo because GM was arrogant, myopic, and resting on laurels - saying it was miserable was about the nicest compliment you could give GM.

Questions: What were the profits from Lynch's major auto positions?
Answers: Well over $100 million each from Ford and Chrysler, plus $79 million from Volvo over the six-year stretch from 1982-1988.

Questions: What was the key to Magellan's superior results according to Lynch?
Answers: Huge gains in a few huge positions, not diversification across many small positions.

Questions: How does Lynch respond to concerns about 'liquidity' in stock selection?
Answers: In stocks as in romance, ease of divorce is not a sound basis for commitment - if you've chosen wisely, you won't want a divorce.

Questions: What examples does Lynch give of liquid stocks that still lost money?
Answers: Polaroid (lost 90% in 1973) and Xerox - both were actively traded and easy to sell, but fund managers still lost money by not wanting to get out.

Questions: What percentage of stocks trade fewer than 10,000 shares daily?
Answers: 99% of all stocks trade fewer than 10,000 shares daily, so liquidity-focused managers confine themselves to only 1% of all companies.

Questions: How did Lynch acquire large positions in some stocks?
Answers: Occasionally through large institutional blocks (2 million shares of Owens-Corning, 2 million of BankAmerica), but usually through constant nibbling over months.

Questions: What determined Lynch's vacation destinations?
Answers: Time zones and phone booth locations - Austria was good because it was afternoon there before U.S. markets opened.

Questions: Where was Lynch's favorite U.S. ski location and why?
Answers: Balsam's in Dixville Notch, New Hampshire, because it had a phone at the bottom of the lift for calling in trades.

Questions: When did Lynch begin investing heavily in foreign stocks?
Answers: Foreign buying began in earnest in 1984, with Lynch being the first domestic fund manager after John Templeton to invest heavily abroad.

Questions: What percentage of Magellan was in foreign stocks by 1986?
Answers: 10% of Magellan's assets were invested in foreign equities by 1986.

Questions: What was Lynch's most successful research trip?
Answers: Mid-September 1985: three weeks, 23 companies across Europe, leading to over $200 million in profits from foreign stock picks.

Questions: What happened to Lynch's luggage on the European trip?
Answers: Sabena airline lost his luggage, but he was outfitted in a proper Swedish suit by his host's husband who had his exact measurements.

Questions: What companies did Lynch visit in Sweden?
Answers: Esselte (office equipment), ASEA (conglomerate), Alfa Laval (milking machines/biogenetics), Electrolux (appliances), Aga (gases), Ericsson (telephones), Skandia (insurance).

Questions: What made Skandia an attractive investment?
Answers: A rate increase had been approved which should have boosted the stock, but Swedish investors ignored good news and focused on lousy current earnings.

Questions: What was special about Lynch's Volvo discovery?
Answers: The stock price was $34 and the company had $34 per share in cash, so he was getting the auto business and subsidiaries for nothing.

Questions: What lesson did Lynch learn about driving on the German autobahn?
Answers: Peter's Principle #10: Never look back when you're driving on the autobahn - he found a Mercedes three inches from his bumper at 120 mph.

Questions: Why couldn't Lynch visit Sandoz in Switzerland?
Answers: When he called to arrange a meeting, the vice-president kept asking 'Why?' to every explanation until Lynch gave up and said goodbye.

Questions: What Italian companies did Lynch visit?
Answers: Montedison (hydroelectric), IFI, and Olivetti, plus he saw The Last Supper - listing all four as his favorite northern Italian attractions.

Questions: What was Lynch's insight about Italy in 1985?
Answers: Italy was like America in the 1940s-50s - a place where appliance companies, electric companies, and supermarkets would be future fast growers.

Questions: What were Lynch's top eleven foreign stock gains?
Answers: Peugeot, Volvo, Skandia, Esselte, Electrolux, Aga, Norsk Hydro, Montedison, IFI, Tobu Railway, and Kinki Nippon Railway made over $200 million in profits.

Questions: Which was Lynch's biggest foreign stock winner?
Answers: Tobu Railway with 386% gain in five years, though it was only 0.13% of Magellan's assets.

Questions: When did Magellan pass the $5 billion mark?
Answers: February 1986, requiring Lynch to buy more Ford, Chrysler, and Volvo to maintain their weightings.

Questions: What was Lynch's experience calling trades from Yosemite?
Answers: Standing in a phone booth overlooking mountains, he spent two hours giving trades and only got from A's through L's in his alphabetical holdings list.

Questions: What happened to Carlene DeLuca?
Answers: She left the trading desk to marry Fidelity's former president Jack O'Brien; on her last day they let her do buys instead of sells.

Questions: What major tactical shift did Lynch make in 1987?
Answers: He began deemphasizing autos and upgrading financial companies, particularly Fannie Mae and S&Ls, as the economic recovery matured.

Questions: When did Magellan become a $10 billion fund?
Answers: May 1987, providing more ammunition for critics saying it was too big to beat the market.

Questions: What kept Lynch motivated despite the 'too big' criticism?
Answers: Skeptics said $1B, $2B, $4B, $6B, $8B, and $10B were all too big, and he was determined to prove them wrong.

Questions: What is Peter's Principle #12?
Answers: A sure cure for taking a stock for granted is a big drop in the price.

Questions: How did Magellan perform during market declines vs. rebounds?
Answers: During nine major declines, Magellan fell more than the market average, but outperformed on the rebound - a consistent pattern.

Questions: What was Lynch's approach to preparing shareholders for volatility?
Answers: He warned in annual reports of Magellan's tendency to get swamped in choppy waters, believing preparation prevents panic.

Questions: How did the Great Correction affect Magellan's size?
Answers: What was an $11 billion fund in August became a $7.2 billion fund by October - the GNP of Costa Rica was lost in a week.

Questions: What forced Lynch to sell during the 1987 crash?
Answers: $689 million in sales and $1.3 billion in redemptions in October, forcing him to be a seller when he'd prefer to be a buyer.

Questions: What lesson does Lynch draw about shareholders and fund performance?
Answers: Shareholders play a major role in success or failure - if they refuse to panic, fund managers won't have to liquidate at unfavorable prices.
