Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Morris County Savings Bank example?
Answers: Initial offering 1983 at $10.75/share, bought out three years later for $65 - excellent return for shareholders.

Questions: How did you approach S&L investing during this period?
Answers: He was so indiscriminate that he bought anything with 'first' or 'trust' in the name, investing in 135 of 145 thrifts whose prospectuses reached his desk.

Questions: What were your two explanations for his S&L attraction?
Answers: 1) Fund was so big and S&Ls so small he needed large quantities like whales surviving on plankton, 2) Unique way S&Ls came public made them automatic bargains.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what created the perfect atmosphere for S&L bargains in 1992?
Answers: S&L fraud story off front pages, replaced by housing market collapse fears, yet National Association of Home Builders showed median home prices still rising.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why had Wall Street lost interest in S&L coverage?
Answers: Fidelity's Select S&L Fund dwindled from $66M (Feb 1987) to $3M (Oct 1990), brokerage houses reduced or stopped coverage entirely.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many analysts track different types of companies?
Answers: Nearly 50 analysts track Wal-Mart, 46 track Philip Morris, but only a few devote themselves to publicly traded S&Ls.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #18?
Answers: When even the analysts are bored, it's time to start buying.

Questions: What publication did you use for S&L research?
Answers: The Thrift Digest, published by SNL Securities, thick as Boston phone directory, costs $700/year for monthly updates.

Questions: What are the key factors in your S&L scorecard?
Answers: Current price, initial offering price, equity-to-assets ratio, dividend, book value, P/E ratio, high-risk real estate assets, 90-day nonperforming assets, real estate owned.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the most important number for S&L analysis?
Answers: Equity-to-Assets ratio - measures financial strength and survivability. Higher is better, with 5.5-6% average, below 5% danger zone.

Questions: What E/A ratio does you prefer before investing?
Answers: At least 7.5% E/A ratio for disaster protection and because high E/A makes attractive takeover candidate.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are high-risk real estate assets problematic?
Answers: Commercial and construction loans have been ruination of many S&Ls. When high-risk assets exceed 5-10%, Lynch gets nervous.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are 90-day nonperforming assets?
Answers: Loans that have already defaulted. Want very low number, preferably less than 2% of S&L's total assets, and falling not rising.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Real Estate Owned (REO)?
Answers: Property on which S&L has foreclosed - index of yesterday's problems since it's been written off, but worrisome when rising.

Questions: How many S&Ls did you end up recommending in Barron's?
Answers: Seven S&Ls: five strong Jimmy Stewart types and two long shots (born-agains) coming back from Chapter 11 edge.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what made the five Jimmy Stewart S&Ls attractive?
Answers: Excellent marks in book value (four at discount), E/A ratio (all 6.0+), high-risk loans (under 10%), delinquencies (2% or less), REO (under 1%), P/E (below 11).

Questions: Why did you pick two 'born-again' S&Ls despite poor numbers?
Answers: They maintained high E/A ratios despite problems, giving leeway to work out troubles, and stock prices had fallen so low that survival meant big gains.

Questions: What is an example of your bottom-fishing approach?
Answers: Lawrence Savings fell from $13 to 75 cents - if it survived, bottom fishers would make substantial money.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how do commercial banks benefit from acquiring strong S&Ls?
Answers: Banks can take deposits only in home states but lend anywhere, so acquiring S&L with excess equity and deposits provides valuable lending capacity.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many banks and deposit takers does the U.S. have compared to need?
Answers: More than 7,000 banks, thrifts, and deposit takers - about 6,500 too many (Lynch's town of Marblehead has 6, half the number in all of England).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what will drive continued S&L consolidation?
Answers: Banks and thrifts will consolidate rapidly because there are far too many institutions, and strong ones with excess capacity make attractive acquisition targets.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what could casual S&L stockpickers do without detailed research?
Answers: Pick five S&Ls fitting the Jimmy Stewart profile, invest equally in each, and await favorable returns - one better than expected, three OK, one worse.

Questions: Why do you usually call companies before investing?
Answers: To improve odds by finding specific information or fishing for surprises that haven't come to Wall Street analysts' attention.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what basic knowledge do you need to talk to an S&L?
Answers: How the business works: needs loyal depositors, must make money on that money by lending (but not to defaulters), needs low operating expenses.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the bankers' favorite saying about their business model?
Answers: Bankers like to live on threes and sixes: borrow money at 3, lend money at 6, play golf at 3.

Questions: How many S&Ls did you call for his detailed research?
Answers: Six S&Ls: four strong ones plus two born-agains (he didn't call Eagle Financial because annual report arrived in time).

Questions: When did you call Glacier Bancorp and what was he wearing?
Answers: Day after Christmas, wearing plaid pants and sweatshirt in the empty Fidelity building except for security guard.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are holidays excellent times for research calls?
Answers: Lynch is always impressed when he finds executives sitting at their desks on December 26, showing dedication.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Glacier Bancorp formerly called?
Answers: First Federal Savings and Loan of Kalispell - Lynch wishes they'd kept the antiquated, parochial name.

Questions: Why do you prefer antiquated names over trendy ones?
Answers: He'd rather have antiquated and parochial than trendy and sophisticated, which usually means desperate to improve image.

Questions: What is your concern about 'bancorp' vs 'bank' names?
Answers: He knows what a bank is, but 'bancorp' makes him nervous - prefers companies that stick to business and let images take care of themselves.

Questions: How do you establish rapport before asking serious questions?
Answers: Started with mountains, mentioned family trips to Western states and national parks, discussed timber industry, spotted owl, ski areas.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Glacier's impressive loan loss record?
Answers: In all of 1991, had to write off only $16,000 in bad loans - almost nonexistent nonperforming loans.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how has Glacier been growing through acquisitions?
Answers: Just bought First National Banks of Whitefish and Eureka, acquiring valuable deposits to make more loans with additional capacity.

Questions: What was your concern about Glacier's 9.2% commercial loans?
Answers: In New England that would be scary, but Montana wasn't Massachusetts - mostly multifamily housing in growing area with California escapees.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who did Glacier's chairman recommend as other strong S&Ls?
Answers: United Savings and Security Federal, both Montana thrifts with impressive equity-to-assets ratios (20% at Security Federal).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Germantown Savings' key financial metrics?
Answers: $10 stock earning $2/share (P/E under 7), book value $26, equity-to-assets ratio 7.5%, less than 1% nonperforming loans.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Germantown notable from a Wall Street perspective?
Answers: $1.4 billion in assets with wonderful record, yet not a single brokerage firm bothered to cover the story.

Questions: What did you find in Germantown's balance sheet analysis?
Answers: Deposits up (customers keeping money there), loans down (bankers being conservative), investment securities up $50M (parking assets in bonds).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Germantown's CEO Martin Kleppe say about their story?
Answers: 'We have a very boring story. We also have a fortress balance sheet. When we get in trouble, other guys are walking the plank.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how was Germantown positioned for economic improvement?
Answers: When economy improves and it's safe to lend, they'll sell investment securities and make more loans, causing surge in earnings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sovereign Bancorp's dividend strategy?
Answers: Pays 8% dividend beginning immediately, and the bell goes off in branches every time a mortgage loan is approved.

Questions: How did you learn about Sovereign Bancorp?
Answers: Through November 25, 1991 Barron's article entitled 'Hometown Lender to the Well-Heeled' about serving wealthy southeastern Pennsylvania.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sovereign's growth strategy according to CEO Jay Sidhu?
Answers: Determined to 'grow' business by at least 12% annually, using Golden West as model for success.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why had Sovereign sold additional shares in 1991?
Answers: Used proceeds to buy troubled thrifts from Resolution Trust rather than squandering money, though this diluted existing shares.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sovereign's loan strategy vs traditional S&Ls?
Answers: Specialized in making loans then selling them to Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac for quick money recovery and up-front fees, transferring ownership risk.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what lending standards did Sovereign maintain?
Answers: Devoted to residential mortgages, no commercial loans since 1989, average loan didn't exceed 69% of property value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what sneaky practice did Sidhu describe for camouflaging problem loans?
Answers: Banks offer borrowers more than requested based on inflated appraisals, hold excess in reserve to cover payments if borrower defaults, keeping bad loans appearing good temporarily.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was People's Savings Financial's competitive advantage?
Answers: Advertised security with 13% equity-to-assets ratio as weak banks failed, growing deposits from $220M (1990) to $242M (1991).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how had People's Savings enhanced shareholder value?
Answers: Bought back 16% of shares in two phases, spending $4.4M - making remaining shares scarce and valuable.

Questions: Why do you prefer share buybacks over acquisitions for enhancing value?
Answers: Share buybacks are simplest, most direct way to reward shareholders, while companies often squander money on fanciful acquisitions instead.

Questions: What examples does you give of successful buyback strategies?
Answers: International Dairy Queen and Crown Cork & Seal became spectacular performers because management committed to buying back shares - that's how Teledyne became 100-bagger.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did People's Savings first go public and at what price?
Answers: 1986 at $10.25 per share, five years later selling for $11 despite being bigger, more profitable with fewer shares outstanding.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what depressed People's Savings stock price?
Answers: Operating in Connecticut, a depressed state - Lynch prefers S&Ls proven to survive in depressed states over those thriving in booming economies.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the source of People's Savings' nonperforming loans?
Answers: Most of 2% problem caused by single construction loan; company wasn't making new loans of this type.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how long does the foreclosure process take according to Medvec?
Answers: May take two years to oust defaulting borrower - drawn-out and expensive process.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was First Essex's frightening financial situation?
Answers: 10% nonperforming assets, 3.5% real estate owned, 13% commercial/construction loans, lost $11M (1989) and $28M (1990).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did First Essex CEO Leonard Wilson describe their situation?
Answers: 'Bottom fishing with a six-hundred-foot line' - facing procession of foreclosures, owning unoccupied buildings nobody wanted.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was First Essex's equity cushion for survival?
Answers: $46M equity vs $46M commercial loans - if 50% of remaining commercial loans went bad, would lose 50% equity but still survive.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Lawrence Savings' riskier position compared to First Essex?
Answers: $55M commercial loans vs only $27M equity, and 21% of portfolio in commercial real estate vs First Essex's 13%.

Questions: How do you analyze long-shot S&Ls?
Answers: Find equity amount, compare to commercial loans outstanding, assume the worst - if half go bad, does S&L survive?

Questions: What is the 'can't-lose proposition' you describes about S&L IPOs?
Answers: Like buying a house and finding former owners left your down payment money in kitchen drawer with note 'Keep this, it belonged to you anyway.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how do S&L public offerings differ from other IPOs?
Answers: Every dollar raised (minus fees) returns to S&L's vault as equity, unlike other companies where founders take money and buy palazzos.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happens to book value when mutual S&L goes public?
Answers: If S&L had $10M book value, sells $10M stock (1M shares at $10), the $10M returns to vault, doubling book value to $20 while stock sells for $10.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many mutual S&Ls have yet to go public?
Answers: 1,178 S&Ls have yet to take this step, providing many more chances for investors to be surprised.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the 1991 mutual thrift IPO results?
Answers: 16 came public: 2 taken over at 4x+ offering price, worst performer up 87%, all others doubled or better, including one 10-bagger.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the 1992 mutual thrift conversion results?
Answers: 42 came public: only 1 loser (down 7.5%), all others advanced, 38 up 50%+, 23 up 100%+ in just 20 months.

Questions: What examples does you give of outstanding 1992 mutual thrift performance?
Answers: Mutual Savings Bank of Bay City, Michigan and United Postal Bancorp in St. Louis both quadrupled in value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did even the worst 1992 mutual thrift performers do?
Answers: Portfolio of five worst performers produced 31% return, beating S&P 500 and most equity mutual funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were early 1993 mutual thrift results through nine months?
Answers: 34 came public: worst up 5%, 26 up 30%+, 20 up 40%+, 9 up 50%+ in shorter period.

Questions: What is your advice about participating in local S&L conversions?
Answers: Open savings account in any mutual savings bank in your area to get right to participate in IPO when it happens.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many mutual savings banks haven't yet converted?
Answers: 1,372 mutual savings banks have not yet come public - check if any are in your area.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what can investors do while waiting for conversions?
Answers: Sit back and await developments after opening accounts, getting all information needed to make informed decisions when IPO happens.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what makes these local S&L investments particularly attractive?
Answers: Ultimate example of how individuals can succeed by investigating what's close to home rather than widely-held institutional stocks.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are Master Limited Partnerships being ignored by Wall Street?
Answers: The name 'limited partnership' brings back memories of tax-shelter boondoggles where losses far exceeded tax savings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what types of partnerships caused the bad publicity?
Answers: Oil and gas partnerships, real-estate partnerships, movie partnerships, farming partnerships, and gravesite partnerships where investors lost money.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how do Master Limited Partnerships differ from tax shelter partnerships?
Answers: MLPs are ongoing enterprises whose purpose is to make money, not lose it to outsmart the IRS.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many MLPs trade on stock exchanges?
Answers: More than 100 MLPs trade on various stock exchanges.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what extra requirement do MLP shareholders face?
Answers: Special tax forms have to be prepared, though the investor relations department fills in all the blanks.

Questions: Why do you welcome the MLP paperwork requirement?
Answers: The nuisance dissuades many investors, particularly fund managers, keeping prices down and creating bargains.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what types of activities are MLPs typically involved in?
Answers: Down-to-earth activities like playing basketball (Boston Celtics), pumping oil and gas, janitorial services (ServiceMaster), auto parts (Sun Distributors), amusement parks (Cedar Fair).

Questions: What is appealing about MLP names in your investment approach?
Answers: Names seem antiquated and out of sync with high-tech culture - Cedar Fair could be from Thackeray, Green Acres from Jane Austen.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what type of investor is attracted to MLPs?
Answers: Takes an imaginative person attracted to romantic names, mundane activities, and complicated structure requiring extra paperwork - a small minority reaps rewards.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the biggest difference between MLPs and regular corporations?
Answers: MLPs distribute ALL earnings to shareholders, either as dividends or return of capital, with unusually high dividends.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what tax advantage do MLPs offer?
Answers: Return of capital feature allows certain percentage of annual distribution to be exempt from federal tax.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did most MLPs come onto the scene?
Answers: First appeared in 1981, majority appeared in 1986 after tax law changes made this organization form more advantageous.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happens to MLPs in 1997-98?
Answers: All except real estate and natural resource partnerships must be closed out as they lose tax benefits - earnings might drop from $1.80 to $1.20.

Questions: What brought EQK Green Acres to your attention?
Answers: The stock dropped during Saddam Sell-off from $13.75 high to $9.75, offering 13.5% yield - as good as junk bonds but more secure.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what does EQK stand for and who are the partners?
Answers: EQ comes from Equitable Life Assurance Society, K stands for Kravco - partners in this enterprise.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is EQK Green Acres' principal asset?
Answers: Its huge enclosed mall on Long Island, situated in densely populated Nassau County.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many people live within five miles of Green Acres mall?
Answers: 750,000 insiders on Long Island - showing how many people could have discovered this investment opportunity.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are enclosed malls attractive investments?
Answers: Only 450 exist in entire country, not many new ones being built, would face zoning problems and need 92 empty acres for parking.

Questions: What was your key concern about any mall investment?
Answers: Vacancies - malls averaged 4% vacancy rate while Green Acres was lower.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what positive developments were occurring at Green Acres?
Answers: Waldbaum's supermarket and Pergament Home Center moving in, one-third of stores subject to large rent increases in 1992-93.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the worrisome elements about Green Acres?
Answers: Highly leveraged balance sheet (company must pay back all debts in 1997), high P/E ratio, vulnerability to recession.

Questions: What warning sign did you see in Green Acres' third-quarter 1991 report?
Answers: Company was debating whether to pay regular quarterly dividend increase of one cent to save $100,000 - breaking 13-quarter string for paltry savings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what potential good news was Green Acres negotiating?
Answers: Potential agreements with Sears and J.C. Penney to lease space in second floor expansion - though not yet signed contracts.

Questions: Why didn't you recommend Green Acres for a second time?
Answers: Potential agreements weren't signed contracts - he preferred waiting for proof rather than buying on rumors.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what owns and operates Cedar Fair's amusement parks?
Answers: Cedar Point on Ohio shore of Lake Erie and Valley Fair in Minnesota, open May to Labor Day plus fall weekends.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many roller coasters does Cedar Point have?
Answers: 10 different roller coasters, including Magnum (highest drop in world) and Mean Streak (highest wooden roller coaster in world).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what historical significance does Cedar Point have?
Answers: 120th year of operation, had roller coasters for 100 years, seven U.S. presidents visited, Knute Rockne had summer jobs and invented forward pass there.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are amusement parks protected from competition?
Answers: Nobody will sneak up and install $500 million worth of rides on Lake Erie shores - unlike electronics where new products can destroy competitors overnight.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many people live within three hours of Cedar Point?
Answers: About 6 million people, providing a substantial customer base for the amusement park.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Cedar Fair's stock performance in 1991?
Answers: Rose from $11.50 to $18, which with dividend gave shareholders over 60% one-year return.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why might amusement parks benefit from recession?
Answers: People might forgo summer trip to France in favor of staying at Cedar Point Hotel and riding world's highest roller coaster.

Questions: What did you ask about Cedar Fair's 1992 prospects?
Answers: He looks for reasons next year will be better than last - if he can't find such reason, he questions why own the stock.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was missing from Cedar Fair's 1992 outlook?
Answers: No major new attractions like previous years' new roller coasters - attendance usually drops year after new ride introduced.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what does Sun Distributors sell?
Answers: Auto glass, sheet glass, insulated glass, cables, mirrors, windshield glass, fasteners, ball bearings, hydraulic systems to builders and auto repair shops.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Sun Distributors being ignored by Wall Street?
Answers: Activities put business school graduates to sleep, financial analysts would rather count ceiling tiles than follow auto parts company.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who was the lone analyst covering Sun Distributors?
Answers: Karen Payne of Wheat First Securities, but her April 1990 report was apparently her last.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what complicated Sun Distributors' structure?
Answers: Two classes of shares: Class A (big dividend), Class B (no dividend), both NYSE-traded, plus MLP paperwork requirements.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Karen Payne describe Sun Distributors?
Answers: 'A simple, well-run business hiding in a complicated financial structure.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the difference between Sun's Class A and Class B shares?
Answers: Class A offered little upside (company will buy back for $10), all action was in Class B shares that fell 50% from $4 to $2.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who owned 52% of Sun's Class B shares?
Answers: Shearson Lehman owned 52%, and management had option to buy up to half at fixed price, giving powerful incentive for success.

Questions: What evidence did you see of management dedication?
Answers: President was in office taking phone calls on December 23, two days before Christmas.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Sun Distributors survive the recession?
Answers: Made money every year since 1986 independence, even in 1991 when glass and electrical parts businesses were terrible.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sun Distributors' competitive advantage?
Answers: Low-cost operator surviving while competitors faltered - bad times worked to its benefit as rivals disappeared.

Questions: How did you determine Sun was a low-cost operator?
Answers: Gross margin of 60% (dividing cost of sales by net sales) - making $40 profit on every $100 of sales, tops among distributors.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sun's capital spending requirement?
Answers: Only $3-4 million annually compared to revenues - unlike steel companies that might make $1B but spend $950M.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sun's growth strategy?
Answers: Buying related enterprises (36 since 1986) and folding them into operation, reducing overhead and making them more profitable.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how much goodwill did Sun have to write off?
Answers: $57 million in goodwill reduced reported earnings to $1.25/share when actual earnings were nearly twice that amount.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the phantom earnings called that companies have but can't claim?
Answers: Free cash flow - healthy free cash flow gives flexibility to change course in good and bad times.

Questions: How did Sun's debt situation affect your analysis?
Answers: High debt (60% of capitalization) was concerning, but cash flow sufficient to cover interest four times over.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sun's recession strategy vs expansion strategy?
Answers: Expansion: used cash flow to buy $41M of businesses. Recession: curtailed acquisitions, devoted cash flow to reducing debt.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how quickly could Sun retire its debt?
Answers: The $110 million borrowed at 9.5% could be retired within two years using all excess cash flow.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Tenera Limited Partners' main problems?
Answers: Squabbling with federal government (major revenue source), expensive software program not paying off, forced to cut workforce drastically.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why had Tenera's stock collapsed from $9 to $1.25?
Answers: Feds accused company of overcharging, canceled contracts, key executives including president resigned, competitors bad-mouthing to customers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was canceled in June 1991 at Tenera?
Answers: Dividend was canceled, company said it would 'take a long time' to restore to former 20 cents quarterly level.

Questions: Why didn't you dismiss Tenera completely?
Answers: Zero debt and no large expenses meant it wasn't going out of business immediately, had well-regarded nuclear services division.

Questions: What were Tenera's positives for your analysis?
Answers: Zero debt, no capital spending needed (consultants need desk, calculator, phone), earning power of 77-81 cents/share in prior four years.

Questions: How did you value Tenera as potential liquidation?
Answers: Figured auction value worth more than $1.50/share with no debts, entire amount minus legal fees would go to shareholders.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who was brought in to oversee Tenera's recovery?
Answers: Bob Dahl, whom Lynch had met in telecommunications industry, suggested turnaround possible within 6-12 months.

Questions: What convinced you that Tenera had remaining value?
Answers: Insiders were holding onto shares and new management believed turnaround was possible within reasonable timeframe.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when do professional money managers begin thinking about cyclicals?
Answers: When the economy is in the doldrums, they think about investing in aluminums, steels, paper producers, auto manufacturers, chemicals, and airlines.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what makes investing in cyclicals increasingly tricky?
Answers: Wall Street is anticipating cyclical industry revivals earlier and earlier before the fact, making timing more difficult.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how do low P/E ratios affect cyclical stock investing?
Answers: With cyclicals, low P/E ratios are usually a bad sign - they indicate companies are at the end of a prosperous interlude.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why might a low P/E ratio be dangerous for cyclicals?
Answers: Business is still good with high earnings, but smart investors are selling. When economy falters, earnings decline at breathtaking speed.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the misconception about buying cyclicals with low P/E ratios?
Answers: Buying after several years of record earnings when P/E hits low point is a proven method for losing half your money quickly.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how should investors interpret high P/E ratios for cyclicals?
Answers: Often good news - may mean company is passing through worst doldrums and business will improve, earnings will exceed expectations.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what makes the cyclical game doubly hard?
Answers: It's a game of anticipation - principal danger is buying too early, getting discouraged, and selling before the turnaround.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what knowledge is essential for successful cyclical investing?
Answers: You must have working knowledge of the specific industry (copper, aluminum, steel, autos, paper) and its rhythms.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #19?
Answers: Unless you're a short seller or a poet looking for a wealthy spouse, it never pays to be pessimistic.

Questions: What led you to Phelps Dodge in 1992?
Answers: He was foiled in housing rebound plays by other buyers, but they hadn't anticipated copper market rebound - his plumber confirmed copper pipe prices rising.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why had Phelps Dodge gone nowhere in 1991?
Answers: Stock's going nowhere isn't necessarily reason to abandon it - may be reason to buy more if story improves.

Questions: What makes copper more valuable than aluminum in your investment approach?
Answers: Aluminum is 8% of earth's crust and easy to extract; copper is scarcer and vanishing asset - mines run out or flood and close.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how have environmental regulations affected the copper industry?
Answers: Forced closing of many U.S. smelters, many companies gave up smelting for good, creating smelter shortage.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what global trend supports copper demand?
Answers: All developing nations including former Soviet republics want improved phone systems, traditional systems require miles of copper wire.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are developing countries more important for copper than mature ones?
Answers: Developing countries are much more copper intensive than mature countries, and there are more of the former.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Phelps Dodge's stock pattern from 1990-1991?
Answers: 1990: earned $6.50, stock ranged $23-36 (low P/E 3.5-5.5). 1991: earnings dropped to $3.90, stock retreated from $39 to $26.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the most important question about any cyclical?
Answers: Whether the company's balance sheet is strong enough to survive the next downturn.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were Phelps Dodge's balance sheet strengths?
Answers: Equity of $1.68 billion, total debt (minus cash) only $318 million - clearly no bankruptcy candidate even if copper prices fell.

Questions: How did you evaluate Phelps Dodge's subsidiary businesses?
Answers: Carbon black OK, magnet wire OK, truck wheels OK, Canyon Resources gold mine could become big moneymaker.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what could Phelps Dodge's non-copper businesses be worth?
Answers: Subsidiaries earning less than $1/share in bad year, could earn $2 in decent year, worth $10-16/share at modest P/E of 5-8.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how much could the gold operations add to Phelps Dodge's value?
Answers: Gold operations could be worth $5/share to Phelps Dodge.

Questions: What technique does you use for valuing diversified companies?
Answers: Thumbnail appraisal of various divisions - take earnings of each division, multiply by generic P/E ratio to get rough value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how was Phelps Dodge's capital spending situation?
Answers: 1990: spent $290 million upgrading plants, less than half its cash flow - even in bad 1991, cash flow exceeded capital spending.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the basic math of copper prices and Phelps Dodge earnings?
Answers: Company produces 1.1 billion pounds copper annually, so penny increase in price creates $11 million pretax earnings, or 10 cents/share after taxes.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how much could copper price increases affect Phelps Dodge earnings?
Answers: If copper goes up 50 cents/pound, earnings improve by $5/share - dramatic leverage to commodity prices.

Questions: Why do you classify autos as cyclicals rather than blue chips?
Answers: Buying auto stock for 25 years is like flying over Alps - you may get something, but not as much as the hiker experiencing ups and downs.

Questions: What convinced you to look at autos again in 1991?
Answers: Auto stocks down 50% from recent highs, widespread showroom gloom, but certain that Americans will continue replacing cars.

Questions: What is your certainty about American car buying habits?
Answers: Until someone invents reliable Hovercraft for home use, cars will continue being America's most beloved personal possession.

Questions: What forces eventual car replacement in your investment approach?
Answers: Cars eventually need replacement due to being tired of old ones, brakes shot, road visible through rusted floorboards, plus mandatory inspections.

Questions: What was the car sales decline that led to your 1980s auto investment?
Answers: Annual sales declined from 15.4 million vehicles (1977) to 10.5 million (1982), but couldn't go to zero.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how have 60-month auto loans affected the replacement cycle?
Answers: Old 36-month loans meant cars were paid off when owners wanted to trade; 60-month loans mean many cars worth less than outstanding balance.

Questions: What is the key indicator you uses for auto stock timing?
Answers: Used-car prices - when dealers lower prices, new car market is worse; when used prices rise, good times ahead for automakers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the 'units of pent-up demand' indicator?
Answers: Chart showing actual car sales vs. trend - difference between what should have been sold vs. actual sales shows built-up demand.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what pent-up demand existed from 1980-1983?
Answers: Actual sales lagged trend by 7 million vehicles - 7 million people delayed purchases, predicting coming boom.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how long did the 1984-1989 auto boom last?
Answers: Auto sales exceeded trend by combined 7.8 million units over those years, working off the pent-up demand.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when was the right time to sell auto stocks according to the indicator?
Answers: 1988, when pent-up demand from early 1980s was exhausted after public bought 74 million vehicles in five years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what pent-up demand has been building since 1990?
Answers: Two years under trend, building toward 5.6 million units of pent-up demand by end of 1993, suggesting 1994-96 boom.

Questions: Why did you favor Chrysler, Ford, and Volvo over General Motors?
Answers: GM's reputation for excellence far exceeded desire to live up to it - company was arrogant, myopic, resting on laurels.

Questions: What was your experience with GM's investor relations?
Answers: Assigned to investor relations guy who couldn't find R&D center (size of big college campus) - took couple hours to locate it.

Questions: How did you view GM in 1991 compared to earlier opinions?
Answers: Previous popular view: powerful company with profitable future. 1991 popular view: weak company with miserable future - I suspected latest view equally misguided.

Questions: What parallel does you draw between GM 1992 and Chrysler 1982?
Answers: Same story: powerful enterprise forgets how to make cars, loses public confidence, lays off thousands, heads for has-been scrap heap.

Questions: What gives you confidence in GM's potential recovery?
Answers: Better balance sheet in 1992 than Chrysler had in 1982, plus profitable non-auto divisions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are GM's most profitable non-auto businesses?
Answers: European operations, financing arm (GMAC), Hughes Aircraft, Delco, Electronic Data Systems (thanks to Ross Perot).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what could GM earn if it just breaks even on U.S. auto business?
Answers: Could earn $6-8/share in 1993 with break-even autos; if auto business improves beyond break-even, could earn $10/share.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is GM's market share situation?
Answers: Upset that share shrunk from 40% to 30%, but that's still bigger than all Japanese carmakers combined.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how could GM succeed even with declining market share?
Answers: Even with 25% of buyers, auto divisions can contribute to earnings by scaling down manufacturing and reducing expenses.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what positive developments had GM achieved by 1993?
Answers: Several cars won major awards including Cadillac, trucks looked good, mid-sized cars improved, company had plenty of cash.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the main attraction of utility stocks in the 1950s vs. since then?
Answers: Utility stocks were great growth stocks of the 1950s, but since then their main attraction has been yield.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what has been more profitable long-term than CDs for income investors?
Answers: Buying utility stocks has been more profitable than buying CDs - you get dividends that increase yearly plus chance at capital gain.

Questions: What examples does you give of big utility winners in recent years?
Answers: Southern Company ($11 to $33 in 5 years), Oklahoma Gas and Electric ($13 to $40), Philadelphia Electric ($9 to $26).

Questions: When did you have 10% of Magellan invested in utilities?
Answers: During brief periods when interest rates were declining and economy was sputtering - he treated utilities as interest-rate cyclicals.

Questions: Which utilities has you done best with?
Answers: The troubled ones: General Public Utilities (Three Mile Island), Public Service of New Hampshire, Long Island Lighting, Gulf States, Middle South (now Entergy).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #20?
Answers: Corporations, like people, change their names for one of two reasons: either they've gotten married, or they've been involved in some fiasco they hope the public will forget.

Questions: Why is your record better with troubled utilities than troubled companies generally?
Answers: Utilities are regulated by government - as long as people need electricity, a way must be found for utility to continue functioning.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what determines a utility's survival and profitability?
Answers: Regulatory system determines prices they can charge, profit allowed, and whether costs of mistakes can be passed to customers.

Questions: Who identified the 'troubled utility cycle' that you references?
Answers: Three analysts at NatWest Investment Banking Group: Kathleen Lally, John Kellenyi, and Philip Smyth.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the four examples of companies that lived through the troubled utility cycle?
Answers: Consolidated Edison (1973 oil crisis), Entergy (lavish nuke plant), Long Island Lighting (unlicensed nuke), General Public Utilities (Three Mile Island).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the stock price drops during the disaster phase?
From Peter Lynch's perspective, at what percentage of book value do distressed utilities trade?
Answers: 20-30% of book value during the disaster phase, as Wall Street worries damage may be fatal.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Stage 2 of the troubled utility cycle?
Answers: 'Crisis management' - utility responds by cutting capital spending, adopting austerity budget, dividend reduced or eliminated.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Stage 3 of the troubled utility cycle?
Answers: 'Financial stabilization' - management succeeds in cutting costs so utility operates on cash from bill-paying customers, survival no longer in doubt.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what characterizes Stage 4 of the utility cycle?
Answers: 'Recovery at last!' - utility capable of earning for shareholders again, Wall Street expects improved earnings and dividend reinstatement.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what determines how utilities progress after Stage 4?
Answers: 1) Reception from capital markets (need capital to expand rate base), 2) Support from regulators (how many costs passed to customers).

Questions: What is your strategy for investing in troubled utilities?
Answers: Buy on omission of dividend and wait for good news, or buy when first good news arrives in second stage.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why shouldn't investors worry about missing the bottom in troubled utilities?
Answers: If stock falls to $4 then rises to $8, don't think you missed it - troubled nukes have long way to go, need psychological Wite-Out.

Questions: What simple strategy does you suggest for troubled utilities?
Answers: Buy when dividend is omitted, hold until dividend is restored - strategy with terrific success ratio.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, which five distressed utilities did NatWest identify in summer 1991?
Answers: Gulf States, Illinois Power, Niagara Mohawk, Pinnacle West, Public Service Company of New Mexico - all in various recovery stages, selling below book values.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was CMS Energy formerly called and why did it change?
Answers: Used to be Consumers Power of Michigan, changed name after building Midland nuclear plant - hoped shareholders would forget.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was CMS's stock performance during the nuclear disaster?
Answers: Sailing in $20s, sank to $4.50 in less than a year, hitting bottom after dividend omitted in October 1984.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the regulatory pattern with nuclear plants?
Answers: Like Lucy with football - state commissions supported nuke plants throughout development until owners fully committed, then snatched projects away at last minute.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what write-off did Consumers Power have to take?
Answers: $4 billion write-off to cover costs of building nuke plant it wasn't allowed to use.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did CMS make the best of the nuclear disaster?
Answers: Converted unusable nuclear plant to natural gas with help of Dow Chemical (biggest customer) at cost of $1,600 per kilowatt, under budget.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was CMS's stock recovery and subsequent decline?
Answers: Came back to $36/share (ninefold gain in 5 years), then unfavorable rate decisions drove price down to $17.

Questions: Who brought CMS to your attention?
Answers: Danny Frank, manager of Fidelity's Special Situations Fund, who had investigated several troubled nukes.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was positive about the converted Midland plant's economics?
Answers: Producing electricity at 6 cents per kilowatt vs. 9.2 cents for new coal plant and 13.3 cents for nuke - low-cost operation.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what demand trend favored CMS in Michigan?
Answers: Electricity demand grew 12 years in a row, even 1% more in recession year 1991, with only 19.6% reserve capacity on peak days.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was the thin reserve capacity significant?
Answers: Very thin margin in utility circles, few new Midwest plants coming online, takes 6-12 years to build from scratch.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what does Economics 101 predict when demand grows faster than supply?
Answers: Higher prices result, and higher prices produce more profits.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was CMS's debt situation from the nuclear conversion?
Answers: Sold $1 billion bonds to finance Midland conversion plus $500 million senior notes not callable for 10 years.

Questions: How did you verify CMS could handle its debt load?
Answers: Calculated cash flow of $6/share (earnings plus depreciation divided by shares), sufficient to pay interest with money left over.

Questions: What could CMS do with its excess cash in your investment approach?
Answers: Buy back stock, make acquisitions, or increase dividend - all benefiting shareholders.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were CMS's expansion plans for the cash?
Answers: Expand gas plant and improve transmission line efficiency, both adding to generating capacity and automatically adding to earnings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Ecuador oil discovery potential for CMS?
Answers: Joint venture with Conoco scheduled to produce $25 million annual profits by 1995, adding 20 cents/share to earnings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Power Group subsidiary situation?
Answers: CMS subsidiary owning small cogeneration plants, losing money lately but could turn profit by 1993.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what disappointed CMS regarding Long Island Lighting?
Answers: Collaboration to convert LILCO's Shoreham nuke plant to natural gas fell apart in 1991.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was CMS's greatest ongoing disappointment?
Answers: Michigan commission was uncooperative, handing down three unfavorable rate decisions in a row.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what rate commission politics affected CMS?
Answers: Recent appointee expected to be more accommodating (only mildly hostile vs. traditionally hostile), commission staff study favored concessions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what earnings could CMS achieve with reasonable regulatory decision?
Answers: $2/share in upcoming year vs. $1.30 Wall Street expected, with steady growth thereafter.

Questions: Why did you view CMS as more than just regulatory gamble?
Answers: Powerful cash flow would enable reentry to strong utility ranks regardless of commission decisions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were CMS's potential earnings scenarios?
Answers: Best case: $2.20/share if all resolved favorably. Worst case: $1.50/share, but either way would prosper long-run.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how could CMS grow if regulators restricted earnings?
Answers: Could plow cash back into more generating capacity and grow business internally.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, at what price was CMS selling and why was it attractive?
Answers: $18/share, below book value, with lot of potential reward without much risk.

Questions: What alternatives does you mention for distressed utility investing?
Answers: Public Service Company of New Mexico or 'more hapless' Tucson Electric, both with available investor relations staff.

Questions: What is your attitude toward government garage sales?
Answers: When Uncle Sam or the Queen of England is having a garage sale, I always tries to attend.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, which country is ahead in privatization efforts?
Answers: Britain is way ahead, having sold everything from waterworks to airlines.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what might the U.S. have to privatize if deficit spending continues?
Answers: National parks, Kennedy Space Center, even White House Rose Garden just to pay interest on national debt.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the strange concept of privatization?
Answers: You take something owned by the public, sell it back to the public, and from then on it's private.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why have privatizations usually been good deals for buyers?
Answers: In democratic countries, buyers are also voters, and governments can't afford disgruntled investors who lost money on telephone companies or gasworks.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what lesson did the British learn from early privatization mistakes?
Answers: Britoil and Amersham International came out overpriced in 1983, creating ill will, so since then British structured offers so investors unlikely to lose.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #21?
Answers: Whatever the queen is selling, buy it.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did British Telecom perform after privatization?
Answers: Doubled in price in one day, with three million Brits snapping up shares.

Questions: What British privatization did you encounter at Fidelity?
Answers: British contingent with numbered prospectus for water utilities: Northumbrian Water, Severn Trent, Yorkshire Water, Welsh Water PLC.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what advantages did British water utilities have?
Answers: Monopolies, government absorbed most prior debt, came out debt-free with extra capital (green dowry), 10-year upgrade program partially subsidized.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how low were English water bills according to the water lords?
Answers: 100 pounds per year, so low that even doubling wouldn't cause resentment, and customers couldn't stop using water anyway.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the installment plan feature of British water shares?
Answers: Could buy on installment: 40% down, rest in two easy payments (12 months and 20 months), same deal offered on British Telecom.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the partial-paid shares feature work?
Answers: British Telecom came public at $30, buyer paid only $6 down, when price rose to $36, buyer could sell and double money on $6 investment.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what dividend advantage did water companies offer?
Answers: Paid 8% dividend immediately on full value of shares acquired at 40% down, giving 20% return on investment in first 12 months.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did British water utilities perform after privatization?
Answers: Portfolio of all five water utilities doubled in value in three years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what has been the pattern with privatized telephone companies worldwide?
Answers: Every telephone company privatized in any country (Philippines, Mexico, Spain) has given shareholders once-in-a-lifetime rewards.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are privatized telephone companies particularly attractive?
Answers: Growth rate of small growth company, size and stability of blue chip, guaranteed success of monopoly.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the opportunity with Mexican telephones?
Answers: Country knew it needed improved phone service before economy could expand, required well-capitalized company, had to allow decent shareholder profits.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how much had privatization sales reached worldwide by 1990?
Answers: $200 billion in sales of privatized companies worldwide, with more to come.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what countries and assets have been privatized globally?
Answers: France: electric utilities, trains; Scotland: hydroelectric plants; Spain/Argentina: oil companies; Mexico: airlines; potential: Britain's railways/ports, Japan's bullet trains.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the biggest recent U.S. privatization deal?
Answers: Conrail (Consolidated Rail Corporation), assembled from Penn Central and five other bankrupt Northeast lines.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how much had the government spent on Conrail before privatization?
Answers: More than $7 billion in government handouts, plus fortune gold-plating the railroad with upgraded rails and equipment.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Conrail's IPO performance?
Answers: March 1987: largest U.S. public offering at $1.6 billion, initial price $10/share, worth $46/share by time of Lynch's writing.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did President Reagan joke about after Conrail deal?
Answers: 'OK, when do we sell the TVA?' referring to Tennessee Valley Authority.

Questions: What other U.S. privatization possibilities has you considered?
Answers: Amtrak, naval petroleum reserves in California and Wyoming, National Gallery, Marine Band, Niagara Falls.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Allied Capital and its track record?
Answers: One of few publicly traded venture capital firms, lends to small companies for high interest plus equity kickers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Allied Capital I's performance since 1960?
Answers: $10,000 invested when it came public in 1960 is sitting on $1.5 million nest egg by Lynch's writing.

Questions: What tangible result of Allied Capital investment does you mention?
Answers: Air purifier in his bedroom that removes so much grit the room has air quality of genetic engineering lab.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the structure of Allied Capital II?
Answers: $92 million pool, borrows against it to raise another $92 million, total $184 million to buy loans paying 10% while borrowing costs 8%.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how does Allied Capital II's business model work?
Answers: Makes comfortable spread for shareholders plus occasional equity kickers, few employees and expenses.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what has been key to Allied's success?
Answers: Management's ability to get money back - very picky about borrowers, stringent about collateral requirements.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Allied Capital II's planned RTC strategy?
Answers: Buy loans from Resolution Trust Corporation - among bum loans in S&L portfolios, there are actually some good ones to reputable borrowers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why were small RTC loans available to Allied?
Answers: Wall Street firms and big banks bought multimillion-dollar loans, but loans of $1 million or less weren't easy for RTC to unload.

Questions: What was Allied Capital II's dividend and price when you analyzed it?
Answers: Selling for $19 with 6% dividend.

Questions: How do you view Allied Capital II as an investment opportunity?
Answers: Simple way to turn S&L fiasco into something advantageous - chance to make back some taxes paid for S&L bailout.

Questions: Which group on Wall Street did you miss for several years?
Answers: The mutual fund industry - he missed Dreyfus, Franklin Resources, Colonial Group, T. Rowe Price, State Street Bank, Alliance Capital Management, and Eaton Vance.

Questions: How do you compare himself to a mall manager regarding mutual fund stocks?
Answers: Like the mall manager who neglected to buy Gap stock despite seeing sales results daily, I neglected mutual fund companies despite being in the industry.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the distinction between direct mutual fund plays and diversified financial companies?
Answers: Direct plays include companies solely focused on funds; diversified include Putnam (subsidiary of Marsh-McLennan) or Kemper (fund business but mostly insurance).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the eight mutual fund companies perform in 1988-1989?
Answers: All did well as fears of mutual fund industry collapse after 1987 correction proved exaggerated.

Questions: What what-if portfolio performance does you present for mutual fund companies?
Answers: If you divided money equally among eight stocks from beginning 1988 to end 1989, you would have outperformed 99% of the funds these companies promote.

Questions: What is your observation about the Gold Rush and mutual fund investing?
Answers: In the Gold Rush, people who sold picks and shovels did better than the prospectors - during fund popularity, investing in fund companies beats their products.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when do different types of mutual fund companies prosper?
Answers: Interest rates declining: bond and equity funds attract cash (Eaton Vance, Colonial prosper). Rates rising: money markets popular (Dreyfus prospers).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Alliance Capital's business model?
Answers: Manages money for institutional clients and mutual funds sold through brokers, been public since 1988.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened during the Saddam Sell-off to mutual fund company stocks?
Answers: Eaton Vance declined 30%, Dreyfus declined 18.86%, others had smaller but significant declines.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what could investors have done to verify mutual fund industry health in 1990-1991?
Answers: Look at sales figures for mutual funds in December 1990 and January 1991 to dispel collapse fears.

Questions: How did you perform with mutual fund stock recommendations in 1991?
Answers: Failed to recommend a single mutual fund company, missing Franklin (75% gain), Dreyfus (55%), T. Rowe Price (116%), UAM (80%).

Questions: Which fund-related stock did you recommend in 1991 and how did it perform?
Answers: Kemper (insurance with fund business via $50 billion managed) - stock doubled in 1991.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what trend was driving mutual fund company success in 1992?
Answers: Interest rates dropping, $200 billion in CDs maturing monthly, great tide of capital emptying from banks into all manner of funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Colonial Group undervalued compared to peers?
Answers: T. Rowe Price and Franklin selling for 20x earnings, but Colonial Group selling for only 10x earnings despite managing more assets.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Colonial Group's 1985 vs 1992 comparison?
Answers: 1985 IPO: $17, managed $5-6 billion, earned $1/share. 1992: same $17 price, managed $9 billion, earned $1.55/share, plus $4/share cash.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what had Colonial Group done to enhance shareholder value?
Answers: Amassed $4/share in cash, bought back 7% of stock, had no debt, yet no Wall Street analyst had mentioned it in two years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Colonial Group undervalued within the attractive mutual fund group?
Answers: Earnings stayed flat for four years while competitors thrived, wasn't household name like Dreyfus or T. Rowe Price.

Questions: Who did you speak with at Colonial Group?
Answers: Corporate treasurer Davey Scoon on January 3, who reported business improvement especially in muni bond funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Colonial Group's new business development?
Answers: Chosen by State Street Bank to market new funds that State Street had created.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is State Street Bank's role in the mutual fund industry?
Answers: Commercial bank doing paperwork ('back office' work) for most mutual fund industry - customer service, recording transactions, tracking ownership.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how profitable has State Street's back office function been?
Answers: Very lucrative - State Street stock had 81% gain in 1991.

Questions: What mistake did you make with his mother-in-law regarding State Street?
Answers: Advised her to sell when money-market assets seemed declining because she'd doubled her money - stock has tripled again since then.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how do stock splits help cover up selling mistakes?
Answers: His mother-in-law thinks State Street went nowhere due to 3-for-1 split, doesn't realize Lynch sold too early - splits can camouflage timing mistakes.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why did State Street want to start its own mutual funds?
Answers: Seeing success in back office work, wanted to get in on front end of bonanza.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why did State Street hire Colonial Group instead of competing directly?
Answers: Didn't want to anger clients by competing against them directly, so camouflaged State Street funds by having Colonial market them.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how would the State Street relationship benefit Colonial Group?
Answers: Extra business from marketing State Street's funds would add to Colonial's revenue and growth.

Questions: What do you say about restaurant stock recommendations in 1992?
Answers: He didn't recommend any restaurant stocks in 1992, but admits he should have.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did fast food become an accessory to the automobile?
Answers: Since the 1960s, when people learned to eat lunches, then breakfasts, and finally dinners on the road.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Kentucky Fried Chicken's origin story?
Answers: Created out of desperation when superhighway diverted traffic from Colonel Sanders's country restaurant, facing bankruptcy, the 66-year-old took to the road offering his recipe.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Colonel Sanders wearing when he started franchising?
Answers: A dark suit, not the white planter's costume that later became his trademark.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did major restaurant chains go public?
Answers: KFC: 1965, Dunkin' Donuts and Howard Johnson earlier, Bob Evans Farms: 1963, McDonald's and Shoney's: mid-1960s.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Shoney's stock performance as a bagger?
Answers: 168-bagger, rising from 22 cents per share (adjusted for splits) to high of $367⁄8.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was McDonald's performance compared to other restaurant stocks?
Answers: 400-bagger, making it one of most rewarding stock market performers in modern history.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what would $10,000 invested in five early restaurant stocks have become?
Answers: By end of 1980s, would have become millionaire at least twice over, four times over if entire amount put into McDonald's alone.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what types of restaurant categories have produced big stock winners?
Answers: Hamburger joints, cafeterias (Luby's, Morrison's), family steak houses (Ponderosa, Bonanza), all-purpose eateries (Denny's, Shoney's), ice cream, yogurt, coffee bars, pizza.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what advantage do restaurant investors have?
Answers: We all know which places are popular and well-maintained, which are disheveled and passé, which have reached saturation, which have room to grow.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what 1970s restaurant opportunities could have made up for missing 1960s?
Answers: International Dairy Queen, Wendy's, Luby's, Taco Bell, Pizza Hut, Jerrico when Long John Silver appeared.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when was especially good timing for restaurant investments in the 1970s?
Answers: After bear market of 1972 when solid franchises were selling for pittance - Taco Bell dropped to $1/share despite never having disappointing quarter.

Questions: What happened to Taco Bell after you discovered it?
Answers: Rebounded to $40, then acquired by PepsiCo, which likes to own food companies because they help sell Pepsi's soft drinks.

Questions: What 1980s restaurant opportunities does you mention?
Answers: Cracker Barrel (popular gift shop, delicious seafood and biscuits), Chili's (public 1984), Sbarro (1985), Ryan's Family Steak Houses (1982), Uno Restaurants (1987).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how are restaurant chains protected from competition compared to other businesses?
Answers: New fish-and-chips chain in California has zero impact on better one in New York - takes long time to work across country, no foreign competition.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what separates restaurant triumphs from flops?
Answers: Capable management, adequate financing, and methodical approach to expansion - slow but steady wins this race.

Questions: What is the tale of two hamburger franchises you tells?
Answers: Chili's (Dallas) vs. Fuddrucker's (San Antonio) - both featured gourmet burger and distinctive surroundings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why did Chili's succeed while Fuddrucker's failed?
Answers: Chili's diversified menu as hamburgers went out of style, Fuddrucker's stuck with burgers; Chili's expanded methodically, Fuddrucker's expanded too rapidly.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the danger of expanding more than 100 new units per year?
Answers: Company likely to run into problems - can pick wrong sites or managers, pay too much for real estate, fail to train employees properly.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what other restaurant chains fell into the rapid expansion trap?
Answers: Fuddrucker's, Flakey Jake's, Winners, TGI Friday's all moved too fast and suffered.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Chili's sensible expansion pace?
Answers: 30-35 new units per year under experienced Norman Brinker (founder of Chili's, Steak & Ale, and Bennigan's).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Chili's expansion goal?
Answers: Reach ceiling of 400-450 restaurants in 1996-98, hoping to produce $1 billion in sales.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the different ways restaurant chains can increase earnings?
Answers: Add more restaurants, improve existing operations, high turnover with low prices, low turnover with high prices, food vs. gift shop profits, cheap ingredients.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the key elements to follow in restaurant stories?
Answers: Growth rate, debt, and same-store sales - want same-store sales increasing every quarter.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the danger zone for restaurant expansion?
Answers: Above 100 new outlets per year puts company in potential danger zone.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what should restaurant debt levels be?
Answers: Debt should be low to nonexistent if possible.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who provides excellent restaurant industry analysis?
Answers: Montgomery Securities in California keeps regular tabs and produces excellent reports on entire restaurant group.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Montgomery Securities' analysis of current restaurant trends?
Answers: Hamburger joints suffering from overexposure (top 5 chains have 24,000 U.S. locations), baby boomers turning away from fast food.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, where has restaurant momentum shifted according to Montgomery?
Answers: To niche restaurants like Au Bon Pain and Spaghetti Warehouse, and medium-priced family restaurants with varied menus.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the performance of Montgomery's top 8 restaurant recommendations in 1991?
Answers: Would have doubled your money by December: Bertucci's, Cracker Barrel, Brinker International (Chili's), Spaghetti Warehouse, Shoney's, Rally's, Applebee's, Outback Steakhouse.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the overall growth rate of the restaurant group?
Answers: Only 4% per year - soon this will be another nongrowth industry.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who will prosper in the mature restaurant industry?
Answers: Superior operators with strong balance sheets will prosper as they always have, as industry consolidates.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of meals do Americans eat outside the home?
Answers: 50% of meals eaten outside home, ensuring continued opportunities for new 20-baggers in food courts and neighborhoods.

Questions: Where did you spot Au Bon Pain?
Answers: In the Burlington Mall - started in Boston in 1977, went public in 1991 at $10/share.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Au Bon Pain's concept?
Answers: Croissant and coffee shop combining French sensibility with U.S. efficiency - plain croissant for breakfast, filled for lunch, chocolate for dessert in under 3 minutes.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how does Au Bon Pain ensure fresh bread?
Answers: Made at central location, sent uncooked to outlets where it rises and is baked fresh on-site.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what new products has Au Bon Pain introduced?
Answers: Fresh orange juice, fruit salad, and about to launch the state-of-the-art bagel.

Questions: What is your preference between high-tech investments and food?
Answers: If choice between state-of-the-art computer chip and state-of-the-art bagel, he'll take the bagel any time.

Questions: Why didn't you recommend Au Bon Pain initially?
Answers: Stock had doubled to carry P/E ratio of 40 based on expected 1992 earnings.

Questions: At what point would you back up the truck on Au Bon Pain?
Answers: When price fell to $14 (less than 20x 1993 earnings) - any 25% grower selling for 20x earnings is a buy.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what global potential does Au Bon Pain have?
Answers: Company is doing well in recession and can grow long time without running into itself, has lot of potential overseas.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why does a healthy portfolio require regular checkups?
Answers: Even with blue chips and top Fortune 500 companies, the buy-and-forget strategy can be unproductive and downright dangerous.

Questions: What examples does you give of buy-and-forget dangers?
Answers: Investors who bought and forgot IBM, Sears, and Eastman Kodak are sorry they did - these stocks declined significantly over time.

Questions: What is the six-month checkup in your investment approach?
Answers: Not simply looking up stock price in newspaper, but following the stories to get answers to two basic questions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the two basic questions for the six-month checkup?
Answers: 1) Is the stock still attractively priced relative to earnings? 2) What is happening in the company to make earnings go up?

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the three possible conclusions from a six-month checkup?
Answers: 1) Story has gotten better (increase investment), 2) Story has gotten worse (decrease investment), 3) Story unchanged (stick with it or find more exciting prospects).

Questions: How did you's 21 Barron's selections perform in the first six months?
Answers: The portfolio increased 19.2% while the S&P 500 returned only 1.64% - extremely well in a so-so market.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to the Body Shop stock price by July 1992?
Answers: Fallen 12.3% from 325 pence to 263 pence, now selling for 20 times estimated 1993 earnings.

Questions: What is your view on paying 20 times earnings for a 25% grower?
Answers: He doesn't mind it, especially when entire NYSE was selling at 20x earnings for companies growing at only 8-10% rate.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what bad publicity hurt the Body Shop?
Answers: Chieftain from Kayapó Indian tribe (hired to produce Brazil nut hair conditioner) was arrested in London for raping Portuguese nanny.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how often has the Body Shop suffered major setbacks?
Answers: Two major setbacks: 1987 and 1990, both despite company perking along with no letup - Lynch attributes to British unfamiliarity with small growth companies.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Monica Kalmanson at Body Shop report about 1991 performance?
Answers: Same-store sales and earnings both increased in 1991, considerable achievement given four major markets (England, Australia, Canada, U.S.) all in recession.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what strategic move was Body Shop making to improve margins?
Answers: Using cash to buy up suppliers of potions and lotions to cut merchandise costs and improve profit margin.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Cathy Stephenson report about her Body Shop franchises?
Answers: 6% sales gain over previous year at Burlington, Harvard Square too early to tell, customers flocking to new products like Complete Color and mango body butter.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Body Shop's expansion plan?
Answers: 40 new U.S. outlets in 1993, 50 more in 1994, 50/year in Europe, equal number in Far East.

Questions: How do you categorize Body Shop's growth phase?
Answers: Attractive mid-life phase - second decade of 30 years of growth.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Pier 1 stock punished despite meeting expectations?
Answers: Analysts expected 18-20 cents first quarter earnings, Pier 1 earned 17 cents, stock got clobbered - Wall Street deaf to good news.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how had Pier 1 strengthened its financial position?
Answers: Sold $75 million convertible debentures, used proceeds to retire debt, further reducing already-reduced long-term debt.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what competitive advantage was Pier 1 gaining during the recession?
Answers: Major competitors (department stores) getting out of home furnishings business, longer recession lasted, more competitors would drop out.

Questions: What was your earnings projection for Pier 1?
Answers: 80 cents from own stores plus 10-15 cents from revived Sunbelt Nursery = $1/share, making it $14 stock at reasonable 14x P/E.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what disappointing development occurred with General Host?
Answers: Issued $65 million convertible preferred stock with 8% yield, creating more shares that would dilute existing shareholders.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did General Host's use of proceeds differ from Pier 1's?
Answers: Pier 1 used proceeds to pay off debt (reducing interest expense), General Host used proceeds for further Frank's Nursery renovation (chancier proposition).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was General Host's earnings revision?
Answers: Expected to earn 60 cents when stock was $7.75, now $8 stock expected to earn only 45 cents.

Questions: What positives kept General Host as a hold for you?
Answers: Strong cash flow, dividend raised 14th year in a row, stock selling below book value, expansion proceeding as planned.

Questions: Who had bought General Host stock in your investment approach's research?
Answers: Mario Gabelli had bought million shares for his value-oriented fund.

Questions: What happened to Sunbelt Nursery after your recommendation?
Answers: Lost money since January due to more rain in Southwest dampening gardening enthusiasm.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how cheap had Sunbelt become by the six-month checkup?
Answers: $4.50 stock with $1.50/share in cash, so buying all garden outlets for only $3.

Questions: Why did you prefer Calloway's over Sunbelt by the checkup?
Answers: Calloway's also fell in half due to rain, but was best company in industry with better fundamentals.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Dan Reynolds report about Calloway's operations?
Answers: 20 employees sharing 3,000 square feet - no communications gap, management attention available by standing up and yelling.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were Calloway's financial metrics?
Answers: 13 nurseries plus 50 cents/share cash, expected to earn 50 cents in 1993, giving P/E ratio of 10.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was positive about Calloway's Wall Street coverage?
Answers: No followers on Wall Street, and company was buying back its own shares.

Questions: What is your principle about investing within attractive groups?
Answers: Find the undervalued stock within attractive group - technique he's often employed with good results.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to Ed Faber at Supercuts?
Answers: Left the company, with explanation he wanted to devote himself to managing his own Supercuts salon - explanation not entirely convincing.

Questions: What overhang problem did you discover with Supercuts?
Answers: Carlton Investments (part of bankrupt Drexel Burnham Lambert) owns 2.2 million shares that creditors will demand be sold.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what positive developments were happening at Supercuts despite problems?
Answers: Named 'Official Hair Salon Services Supplier for Olympics,' same-store sales up 6.9% in first quarter, expanding into upstate New York.

Questions: What was your concern about Supercuts expansion?
Answers: 80-100 new franchises planned for 1993 - he's seen promising franchises ruined by overeager expansion.

Questions: What advice did you give to Supercuts CEO?
Answers: 'If you have choice between reaching your goal in fifteen years or five years, fifteen is better.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the seven S&Ls perform in the first six months?
Answers: They were the best performers of Lynch's 21 picks - not an accident since he took industry surrounded by most doom and gloom.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why have S&Ls been the best performers?
