Answers: Interest rates falling created happy year for financial institutions making huge earnings on spreads between loan rates and deposit rates.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the specific S&L performance numbers?
Answers: Germantown up 59%, Sovereign up 64.5% (plus two 10% stock dividends), Eagle Financial up from $11 to $16, Glacier up 40%+, People's up 26%.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the long-shot S&Ls perform?
Answers: Lawrence up 37%, First Essex up 70% - proving riskiest stocks often carry greatest rewards.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Leonard Wilson report about First Essex's improvement?
Answers: Reduced 'bottom fishing' line from 600 feet to 60 feet - foreclosed properties selling, nonperforming loans down, mortgage market picking up.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what sign of optimism did Wilson show at First Essex?
Answers: Actually dared to make a new construction loan after being driven close to poorhouse - somebody thinks region has future.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was First Essex's potential if real estate market continued improving?
Answers: Could eventually earn $1/share, making stock worth $7-10 vs. current $35⁄8.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what mixed signals came from Lawrence Savings?
Answers: April: CEO Paul Miller optimistic, seven pages of nonperformers reduced to one. June: sounded discouraged.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Lawrence Savings' precarious position?
Answers: $55 million commercial real estate loans outstanding vs. only $21 million net worth - if half go sour, Lawrence wiped out.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what better S&L opportunity had emerged by the checkup?
Answers: First Federal of Michigan (FFOM) - hadn't budged while other S&Ls increased in value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was FFOM's problem despite being a strong Jimmy Stewart thrift?
Answers: Money borrowed from Federal Home Loan Bank at 8-10% fixed rates through 1994, while borrowers refinancing at lower rates.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when will FFOM's problems resolve?
Answers: Once FHLB debt retired and interest rate futures contracts expire, earnings will explode - resolution could add $2+/share to earnings in 1994-96.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is FFOM's book value and current earnings situation?
Answers: Book value over $26/share, current earnings $2/share making it $12 stock, could earn $4 when problems resolve.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Colonial Group benefit from bond fund popularity?
Answers: Specializes in bond funds, particularly tax-exempt and limited maturity government funds enjoying widespread popularity.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Davey Scoon report about Colonial Group's recent performance?
Answers: Sales up 58% in recent quarter, now manages $9.5 billion vs. $8.1 billion year earlier.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what additional positive news did Colonial Group announce?
Answers: $10 million stock buyback program, plus $4/share in cash with stock selling around $20.

Questions: What is the key to making money in stocks in your investment approach?
Answers: The key to making money in stocks is not to get scared out of them. This point cannot be overemphasized.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what determines success in both dieting and stocks?
Answers: In dieting and in stocks, it is the gut and not the head that determines the results.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who is better off - the person who studies the market or the person who ignores it?
Answers: The person who never bothers to think about the economy, blithely ignores market conditions, and invests on a regular schedule is better off than the person who tries to time investments.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: An annual gathering where supposed experts meet for eight hours to trade quips and tips, published in three weekly issues of Barron's magazine.

Questions: How long has you participated in the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: I has participated in the Barron's Roundtable every year since 1986.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who is Alan Abelson and what is his role?
Answers: Alan Abelson is Barron's editor and the resident wit who directs the friendly inquisition at the Roundtable, having done for finance what Dorothy Parker did for romance.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the regular panelists on the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: Mario Gabelli, Michael Price, John Neff, Paul Tudor Jones, Felix Zulauf, Marc Perkins, Oscar Schafer, Ron Baron, and Archie MacAllaster.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to Jimmy Rogers from the panel?
Answers: Jimmy Rogers gave up Wall Street to follow the old silk trade route across China on a motorcycle, later shipping it to Peru to ride around the Andes.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the format of the Barron's Roundtable?
Answers: It starts at noon with two parts: first an overview of financial markets and economy, then individual stock recommendations. The overview discussions get them into trouble.

Questions: What do you say about weekend worrying?
Answers: Weekend worrying is dangerous for investors because they have extra time to ponder distressing news, leading to emotional decisions that spoil nest eggs.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what types of scary news do people encounter on weekends?
Answers: Global warming, Soviet empire collapse, recession, inflation, health care costs, budget deficits, tribal warfare, organized crime, sex and money scandals.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why are Mondays historically the biggest down days in stocks?
Answers: Because weekend logic leads to sell orders pouring in on Mondays after people have had time to worry about world events over the weekend.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the panel's worries in 1986?
Answers: M-1 versus M-3, Gramm-Rudman deficit reduction, what the Group of Seven would do, and whether the J Curve effect would reduce the trade deficit.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the main concerns in 1987?
Answers: Dollar collapsing, foreign dumping, Iran-Iraq War causing oil shortage, foreigners stopping bond purchases, over-indebted consumers, and Reagan term limits.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #4?
Answers: You can't see the future through a rearview mirror.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Felix Zulauf's pessimistic 1988 statement?
Answers: 'The honeymoon, from 1982 to 1987, is over' - which was the most optimistic thing said all day.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the two types of bear markets the panel debated in 1988?
Answers: A standard bear market taking the Dow to 1500 or lower, versus a killer bear market that would 'wipe out most people in the financial community.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what Chinese cosmological concern did Zulauf raise in 1989?
Answers: He noted that 1989 was the Year of the Snake, which was a bad sign in Chinese cosmology.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the panel's concern in 1990 despite the Dow reaching 2500?
Answers: They worried about real estate collapse and that after seven straight up years, a down market was inevitable - worrying that things had been going too well.

Questions: What extreme behavior did you observe in 1990?
Answers: He heard cabdrivers recommending bonds and barbers bragging about buying 'puts' (options that increase in value as stocks decline).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what does Bernard Baruch's saying about shoeshine boys suggest?
Answers: If Baruch was right about selling when shoeshine boys are buying stocks, then the right time to buy is when barbers discover put options.

Questions: What were some of the pessimistic headlines you collected from fall 1990?
Answers: 'Layoffs Hit Professional Ranks,' 'How Safe Is Your Job?,' 'The Real Estate Bust,' 'Housing Slump Hammering Remodelers,' 'Can Your Bank Stay Afloat?'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Mother of All Worries in 1991?
Answers: The Gulf War, with fears about chemical and biological weapons, body bags, and the well-trained Iraqi army in reinforced bunkers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the Roundtable's dire predictions for 1991?
Answers: Zulauf saw Dow falling to 2000-2700, Michael Price saw 500-point downside, Marc Perkins predicted 1600-1700, Lynch feared 33% drop if war was terrible.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, despite the dire predictions, what actually happened in 1991?
Answers: Instead of a 33% drop, there was a 30% gain in S&P 500, 25% gain in Dow, and 60% gain in smaller stocks - making 1991 the best year in two decades.

Questions: What was you doing personally during the pessimistic predictions?
Answers: I was actually buying stocks, adding to holdings in his personal account and for charitable trusts, increasing stakes in W.R. Grace and Morrison-Knudsen.

Questions: What do you say about preparing for total disaster?
Answers: It's beyond him why investors bail out of best investments to prepare for total disaster - if disaster strikes, cash will be as useless as stock certificates.

Questions: What is the Even Bigger Picture in your investment approach?
Answers: Over 70 years, stocks have provided 11% annual gains while Treasury bills, bonds, and CDs returned less than half that amount.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many scary market declines have occurred in 70 years?
Answers: There have been 40 scary declines of 10% or more, including 13 terrifying declines of 33% or more, including the 1929-33 sell-off.

Questions: What do you identify as the main factor keeping people away from stocks?
Answers: The cultural memory of the 1929 Crash, which continues to scare people 60 years later, including people who weren't even born in 1929.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how costly has the post-Crash trauma syndrome been?
Answers: People avoiding stocks for 60 years have missed stock market gains and suffered inflation damage that exceeded what another crash would have done.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what misconception persists about market crashes and economic collapses?
Answers: People believe stock market collapses lead to economic collapses, even though crashes in 1972 and 1987 didn't cause economic disasters.

Questions: How do you compare market declines to Minnesota weather?
Answers: A decline in stocks is as normal as frigid air in Minnesota - you expect it, prepare for it, and know that warmer weather will return.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what should a successful stockpicker do during market drops?
Answers: Like a Minnesotan with freezing weather, you know it's coming, you're ready to ride it out, and when favorites go down, you buy more.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how severe was the Great Correction of 1987?
Answers: 508 points were shaved from the Dow in a single day, representing a 1000-point decline (33% from August high).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, was the 1987 crash as apocalyptic as predicted?
Answers: No, it was a normal, albeit severe, correction - the 13th such 33% drop in the century, not the end of civilization many expected.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what will be the significance of the next 10% market decline?
Answers: It will be the 41st in recent history, or if it's 33%, the 14th - just another in a long string of chances to buy great companies at bargain prices.

Questions: How did you prepare Magellan shareholders for inevitable setbacks?
Answers: In annual reports, he often reminded shareholders that such setbacks were inevitable and normal parts of market cycles.

Questions: What comfort does you find in the story of 40 market declines?
Answers: The story continues to comfort him during gloomy periods when there's another chance to buy great companies at bargain prices.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what mistake do investors make regarding market timing?
Answers: They feel better after the market gains 600 points (when stocks are overvalued) and worse after it drops 600 points (when bargains abound).

Questions: What type of faith does you say stockpickers need?
Answers: Faith that America will survive, people will keep getting up and putting on pants, and corporations making pants will profit for shareholders.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what faith should investors have about American business?
Answers: Faith that as old enterprises lose momentum, exciting new ones like Wal-Mart, Federal Express, and Apple Computer will emerge to replace them.

Questions: What is your view on American workers and entrepreneurs?
Answers: I has faith that America is a nation of hardworking and inventive people, and that even yuppies have gotten a bad rap for being lazy.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how should investors think about the Even Bigger Picture during doubt?
Answers: Focus on 70 years of stocks providing 11% annual returns versus bonds and CDs providing less than half that, despite all the calamities.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what will be more lucrative than following 200 commentators predicting depression?
Answers: Acting on the information that stocks have outperformed other investments for 70 years will be far more lucrative long-term.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many times has the market declined 33% or more in this century?
Answers: The market has had 13 terrifying declines of 33% or more, including the Mother of All Terrifying Declines from 1929-33.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what would have happened in 39 out of 40 market corrections if you sold everything?
Answers: You would have sold all your stocks and been sorry, since stocks eventually came back even from the Big One.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how should investors view market corrections?
Answers: As recurring events, not surprising events - as normal as frigid air in Minnesota, requiring preparation but not panic.

Questions: How many mutual funds existed when you wrote this book?
Answers: There were 3,565 mutual funds: 1,266 equity funds, 1,457 bond and income funds, 566 taxable money-market funds, and 276 short-term municipal bond funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how does the number of funds in 1992 compare to 1976?
Answers: In 1976 there were only 452 funds (278 equity), compared to 3,565 in 1992 - nearly an 8-fold increase.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what milestone has been reached in fund-making history?
Answers: The number of funds now exceeds the number of individual stocks traded on the New York and American stock exchanges combined.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the first decision investors must make when structuring a portfolio?
Answers: Whether the mix of stocks and bonds should be changed - the initial growth-versus-income decision, which has the greatest consequence for future net worth.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of mutual fund money went into stock funds in 1980 vs 1990?
Answers: In 1980, 69% went into stock funds. By 1990, only 43% of mutual-fund assets were invested in stocks.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of mutual fund dollars was parked in bond and money-market funds?
Answers: Approximately 75% of all mutual-fund dollars was parked in bond and money-market funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why do stocks do better than bonds over time?
Answers: As companies grow larger and more profitable, stockholders share in increased profits through raised dividends, while no company has ever rewarded bondholders by raising interest rates.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many companies have raised dividends for 20 years in a row?
Answers: 134 companies have an unbroken 20-year record of dividend increases, and 362 have a 10-year record.

Questions: What is your simple strategy for Wall Street success?
Answers: Buy stocks from Moody's Dividend Achievers list and stick with them as long as they stay on the list.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why is the stocks-for-young, bonds-for-old prescription becoming obsolete?
Answers: People aren't dying as readily - a healthy 62-year-old faces 20 more years of spending and inflation, requiring growth to maintain living standards.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what problem do senior citizens face with low interest rates?
Answers: With CDs paying 3.5%, even people with huge portfolios have trouble living off interest alone.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happens to a retired couple with $500,000 in bonds paying 7% with 5% inflation?
Answers: Their $35,000 annual income will be cut in half in 10 years and cut by two-thirds in 15 years due to inflation.

Questions: What advice does you give about stock allocation?
Answers: Increase the stock part of the mix to the limit of your tolerance for the best long-term results.

Questions: What was the bond/stock mix your nonprofit organization had before restructuring?
Answers: 50% stocks and 50% bonds, yielding about 6% return with 4% growth rate - barely enough to keep up with inflation.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the historical returns from stocks vs other investments?
Answers: Stocks return nearly 11% (3% dividends, 8% price appreciation), while bonds don't appreciate at all over time.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what would happen to portfolio growth by adjusting stock/bond percentages?
Answers: Table 3-1 shows that increasing stock allocation sacrifices short-term income but provides much better long-term growth and eventually higher income.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, in Case C (100% stocks), what were the 20-year results vs Case A (100% bonds)?
Answers: Case C: $13,729 dividend income, portfolio worth $46,610. Case A: $14,000 interest income, original $10,000 returned.

Questions: What do you's radical conclusion suggest about bonds for income?
Answers: Theoretically, it makes no sense to put any money into bonds, even if you need income - you're better off with stocks even when dipping into capital.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #5?
Answers: There's no point paying Yo-Yo Ma to play a radio (referring to paying loads for government bond funds).

Questions: What do you say about government bond funds?
Answers: He can't figure out why anyone would invest in intermediate or long-term government bond funds when they could buy Treasury bonds directly with no fees.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how can you buy Treasury bonds without fees?
Answers: Treasury bonds and bills can be purchased through a broker or directly from a Federal Reserve bank, which charges no commission.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what study shows bond funds underperforming individual bonds?
Answers: Gabriele, Hueglin & Cashman found that from 1980-1986, bond funds were consistently outperformed by individual bonds, sometimes by 2% annually.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Warren Buffett's advice about stock volatility?
Answers: People who can't tolerate seeing their stocks lose 50% of their value shouldn't own stocks (this also applies to stock funds).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #6?
Answers: As long as you're picking a fund, you might as well pick a good one.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of equity funds failed to outperform market indexes in the 1980s?
Answers: Up to 75% of equity funds have been worse than mediocre, failing to outgain random baskets of stocks in market indexes.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the modern paradox of fund management?
Answers: Most fund managers investing in stocks that make up the averages somehow manage to do worse than the averages themselves.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the theories for why funds underperform indexes?
Answers: Fund managers are lousy stockpickers, herd instinct creates closet indexers, large company stocks had a great run, or popularity of index funds creates self-fulfilling prophecy.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what would $100,000 in Vanguard 500 index fund be worth from 1983-1991?
Answers: $308,450, compared to only $236,367 in the average managed equity fund over the same 8-year period.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what does the Investment Vision study show about chasing past performance?
Answers: Investing in prior 3-year best performers lagged S&P by 2.05%. Even 5- and 10-year best performers only beat S&P by 0.88% and 1.02% respectively.

Questions: What is your advice about past performance charts?
Answers: Don't spend a lot of time poring over past performance charts - it's better to stick with steady, consistent performers than move in and out trying to catch waves.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many funds have shown gains in every calendar year since 1978?
Answers: Only 9 out of 264 funds that go back to 1978 have shown gains every calendar year since then.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the best performer among funds with gains every year since 1977?
Answers: Phoenix Growth, with a compound annual gain of 20.2% since 1977.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, does paying a load mean you get a better fund?
Answers: Not necessarily. Some successful funds charge loads while others don't. If you plan to stick with a fund for several years, the 2-5% load becomes insignificant.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the 'too big to succeed' criticism of Magellan?
Answers: Beginning in 1983 at $1 billion, critics said Magellan was too big to succeed at $2B, $4B, $10B, and $14B, but it continued to outperform.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the drawbacks of running a big fund?
Answers: Like a linebacker on petits fours - you need considerable quantities to get nourishment. Can't buy enough small company shares to matter, takes months to build positions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are sector funds designed for?
Answers: For investors with special knowledge about a commodity or business prospects, not for whimsical speculation.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who are the best candidates for sector fund investing?
Answers: Jewelry store owners (gold), builders (lumber), insurance adjusters (rates), gas station managers (oil), doctors (drug approvals), scientists (biotech products).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Fidelity Biotechnology's performance in 1991 and 1992?
Answers: 99.05% gain in 1991, but down 21.5% through first nine months of 1992, showing the volatility of sector investing.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what have been the most and least profitable sectors over the past decade?
Answers: Most profitable: health care, financial services, utilities. Least profitable: precious metals.

Questions: Why is you getting interested in gold sector again?
Answers: Gold supply from new mines running out, decade of low prices discouraged exploration, demand increasing (especially China factor), potential inflation hedge.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are convertible funds and their advantage?
Answers: Funds investing in convertible bonds that combine high performance of small-cap stocks with stability of bonds, offering best of both worlds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how do convertible bonds work?
Answers: They pay lower interest than regular bonds but allow conversion to common stock at a specific price, usually 20-25% above current stock price.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the performance comparison in 1990 between convertible bonds and common stocks?
Answers: Common stocks connected to convertibles were down 27.3%, while convertible bonds themselves lost only 13% of value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the key difference between closed-end and open-ended funds?
Answers: Closed-end funds have static share counts and trade like stocks; open-ended funds create/retire shares as investors buy/sell.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what advantage do closed-end fund managers have?
Answers: Job security - the fund can't shrink due to customer exodus, so they can only fail by generating portfolio losses.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what opportunity exists with closed-end funds during market sell-offs?
Answers: Bargain hunters can buy closed-end funds at substantial discounts to their net asset value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are country funds and how many exist?
Answers: Funds that invest in specific countries, with at least 75 country and/or region funds in existence, growing with communist bloc breakup.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the best argument for country funds as long-term investments?
Answers: Foreign economies are growing faster than the U.S., causing their stock markets to advance faster than ours.

Questions: What example does you give of country fund overenthusiasm?
Answers: Germany Fund was bid up 25% above underlying stock values as Berlin Wall fell, then sold at 20-25% discount when reality set in.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when is the best time to buy a country fund?
Answers: When it's unpopular and you can get it for a 20-25% discount to underlying asset value.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the drawbacks of country funds?
Answers: High fees, currency risk, government policy risk, and need for knowledgeable managers who understand the local market.

Questions: What is your view on U.S. vs foreign companies?
Answers: The U.S. still has the best companies and system for investing - Europe lacks growth companies, information is sketchy, earnings estimates are unreliable.

Questions: What do you say about Japanese superiority claims?
Answers: It's malarkey - Japan is the richest country where people have trouble making ends meet, with $5 apples, $100 dinners, and $1 million, 1000-square-foot homes.

Questions: What was the problem with the Japanese market in your investment approach?
Answers: It was subject to behind-the-scenes manipulation unknown since the 1920s, with money-back guarantees from brokers and controlled stock prices.

Questions: What do you recommend for mutual fund strategies?
Answers: Put as much money into stock funds as possible, know what kinds you own, divide among 3-4 types, add money to lagging sectors, stick with solid performers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did the Magellan Fund originally start and what was it called?
Answers: The fund started in 1963 as the Fidelity International Fund, founded by Ned Johnson.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why did the International Fund become a domestic fund?
Answers: A tax on foreign investments promoted by President Kennedy forced international fund managers to sell foreign stocks and buy domestic stocks.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did the fund officially become Magellan?
Answers: It became Magellan on March 31, 1965, after two years as a domestic fund in disguise.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Magellan's biggest position when it launched in 1965?
Answers: Chrysler was the biggest position, which came back from bankruptcy 20 years later to become Lynch's biggest position.

Questions: What was you doing when Magellan was launched in 1965?
Answers: I was a student at Boston College, caddying golf games on weekends.

Questions: How did you's mother get involved in mutual funds?
Answers: A schoolteacher moonlighting as a fund salesman convinced her to buy Fidelity Capital because 'a Chinese guy' (Gerry Tsai) was running it.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to Magellan's assets from 1966 to 1976?
Answers: The fund declined from $20 million in 1966 to only $6 million by 1976 due to steady outflow from customer redemptions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was the Essex Fund merged with Magellan in 1976?
Answers: Essex had shrunk from $100 million to $12 million but had a valuable $50 million tax-loss carryforward that could benefit Magellan.

Questions: What was your situation when he took over Magellan in 1977?
Answers: $18 million in assets, $50 million tax-loss carryforward, terrible stock market, declining customers, and the fund was closed to new buyers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Magellan closed to new investors for four years?
Answers: Not by design - there was simply no interest. The fund business was so dismal that brokerage houses had disbanded sales departments.

Questions: What do you say about being brought along slowly as a fund manager?
Answers: The obscurity for the first four years was a blessing, enabling him to learn and make mistakes without being in a spotlight.

Questions: What was your background before managing Magellan?
Answers: He was director of research at Fidelity from 1974-1977, served on the investment committee, and had begun helping a Boston charity manage its portfolio in 1975.

Questions: What was your first stock pick that he missed as a 30-bagger?
Answers: General Cinema, which was selling for less than $1 when he visited on October 12, 1977, and went to over $30.

Questions: What were your biggest positions by December 1977?
Answers: Congoleum (51,000 shares worth $833,000), Transamerica, Union Oil, and Aetna Life and Casualty.

Questions: How did you discover Hanes stock?
Answers: Through his wife Carolyn, who was crazy about their L'eggs pantyhose product.

Questions: What was your reaction when he first ordered Taco Bell stock?
Answers: His trader Charlie Maxfield asked 'What's that, the Mexican telephone company?' showing how unknown the company was.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #7?
Answers: The extravagance of any corporate office is directly proportional to management's reluctance to reward the shareholders.

Questions: What attracted you to Congoleum?
Answers: It had invented seamless vinyl flooring that could be rolled out like carpet, and was building naval frigates using modular prefab techniques.

Questions: Why did you like Taco Bell initially?
Answers: Tasty tacos, 90% of country not yet exposed to them, good record, strong balance sheet, and home office that resembled a neighborhood garage.

Questions: What was Magellan's performance in your first 12 months?
Answers: The fund was up 20% while the Dow Jones average lost 17.6% and S&P 500 lost 9.4% in the same period.

Questions: How did you describe his early strategy in 1978?
Answers: 'Reduced holdings in autos, aerospace, railroads, pollution, utilities, chemicals, electronics, energy; added to financial institutions, broadcasting, entertainment, insurance, banking, consumer products, lodging, leasing.'

Questions: Did you have an overall strategy when he started?
Answers: No, I never had an overall strategy. His stockpicking was entirely empirical, going from case to case like a bloodhound following a scent.

Questions: How did you's approach differ from growth fund managers?
Answers: As a capital appreciation fund manager, he could buy anything when growth sectors were overvalued, while growth fund managers were forced into overpriced inventory.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what five categories did Magellan define for its investments in 1979?
Answers: Small and medium-sized growth companies, companies with improving prospects, depressed cyclicals, high-yielding dividend payers, and undervalued asset companies.

Questions: What was your turnover rate in the early years?
Answers: 343% in the first year with 41 stocks, and 300% in each of the three years thereafter - a very high trading pace.

Questions: Why was you trading so frequently in the early years?
Answers: He was constantly selling to raise cash for redemptions while discovering new prospects, and had to sell something to buy something new in the small fund.

Questions: What do you mean by 'pulling out the flowers and watering the weeds'?
Answers: Selling winning stocks too early while holding onto losing stocks - a common and expensive mistake he made early on.

Questions: Which great stocks did you sell too early?
Answers: Albertson's (300-bagger), Toys 'R' Us, Pic 'N' Save, Warner Communications, Federal Express ($5 to $70 in two years), and Home Depot.

Questions: How did you learn about companies in his early years?
Answers: He visited dozens at headquarters, attended regional investment conferences, and companies came to Fidelity for lunches, breakfasts, and dinners.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Fidelity's policy of 'taking a corporation to lunch'?
Answers: This replaced lunches with cronies - every week they had printed menus of corporate guests, enabling access to hundreds of companies annually.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Boston advantageous for seeing companies?
Answers: As the mutual fund capital, executives could make rounds of multiple firms in one trip, and both sides initiated these educational exchanges.

Questions: What was your monthly rule for industry contact?
Answers: Once a month he tried to have at least one conversation with a representative of each major industry group as an early-warning system.

Questions: What question did you always ask at the end of company meetings?
Answers: Which of your competitors do you respect the most? When a CEO admits a rival is doing better, it's a powerful endorsement.

Questions: What do you say about being lied to in corporate meetings?
Answers: In thousands of encounters, he was lied to only a handful of times - there may be fewer liars on Wall Street than Main Street.

Questions: Why are there fewer liars on Wall Street in your investment approach?
Answers: Financial types are so widely distrusted that every claim is reviewed by the SEC, so they aren't allowed to lie, and lies can't survive quarterly earnings reports.

Questions: How did you learn about the insurance industry?
Answers: Through crash courses from executives at Aetna, Travelers, and Connecticut General in Hartford over a couple of days.

Questions: What was your insurance allocation in March 1980?
Answers: 25.4% of the fund was in property or casualty underwriters, making him insurance's best friend.

Questions: How did you discover the potential in bank stocks?
Answers: At a Robinson-Humphrey conference in Atlanta, he took a side trip to visit First Atlanta, which had 12 years of continuously higher earnings.

Questions: What impressed you about regional banks?
Answers: First Atlanta had earnings greater than the sales of many flashy companies, yet solid banks were selling for half the P/E ratio of the market.

Questions: Which banks does you show as examples of great performance?
Answers: Wachovia (10-fold increase in 10 years), Norwest of Minneapolis, and NBD Bancorp of Detroit - all looking like fast-growth company charts.

Questions: Why are regional banks mispriced in your investment approach?
Answers: Banks growing at 15% like Pep Boys or Dunkin' Donuts get low P/E multiples, treated like mature utilities instead of growth companies.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Magellan's bank allocation strategy?
Answers: Lynch consistently had four or five times the market weighting in bank stocks due to these mispricings.

Questions: What was your bond strategy in early 1982?
Answers: With Treasury bonds paying 13-14%, I made them his biggest position because yields exceeded normal stock returns.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #8?
Answers: When yields on long-term government bonds exceed the dividend yield of the S&P 500 by 6% or more, sell your stocks and buy bonds.

Questions: Why doesn't you recommend preparing for total disaster?
Answers: If total disaster strikes, cash will be as useless as stock certificates, but if it doesn't (more likely), the 'cautious' become reckless by selling valuable assets.

Questions: How did you approach the 1982 recession fears?
Answers: He focused on the Even Bigger Picture, assumed the worst wouldn't happen, and asked what would happen if it didn't - leading him to both stocks and bonds.

Questions: What led you to Chrysler in March 1982?
Answers: He got interested in Ford as an auto rebound play, and talking to Ford convinced him Chrysler would benefit even more.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Chrysler selling for only $2 in 1982?
Answers: Wall Street expected the number-three automaker to go bankrupt like Penn Central, but Lynch found over $1 billion in cash on the balance sheet.

Questions: What convinced you that Chrysler could survive?
Answers: The company had capacity to survive at least a couple of years, the government had guaranteed loans, and the entire industry was due for a rebound.

Questions: What new products excited you about Chrysler's future?
Answers: The Dodge Daytona, Chrysler Laser, G-124 Turbo Car, convertibles, sportier New Yorker, and especially the T-115 minivan.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what did Iacocca call 'the first new thing in the auto industry in twenty years'?
Answers: The T-115, which became the Chrysler minivan and sold over 3 million copies in nine years, saving the company.

Questions: What time did your working day begin?
Answers: my working day began at 6:05 A.M. when he met his carpool ride with radiologists Jeff and Bobbie Moore.

Questions: What was you doing during his carpool ride?
Answers: I sat in the back with a small light, perusing annual reports and chart books, while Bobbie held X-rays up to a light in the front seat.

Questions: What time did you arrive at the office?
Answers: By 6:45 A.M., but he wasn't alone - Fidelity was full of analysts and fund managers who arrived before dawn.

Questions: What were your 'sophisticated tools of the trade'?
Answers: The S&P stock guide (free from brokers), antique Rolodex, empty yellow legal pads, 21⁄2 pencils, and clunky Sharp calculator with oversize buttons.

Questions: Why did you prefer the old Quotron system?
Answers: The blank screen was better because you couldn't stare at it all day watching stocks go up and down - he had to turn off the newer versions.

Questions: What did you do in the precious morning hours before market opened?
Answers: Reviewed buy/sell summaries from the day before, read in-house analyst reports, read Wall Street Journal, and wrote out new buy/sell lists.

Questions: Who were your head traders?
Answers: Barry Lyden handled buys, and later Carlene DeLuca was assigned to handle sells, both very patient with my extensive trading lists.

Questions: How much time did you spend on trading?
Answers: About an hour a day instead of 10 minutes - he admits he should have used the extra 50 minutes to call two more companies.

Questions: What is your key insight about successful investing?
Answers: Focus on the companies, not on the stocks - this is one of the keys to successful investing.

Questions: How did you keep track of his company contacts?
Answers: He wrote down the name of everyone he met and kept detailed notes in loose-leaf binders with company names, stock prices, and story summaries.

Questions: Why did you avoid the lobby when going to the bathroom?
Answers: Corporate guests and analysts waited there, and he'd have to waste time on small talk or snub friends, so he snuck down a back stairway.

Questions: Who was your first assistant and what happened to him?
Answers: Rich Fentin set the standard for quality and went on to run the Fidelity Growth and Fidelity Puritan funds.

Questions: What other successful fund managers came from your assistant program?
Answers: Danny Frank (Special Situations), George Noble (Overseas Fund), Bob Stansky (Growth), Will Danoff (Contrafund), and Jeff Vinik (later ran Magellan).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was revolutionary about Fidelity's research approach?
Answers: Fund managers were required to do their own research rather than relying on analysts' recommendations, making them accountable for results.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Fidelity's system differ from traditional fund management?
Answers: Traditional managers choose stocks from analyst recommendations and blame analysts when stocks fail; Fidelity managers did independent research.

Questions: What advantage did you have as a capital appreciation fund manager?
Answers: He had the widest latitude to buy stocks recommended by special situations, small-stock, growth, value, and over-the-counter specialists.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Fidelity formalize information sharing?
Answers: Random hallway powwows were replaced by scheduled conference room meetings where all analysts and fund managers presented weekly picks.

Questions: What was your innovation with the kitchen timer?
Answers: He pretended to set it at three minutes for presentations but actually shortened it to 90 seconds to keep discussions focused.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why were the presentations non-combative?
Answers: Combat isn't the best way to arrive at truth about stocks; hostile receptions might undermine confidence in future recommendations.

Questions: What was your approach to feedback at presentations?
Answers: No feedback was allowed - listeners could follow up on leads or ignore them, focusing on idea quality rather than speaker quality.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did fund managers share information with competitors?
Answers: They eagerly shared buy lists with each other after acquiring their planned positions, with competitors returning the favor.

Questions: How did you evaluate outside analysts?
Answers: He was selective, noting great variation in quality and preferring analysts who called companies regularly and visited them in person.

Questions: Who were some of your trusted outside analysts?
Answers: Maggie Gilliam at First Boston (Home Depot, Limited), John Kellenyi at NatWest (utilities), Elliot Schneider at Gruntal (financial services).

Questions: What made certain analysts valuable to you?
Answers: Analysts who reinforced opinions with multiple reports as stocks rose, not just initial buy signals that were quickly forgotten.

Questions: How did you's patience change by 1981?
Answers: He became more patient, redemptions were down so he wasn't forced to sell for cash, and turnover dropped from 300% to 110%.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Magellan's size and ranking in 1981?
Answers: $100 million in assets, putting it in the bottom fifth of all general equity funds, with 200 different stocks.

Questions: What types of companies did you favor in 1981?
Answers: John Blair (broadcaster), Tandy (Radio Shack), Quixote (plastic barriers), Telecredit, ChemLawn, Seven Oaks (coupon processor), various restaurant chains.

Questions: Why was you impressed with restaurant chains and retailers?
Answers: By expanding across the country, these companies could maintain 20% growth rates for 10-15 years with favorable math.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the Rule of 72?
Answers: Divide 72 by the annual return percentage to get the number of years it takes to double your money.

Questions: Why did you prefer retailers and restaurants over high-tech companies?
Answers: They were less risky - a computer company can lose half its value overnight, but a donut chain won't lose business when a competitor opens in another state.

Questions: What was your biggest holding at the end of 1981?
Answers: Mattel, the toy maker, which was 3% of the fund.

Questions: What characterized your top 10 holdings in early 1982?
Answers: Companies like Chemical Bank, Pic 'N' Save, Verbatim, Horn & Hardart, and Pep Boys - strong balance sheets with favorable prospects.

Questions: Why could you buy offbeat companies like Seven Oaks?
Answers: In a wide-open fund like Magellan, nobody was looking over his shoulder, unlike managers subject to hierarchical second-guessing.

Questions: What do you say about professional responsibility and monitoring?
Answers: When you have to worry about what someone behind you thinks, you cease to be professional and doubt your ability to succeed.

Questions: What luxury did you have by 1982?
Answers: Instead of selling one stock to buy another, new money was pouring in at $40-71 million per month, allowing him to maintain old positions while initiating new ones.

Questions: How did you's stock focus change as Magellan grew?
Answers: Ironically, when Magellan was small he concentrated on bigger stocks, and when it became bigger he found himself concentrating on smaller stocks.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to Magellan's popularity in 1983?
Answers: Another $76 million in February, $100 million in March had to be invested, making fund growth and stock selection increasingly challenging.

Questions: Why was you depressed by the early 1983 market?
Answers: The Dow had advanced 300 points from 1982 lows, technology issues reached giddy heights - he preferred corrections that created bargains.

Questions: What do you say about bargains and market sell-offs?
Answers: Bargains are the holy grail of the true stockpicker; corrections are opportunities to acquire more shares at low prices, not disasters.

Questions: What remained your biggest holding through 1983?
Answers: Chrysler remained at 5% of the fund (SEC maximum) and stayed his biggest holding for most of the year.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did Magellan hit the $1 billion milestone?
Answers: April 1983, which elicited a 'great ho-hum' at the office, soon followed by criticism that it was too big to succeed.

Questions: What was the structure of your day by the mid-1980s?
Answers: 6:05 AM carpool, 6:45 arrival, morning preparation, trading orders by 8 AM, then constant phone calls and company research until late.

Questions: How many companies did you visit annually?
Answers: His visits escalated from 214 in 1980 to 330 in 1982, 489 in 1983, 411 in 1984, 463 in 1985, and 570 in 1986.

Questions: What was your approach to corporate lunches as Magellan grew?
Answers: He cut back on lunches in favor of more efficient phone calls while eating sandwiches, having developed enough sources from earlier lunches.

Questions: How did you's office setup facilitate his work style?
Answers: Four secretaries led by Paula Sullivan routed calls, chairs had become file cabinets so visitors couldn't sit, forcing brief interactions.

Questions: What was your rule about keeping up with companies?
Answers: He kept detailed notebooks of every contact with companies, including stock prices and story summaries, essential for tracking hundreds of investments.

Questions: How did you use his Saturday work time?
Answers: Devoted to cleaning his desk, reviewing three-foot-high stacks of mail, perusing annual reports in February/March, and reviewing company notebooks.

Questions: What was your Saturday goal?
Answers: To see some wood (desktop) at the end of the afternoon, though he didn't always achieve it.

Questions: How did you handle the terrible first half of 1982?
Answers: Prime rate hit double digits along with inflation and unemployment; he bought Treasury bonds paying 13-14% as his biggest position.

Questions: Why did you buy bonds in 1982?
Answers: Not for defensive purposes due to fear of stocks, but because bond yields exceeded normal expected returns from stocks.

Questions: What convinced you not to prepare for total economic collapse?
Answers: If the economy collapsed, he'd be fishing with everyone else and portfolio strategy would be irrelevant; if not, he wanted to be in stocks and bonds.

Questions: How did you approach the 1982 recession?
Answers: He assumed the worst wouldn't happen and asked 'what then?' - figuring interest rates had to come down and both stocks and bonds would profit.

Questions: How do you describe the relationship between research time and number of stocks owned?
Answers: How much time you spend researching stocks is directly proportional to how many stocks you own. It takes a few hours a year to keep up with each one.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many stocks did Magellan have by mid-1983 and fall 1983?
Answers: By mid-1983 there were 450 stocks, and by fall the number had doubled to 900 stocks in the portfolio.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Magellan's size ranking by end of 1983?
Answers: Magellan was running a close second to John Neff's Vanguard Windsor as the largest mutual fund, with $1.6 billion in assets.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #9?
Answers: Not all common stocks are equally common.

Questions: How do you defend having 900 stocks in the portfolio?
Answers: An imaginative fund manager can pick 1,000+ stocks in unusual companies that will never appear in standard Wall Street portfolios, 'flying off the radar scope.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of Magellan's 900 stocks in 1983 were tiny positions?
Answers: 700 of the 900 stocks accounted for less than 10% of the fund's total assets.

Questions: What were your two reasons for taking tiny positions?
Answers: 1) Companies were quite small, so even owning 10% didn't amount to much, or 2) He wasn't convinced they deserved substantial commitment.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the Jan Bell Marketing meeting lead to a major opportunity?
Answers: Jan Bell executives mentioned their best customers were discount clubs ordering tremendous jewelry, leading Lynch to invest in Costco, Wholesale Club, and Pace.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Will Danoff's role in the discount club discovery?
Answers: Lynch asked Danoff, the retail analyst who later took over Contrafund, to research the discount clubs after the Jan Bell tip.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why were discount club stocks available at bargain prices?
Answers: After IPO euphoria faded, expectations were too lofty, stocks sold off, and Wall Street lost interest with no analysts following them.

Questions: What were the results from your discount club investments?
Answers: All three made money - Costco was a triple, proving the value of following up on unexpected leads.

Questions: How many S&Ls did you buy in April 1983?
Answers: 39 of his 83 new acquisitions in April 1983 were banks or S&Ls, eventually totaling 100 S&Ls making 3% of the fund.

Questions: What was your approach to building positions in auto stocks?
Answers: He made what's known as an 'industry bet' by analyzing each company case-by-case rather than arbitrarily deciding on 8% auto allocation.

Questions: Which auto companies did you favor over General Motors and why?
Answers: Ford, Chrysler, and Volvo because GM was arrogant, myopic, and resting on laurels - saying it was miserable was about the nicest compliment you could give GM.

Questions: What were the profits from your major auto positions?
Answers: Well over $100 million each from Ford and Chrysler, plus $79 million from Volvo over the six-year stretch from 1982-1988.

Questions: What was the key to Magellan's superior results in your investment approach?
Answers: Huge gains in a few huge positions, not diversification across many small positions.

Questions: How do you respond to concerns about 'liquidity' in stock selection?
Answers: In stocks as in romance, ease of divorce is not a sound basis for commitment - if you've chosen wisely, you won't want a divorce.

Questions: What examples does you give of liquid stocks that still lost money?
Answers: Polaroid (lost 90% in 1973) and Xerox - both were actively traded and easy to sell, but fund managers still lost money by not wanting to get out.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of stocks trade fewer than 10,000 shares daily?
Answers: 99% of all stocks trade fewer than 10,000 shares daily, so liquidity-focused managers confine themselves to only 1% of all companies.

Questions: How did you acquire large positions in some stocks?
Answers: Occasionally through large institutional blocks (2 million shares of Owens-Corning, 2 million of BankAmerica), but usually through constant nibbling over months.

Questions: What determined your vacation destinations?
Answers: Time zones and phone booth locations - Austria was good because it was afternoon there before U.S. markets opened.

Questions: Where was your favorite U.S. ski location and why?
Answers: Balsam's in Dixville Notch, New Hampshire, because it had a phone at the bottom of the lift for calling in trades.

Questions: When did you begin investing heavily in foreign stocks?
Answers: Foreign buying began in earnest in 1984, with I being the first domestic fund manager after John Templeton to invest heavily abroad.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of Magellan was in foreign stocks by 1986?
Answers: 10% of Magellan's assets were invested in foreign equities by 1986.

Questions: What was your most successful research trip?
Answers: Mid-September 1985: three weeks, 23 companies across Europe, leading to over $200 million in profits from foreign stock picks.

Questions: What happened to your luggage on the European trip?
Answers: Sabena airline lost his luggage, but he was outfitted in a proper Swedish suit by his host's husband who had his exact measurements.

Questions: What companies did you visit in Sweden?
Answers: Esselte (office equipment), ASEA (conglomerate), Alfa Laval (milking machines/biogenetics), Electrolux (appliances), Aga (gases), Ericsson (telephones), Skandia (insurance).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what made Skandia an attractive investment?
Answers: A rate increase had been approved which should have boosted the stock, but Swedish investors ignored good news and focused on lousy current earnings.

Questions: What was special about your Volvo discovery?
Answers: The stock price was $34 and the company had $34 per share in cash, so he was getting the auto business and subsidiaries for nothing.

Questions: What lesson did you learn about driving on the German autobahn?
Answers: Peter's Principle #10: Never look back when you're driving on the autobahn - he found a Mercedes three inches from his bumper at 120 mph.

Questions: Why couldn't you visit Sandoz in Switzerland?
Answers: When he called to arrange a meeting, the vice-president kept asking 'Why?' to every explanation until I gave up and said goodbye.

Questions: What Italian companies did you visit?
Answers: Montedison (hydroelectric), IFI, and Olivetti, plus he saw The Last Supper - listing all four as his favorite northern Italian attractions.

Questions: What was your insight about Italy in 1985?
Answers: Italy was like America in the 1940s-50s - a place where appliance companies, electric companies, and supermarkets would be future fast growers.

Questions: What were your top eleven foreign stock gains?
Answers: Peugeot, Volvo, Skandia, Esselte, Electrolux, Aga, Norsk Hydro, Montedison, IFI, Tobu Railway, and Kinki Nippon Railway made over $200 million in profits.

Questions: Which was your biggest foreign stock winner?
Answers: Tobu Railway with 386% gain in five years, though it was only 0.13% of Magellan's assets.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did Magellan pass the $5 billion mark?
Answers: February 1986, requiring Lynch to buy more Ford, Chrysler, and Volvo to maintain their weightings.

Questions: What was your experience calling trades from Yosemite?
Answers: Standing in a phone booth overlooking mountains, he spent two hours giving trades and only got from A's through L's in his alphabetical holdings list.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to Carlene DeLuca?
Answers: She left the trading desk to marry Fidelity's former president Jack O'Brien; on her last day they let her do buys instead of sells.

Questions: What major tactical shift did you make in 1987?
Answers: He began deemphasizing autos and upgrading financial companies, particularly Fannie Mae and S&Ls, as the economic recovery matured.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when did Magellan become a $10 billion fund?
Answers: May 1987, providing more ammunition for critics saying it was too big to beat the market.

Questions: What kept you motivated despite the 'too big' criticism?
Answers: Skeptics said $1B, $2B, $4B, $6B, $8B, and $10B were all too big, and he was determined to prove them wrong.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #12?
Answers: A sure cure for taking a stock for granted is a big drop in the price.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Magellan perform during market declines vs. rebounds?
Answers: During nine major declines, Magellan fell more than the market average, but outperformed on the rebound - a consistent pattern.

Questions: What was your approach to preparing shareholders for volatility?
Answers: He warned in annual reports of Magellan's tendency to get swamped in choppy waters, believing preparation prevents panic.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the Great Correction affect Magellan's size?
Answers: What was an $11 billion fund in August became a $7.2 billion fund by October - the GNP of Costa Rica was lost in a week.

Questions: What forced you to sell during the 1987 crash?
Answers: $689 million in sales and $1.3 billion in redemptions in October, forcing him to be a seller when he'd prefer to be a buyer.

Questions: What lesson does you draw about shareholders and fund performance?
Answers: Shareholders play a major role in success or failure - if they refuse to panic, fund managers won't have to liquidate at unfavorable prices.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happened to cyclical stocks after the 1987 correction?
Answers: Cyclicals like Chrysler and Ford rallied strongly initially but disappointed over the next three years, showing the importance of timing exits.

Questions: What is your warning about cyclicals?
Answers: Cyclicals are like blackjack - stay in the game too long and it's bound to take back all your profit.

Questions: What stocks became your focus after reducing autos?
Answers: Growth stocks with high-quality operations: Philip Morris, RJR Nabisco, Eastman Kodak, Merck, Atlantic Richfield, plus General Electric.

Questions: What was your biggest single stock winner?
Answers: Fannie Mae, where Magellan made $500 million profit in five years, while all Fidelity funds combined made over $1 billion - possibly an all-time record.

Questions: What were your second through fourth biggest winners?
Answers: Ford ($199 million from 1985-1989), Philip Morris ($111 million), and MCI ($92 million).

Questions: What characterized your nine all-time winners?
Answers: Two automakers, cigarette/food company, tobacco/insurance conglomerate, electric utility with accident, telephone company, diversified financial company, entertainment company, student loan buyer.

Questions: What do you say about his most consistent losers?
Answers: Technology stocks were his most consistent losers, including $25 million on Digital in 1988, plus losses on Tandem, Motorola, Texas Instruments, and IBM.

Questions: What do you say about stockpicking being reducible to a formula?
Answers: Stockpicking can't be reduced to a simple formula or recipe that guarantees success - the 160+ pages describing his 21 stock picks prove this.

Questions: How do you describe stockpicking as both art and science?
Answers: Stockpicking is both art and science, but too much of either is dangerous - pure measurement or pure intuition both lead to poor results.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happens when someone is infatuated with measurement in investing?
Answers: A person with his head stuck in the sand of balance sheets is not likely to succeed - if you could tell the future from balance sheets, mathematicians would be richest.

Questions: What historical example does you give of measurement obsession?
Answers: Thales, the early Greek philosopher who was so intent on counting stars that he kept falling into potholes in the road.

Questions: How do you describe the 'art' approach to investing?
Answers: The realm of intuition and passion where artistic types believe success is about having a knack and following hunches, leading to neglect of research.

Questions: What tools does you prefer over high-tech trading systems?
Answers: I uses a basic Quotron, not the newfangled workstations with elaborate features - he believes professionals are missing the point with fancy software.

Questions: What do you say about Warren Buffett and technology?
Answers: Trust me, Warren Buffett doesn't use fancy trading software and technology systems.

Questions: Where should professional investors spend more time in your investment approach?
Answers: They should spend more time at the mall rather than scrambling to buy services to find out what other professionals are doing.

Questions: How many stocks did you recommend in previous Barron's panels?
Answers: 1986: over 100 stocks, 1987: 226 stocks, 1988: 122 stocks, 1989: 91 stocks, 1990: 73 stocks.

Questions: What was Alan Abelson's reaction to your extensive recommendations?
Answers: 'Maybe we should have asked you what you don't like' and 'You are an equal-opportunity buyer. You're being nondiscriminatory.'

Questions: What is your philosophy about searching for companies?
Answers: Searching for companies is like looking for grubs under rocks: turn over 10 rocks, find one grub; turn over 20 rocks, find two grubs.

Questions: How many recommendations did you make in 1991 and 1992?
Answers: 21 companies in 1991 and 21 again in 1992, reduced from his full-time days due to part-time status.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the Rule of Five for part-time stockpickers?
Answers: The smallest investor can limit portfolio to five issues. If one is a 10-bagger and four go nowhere, you've still tripled your money.

Questions: How did you feel about the overpriced market in January 1992?
Answers: He was the most depressed person on the panel because overpriced markets with stocks hitting new highs are harder to find bargains in.

Questions: What do you prefer - rising or falling markets?
Answers: The devoted stockpicker is happier when the market drops 300 points than when it rises the same amount, because drops create bargains.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, which large growth stocks had strayed above their earnings lines by 1992?
Answers: Philip Morris, Abbott, Wal-Mart, and Bristol-Myers had risen far above their earnings lines - a bad sign.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what happens to stocks priced higher than their earnings lines?
Answers: They have a regular habit of moving sideways or falling until brought back to reasonable valuations.

Questions: What was your prediction for growth stocks in 1992?
Answers: Much-ballyhooed growth stocks that were 1991 champions would do nothing or go sideways in 1992, or suffer 30% declines in a bad market.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how can you tell if a large growth stock is overvalued?
Answers: Look at a chart book - buy when stock price is at or below the earnings line, not when price diverges into the danger zone above earnings.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what creates bargains in November and December?
Answers: Annual tax-loss selling by disheartened investors drives prices of smaller issues to pathetic lows.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the January effect?
Answers: Prices rebound in January after tax-selling, especially powerful with smaller companies - they've risen 6.86% in January vs 1.6% for stocks generally over 60 years.

Questions: Where did you expect to find bargains in 1992?
Answers: In small stocks, where he expected bargains while large growth stocks were overpriced.

Questions: What do you say about reviewing previous stock picks?
Answers: Don't pick new companies just for another quote to watch - getting involved with manageable numbers and confining buys/sells to these is a good strategy.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why should investors stick with companies they've researched?
Answers: Once you've bought a stock, you've learned about the industry and company's behavior, giving you an advantage when it becomes a bargain again.

Questions: What is the common practice you criticizes about stock trading?
Answers: Buying, selling, and forgetting a long string of companies is not likely to succeed, yet many investors continue this approach.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why do people avoid looking at stocks they once owned?
Answers: Human nature causes avoidance of stocks that went up after selling them, like sneaking around aisles to avoid an old flame in a supermarket.

Questions: How do you keep track of his investment stories?
Answers: He carries large wire-bound notebooks recording important details from quarterly/annual reports plus reasons for buying/selling each stock.

Questions: What do you compare his notebooks to?
Answers: Other people thumbing through love letters found in the attic - he reviews these investment stories at home or on the way to office.

Questions: How did you review his 21 selections from 1991?
Answers: It was a mixed bag that did extremely well, rising 50%+ while S&P rose 30%, including various sectors from insurance to biotechnology.

Questions: What were some of your 1991 stock recommendations?
Answers: Kemper, Household International, Cedar Fair, EQK Green Acres, Reebok, Caesars World, Phelps Dodge, Coca-Cola Enterprises, Genentech, AFLAC, K mart.

Questions: Why did you reject Cedar Fair for 1992?
Answers: The stock had risen from under $12 to $18, reducing yield from 11% to 8.5%, with no indication of improved earnings ahead.

Questions: What warning sign did you see in EQK Green Acres' quarterly report?
Answers: The company was debating whether to pay the regular quarterly dividend increase of one cent to save $100,000 - breaking a 6-year string for paltry savings.

Questions: What do you say about buying on bad news vs. good news?
Answers: 'Buy at sound of cannons, sell at sound of trumpets' can be misguided - buying on bad news can be costly since bad news often gets worse.

Questions: What is your preference regarding news and stock purchases?
Answers: Buying on good news is healthier long-run; wait for proof rather than rumors to improve odds considerably.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how should investors handle loving a company but not the current price?
Answers: Make a small commitment and increase it in the next sell-off rather than avoiding the stock entirely.

Questions: What do you say about year-end bargain hunting?
Answers: Act quickly! Bargain hunters find bargains fast these days, and by the time they're finished buying, stocks aren't bargains anymore.

Questions: What happened to Toll Brothers stock that you identified as a bargain?
Answers: He found it at $2.38 (down from $12.63), put it at top of his list in October, but it quadrupled to $8 before he could publish the recommendation.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Good Guys situation in 1991?
Answers: The stock rose dramatically between January 14 (Barron's meeting) and January 21 (publication), forcing deletion from the published recommendations.

Questions: Why do you look for companies that benefit subtly from overblown crises?
Answers: When markets overreact to news, there are often indirect beneficiaries that get overlooked but will profit when conditions normalize.

Questions: What approach does you take to continuing sagas vs. disconnected events?
Answers: He thinks of investments as continuing sagas needing periodic review for new plot twists rather than disconnected events.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, when is a company's story never over?
Answers: Unless a company goes bankrupt, the story is never over - a stock owned 10 years ago may be worth buying again.

Questions: What do you say about the January 1992 market atmosphere?
Answers: In the festive atmosphere of a recent 300-point Dow gain, optimism abounded, but I was most depressed by the overpriced conditions.

Questions: Where does you find his favorite source of investment ideas?
Answers: The Burlington Mall, located 25 miles from his hometown of Marblehead.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many huge covered malls exist in the United States?
Answers: There are only 450 or so huge covered malls in the United States.

Questions: What investment strategy does you say is superior to taking a stockbroker's advice?
Answers: Hanging out at the mall is far superior to taking a stockbroker's advice on faith or combing financial press for tips.

Questions: What example does you give of retail investment success?
Answers: $10,000 invested in 1986 in each of Home Depot, Limited, Gap, and Wal-Mart, held for 5 years, was worth over $500,000 by end of 1991.

Questions: What retail companies does you pass on his drive to Burlington Mall?
Answers: Two Radio Shacks (Tandy), Toys 'R' Us, Kids 'R' Us, Ames Department Store, LensCrafters, Howard Johnson's, Taco Bell, and Chili's.

Questions: What do you note about Toys 'R' Us performance?
Answers: It went from 25 cents to $36, representing a massive return for early investors.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how is the Burlington Mall laid out?
Answers: In the form of a giant cross, anchored by Jordan Marsh (east), Filene's (south), Lord & Taylor (north), and Sears (west).

Questions: What do you say about the mall's resemblance to an old town square?
Answers: It reminds him of an old town square with ponds, park benches, trees, and promenade, but with 160 enterprises instead of traditional shops.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #14?
Answers: If you like the store, chances are you'll love the stock.

Questions: What makes retail investing particularly profitable in your investment approach?
Answers: The homogeneity of taste in food and fashion that makes for dull culture also makes fortunes for retail and restaurant company owners.

Questions: What examples does you give of successful retail expansion?
Answers: Westward Ho of Home Depot (Atlanta), Eastward Ho of Taco Bell (California), Southward Ho of Lands' End (Wisconsin), Northward Ho of Wal-Mart (Arkansas).

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what advantage do mall employees have in stock picking?
Answers: They see what's going on daily and get word from colleagues about which stores are thriving - better tips than Ivan Boesky ever got.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who has the greatest advantage in retail stock picking?
Answers: Mall managers with access to monthly sales figures used to compute rents.

Questions: How did you's daughters lead him to investment ideas?
Answers: Annie asked 'Is Clearly Canadian a public company?' and they often wore Chili's sweatshirts, but I ignored these signals initially.

Questions: What was your mistake with Clearly Canadian?
Answers: He looked it up, didn't see it in S&P book, and forgot about it. The stock went from $3 to $26.75 (9-bagger) in one year after going public in 1991.

Questions: What do you say about children as investment advisors?
Answers: Children are part of an international tribe with same taste in caps, T-shirts, socks, and jeans - when his daughter shops at Gap, teenagers nationwide are doing the same.

Questions: When did your daughter Mary initiate coverage on the Gap?
Answers: Summer 1990, buying school wardrobe from the Burlington Mall store when Gap had moved beyond just jeans to colorful new merchandise.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, where are the most popular retailers usually located in double-decker malls?
Answers: Upstairs, because managers arrange it so maximum customers pass maximum stores on their way to the busiest, most profitable locations.

Questions: What led you to investigate the Body Shop?
Answers: His three daughters headed there during a 'Christmas present trip' that was actually my research expedition.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what products does the Body Shop sell?
Answers: Lotions and bath oil made from bananas, nuts, berries; beeswax mascara; kiwi-fruit lip balm; carrot moisture cream; Rhassoul mud shampoo.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what made the Body Shop one of the most crowded stores?
Answers: Along with Gap and Nature Company, Body Shop occupied 3,000 square feet but appeared to do as much business as Sears with 100,000 square feet.

Questions: Who first recommended Body Shop to you and when?
Answers: Analyst Monica Kalmanson recommended it at a 1990 Fidelity meeting, and head librarian Cathy Stephenson left to open a Body Shop franchise.

Questions: What was your embarrassing discovery about Body Shop?
Answers: He had already bought shares in 1989 and forgotten - it was one of many 'tune in later' stocks in his 1,400-company portfolio.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, who founded the Body Shop and how?
Answers: Anita Roddick, an ambitious housewife whose husband was frequently out of town, began tinkering with potions in her garage.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Body Shop's initial public offering performance?
Answers: Came public in 1984 for 5 pence (roughly 10 cents), turned into 362 pence - more than 70-fold return in six years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are the Body Shop's socially conscious practices?
Answers: Uses natural ingredients, shuns advertising, gives employees paid community service leave, promotes health over beauty, recycles bags, pays refill rewards.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how successful was Cathy Stephenson's Body Shop franchise?
Answers: She turned a profit in the first year and was preparing to open a second store in Harvard Square during a recession.

Questions: What impressed you about the Body Shop's expansion approach?
Answers: The company was proceeding carefully and expanding with caution, requiring chairman approval even for proven franchisees' second stores.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was concerning about Body Shop's P/E ratio?
Answers: 42 times estimated 1992 earnings, which Lynch considers dangerously high for any growth stock.

Questions: What is your rule of thumb for growth stock pricing?
Answers: A stock should sell at or below its growth rate - even fastest-growing companies rarely achieve more than 25% growth sustainably.

Questions: How did you compare Body Shop to Coca-Cola valuations?
Answers: Body Shop: 30% grower at 40x earnings vs. Coca-Cola: 15% grower at 30x earnings - he preferred the higher growth despite higher multiple.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the key question about Body Shop's future?
Answers: Whether it could maintain 25-30% growth rate long enough for the stock to 'catch up' to its lofty current price.

Questions: What gave you confidence in Body Shop's global potential?
Answers: It was international almost from the start, installed on six continents, had hardly scratched the surface of any of them.

Questions: What do you say about Wal-Mart's long-term success story?
Answers: Shows how stocks that have gone up 10-50 fold can still go higher - Wal-Mart was a great investment in multiple decades.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Wal-Mart's expansion timeline?
Answers: 1970: 38 stores (mostly Arkansas); 1975: 104 stores; 1980: 276 stores; even after 20-fold gain, there were stores in only 15% of country.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what were the returns for Wal-Mart investors who bought after the initial success?
Answers: Bought in 1980 after 20-fold gain: made 30-fold gain 1980-1990, plus another 60% in 1991 - 50-bagger in 11 years total.

Questions: What is your key insight about retail company growth?
Answers: As long as same-store sales increase, company isn't crippled by excessive debt, and follows expansion plans, it usually pays to stick with the stock.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how much time do investors have to catch onto retail success stories?
Answers: You don't have to rush in during garage phase - Lynch found Body Shop 8 years after IPO when it still had room to grow significantly.

Questions: What do you say about getting in 'too late' on successful stocks?
Answers: If anybody tells you a stock that's gone up 10-50 fold can't go higher, show them the Wal-Mart chart.

Questions: What do you say about investing in fearsome places?
Answers: You've got to go into places where other investors and fund managers fear to tread - the most fearsome places in 1991 were connected to housing and real estate.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how long had real estate been the principal national scare?
Answers: Real estate had been the principal national scare for more than two years by the time Lynch was writing.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the popular belief about the real estate collapse?
Answers: The famous collapse of commercial real estate was rumored to be spreading into residential real estate with house prices plummeting rapidly.

Questions: What evidence did you see of real estate despair in his neighborhood?
Answers: So many for-sale signs sprouted in Marblehead that the for-sale sign seemed like the new state flower of Massachusetts.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why did real estate collapse get so much media attention?
Answers: Newspaper editors, TV commentators, and Wall Street money managers owned fat-cat houses, so the collapse got front-page and nightly news coverage.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what quiet fact contradicted the real estate collapse narrative?
Answers: The National Association of Realtors reported that the price of the median house was going up - it had risen in 1989, 1990, and 1991.

Questions: What other quiet facts supported your contrarian view?
Answers: The 'affordability index' from National Association of Home Builders and percentage of mortgage loans in default told a different story than headlines.

Questions: What is your technique for investing in troubled industries?
Answers: Wait until prevailing opinion is that things have gone from bad to worse, then buy shares in the strongest companies in the group.

Questions: When is your technique for troubled industries NOT reliable?
Answers: When quiet facts don't support improvement - oil and gas drilling industries kept getting worse since 1984 despite people saying they couldn't get worse.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what had happened to Toll Brothers stock and why?
