Answers: Dropped from $125⁄8 to $23⁄8 (five-bagger in reverse) due to fat-cat house owners selling amid real estate fears.

Questions: Why did you choose Toll Brothers for further study?
Answers: He remembered it as a strong company with financial wherewithal to survive hard times, recommended by Ken Heebner and Alan Leifer.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Toll Brothers' business model advantage?
Answers: Strictly a home builder, not a developer, so it wasn't risking its own money speculating in real estate.

Questions: What positive factors did you find in Toll Brothers' situation?
Answers: Debt had fallen $28 million, cash was up $22 million, balance sheet improved, and they had a two-year backlog of orders.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was wrong with the picture that justified Toll Brothers' price drop?
Answers: Nothing - the company had little debt, enough orders to keep busy for two years, competitors dropping out, and was well-positioned for recovery.

Questions: How did you approach the Pier 1 investment opportunity?
Answers: He realized people moving into houses would need lamps, room dividers, place mats, rugs, and furniture that Pier 1 sold at affordable prices.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Pier 1's stock price history?
Answers: Great growth in 70s, ran out of steam, great run in 80s, dropped from $14 to $4 in 1987, bounced to $12, hit $3 in Saddam Sell-off.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Intermark's involvement with Pier 1?
Answers: Conglomerate Intermark owned 58% of stock, allegedly rejected $16/share offer holding out for $20, but later forced to sell at $7 before going bankrupt.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what favorable factors did CEO Clark Johnson report about Pier 1?
Answers: Company made money in 1991 despite difficult environment, expanding 25-40 stores yearly, only 500 U.S. stores so nowhere near market saturation.

Questions: What is the key retail indicator you always checks?
Answers: Same-store sales - when they decline in prosperity it's worrying, but decline during recession is normal and even modest positive is good.

Questions: How did you analyze Pier 1's inventory situation?
Answers: Inventories had increased but only because of 25 new stores needing stock; otherwise at acceptable levels, unlike companies covering up poor sales.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the Sunbelt Nursery connection to Pier 1?
Answers: Pier 1 sold 50.5% of Sunbelt in public offering for $31 million, used $21 million to reduce debt and gave $10 million to Sunbelt for expansion.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was unusual about the Sunbelt transaction for Pier 1?
Answers: Pier 1 received $31 million for half of Sunbelt, which was $6 million more than it paid to acquire all of Sunbelt in 1990.

Questions: What was Pier 1's valuation when you recommended it?
Answers: $7 stock with P/E ratio of 10 based on 70-cent earnings estimate, while growing at 15% annual rate.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why was Pier 1 well-positioned for economic recovery?
Answers: Major competitors (department stores) were dropping home furnishing sections, mom-and-pop furniture stores closing, giving Pier 1 huge market share.

Questions: Who does you imagine might want to acquire Pier 1?
Answers: K mart, which was pleased with earlier acquisitions of drug, book, and office supply chains and always looking for expansion opportunities.

Questions: How did Pier 1 lead you to Sunbelt Nursery?
Answers: One stock leads to another - I realized lawn and garden business would benefit from housing rebound just like lampshade and dish rack business.

Questions: What opportunity did you see in the nursery business?
Answers: It was one of the last mom-and-pop enterprises not supplanted by chains - opportunity for well-managed chain to do for flower beds what Dunkin' Donuts did for donuts.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sunbelt's regional presence?
Answers: Operating as Wolfe Nursery (Texas/Oklahoma), Nurseryland Garden Centers (California), Tip Top Nursery (Arizona) in 6 of 11 largest lawn/garden markets.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sunbelt's target customer according to Smith Barney?
Answers: The upscale, quality-conscious lawn and garden customer seeking broader range, quality, and higher service level than discount-oriented retailers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sunbelt's initial public offering price and financial condition?
Answers: $8.50 per share IPO, started independent life with strong balance sheet - no debt and $2 per share in cash.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sunbelt's renovation plan?
Answers: Remodel 98 lawn and garden centers (not updated since Vietnam War), enclose portions so plants survive colder months instead of becoming mulch.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why had tax selling driven Sunbelt to $5 per share?
Answers: After single disappointing quarter caused by natural calamities (premature frost in Arizona, 14 inches of rain in Texas), stock lost half its value.

Questions: How did you value Sunbelt compared to Calloway's?
Answers: Calloway's: 13 stores worth $40 million ($3M per store). Sunbelt: 280 stores, even at half Calloway's value ($1.5M each) = $420M worth.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was Sunbelt's market valuation at $5 per share?
Answers: $5 × 6.2 million shares = $31 million total market value for entire company and 98 lawn and garden centers.

Questions: How did you calculate Sunbelt's intrinsic value?
Answers: $420 million asset value minus $167 million debt = $253 million worth, or $14 per share vs. $5 market price.

Questions: What attracted you to General Host initially?
Answers: The company had a long-term program to buy back its own shares, recently purchasing some for $10/share.

Questions: What is your insight about companies buying back their own shares?
Answers: When you can buy part of a company for less than the company itself has paid, it's a deal worth examining.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #15?
Answers: When insiders are buying, it's a good sign - unless they happen to be New England bankers.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was positive about General Host's CEO Harris Ashton?
Answers: He owned a million shares and hadn't sold a single one during the recent price drop from higher levels.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was General Host's book value situation?
Answers: Book value was $9 per share, exceeding the $7 stock price, meaning buyer got $9 worth of assets for $7.

Questions: How do you approach analyzing book value reliability?
Answers: He asks whether it's based on a true story or fiction, then examines the balance sheet to determine asset quality.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was reliable about General Host's balance sheet?
Answers: $65 million was cash (definitely reliable), and inventory consisted of trees, flowers, and shrubs with decent resale value.

Questions: What concerned you about General Host's debt ratio?
Answers: $167 million debt vs. $148 million equity was troublesome, but mitigated because debt wasn't due for years and wasn't owed to banks.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why is bank debt more dangerous than other debt?
Answers: If company runs into problems, banks will ask for money back immediately, turning manageable situation into potentially fatal one.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what operational improvements was General Host making?
Answers: Adding scanning devices, satellite system for inventory tracking, faster credit card authorization (25 seconds to 3 seconds), enclosing nursery sections.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was General Host's kiosk strategy?
Answers: Installing Christmas kiosks in malls during holidays, leveraging experience from 1,000+ Hickory Farm kiosks, planning 150 Frank's kiosks by Christmas 1992.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was General Host's expansion plan?
Answers: Opening 150 new Frank's Nursery outlets by 1995, bringing total to 430, plus launching private-label fertilizers and seeds.

Questions: How do you describe stockpicking as a dynamic exercise?
Answers: I emphasize that stockpicking is dynamic - a lot happens between making selections and publication, requiring constant monitoring and updates.

Questions: What was your routine for the Barron's Roundtable selections?
Answers: I follows the same routine annually: search for undervalued companies, usually finding them in out-of-favor sectors or industries.

Questions: Where did you consistently find bargains in 1991-1992?
Answers: I found no bargains among blue-chip growth stocks for two years running, including Merck, Abbott Labs, Wal-Mart, and Procter & Gamble.

Questions: How do you's chart-reading technique work for growth stocks?
Answers: I demonstrates that looking at long-term charts showing stock prices straying far beyond earnings lines provides danger signals to back off.

Questions: What do you say about Wall Street's explanations for stock declines?
Answers: I note that when popular stocks drop, Wall Street invents reasons (Clinton health plan for drugs, stronger dollar for Coca-Cola) when real reason is overpricing.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what typically happens to overpriced blue-chip growth stocks?
Answers: Lynch explains the stock price falls or moves sideways for couple years while earnings continue growing, until price and earnings converge again.

Questions: What principle does you emphasize about stock prices and earnings?
Answers: I teache that the price of a stock (the 'p' in P/E) cannot run too far ahead of earnings (the 'e') without something having to give.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how does the New Horizons indicator guide small-stock investing?
Answers: Lynch uses this indicator showing small stocks at bottom of price range relative to S&P 500, suggesting they'll outperform larger companies.

Questions: What sector revived in 1993 in your investment approach?
Answers: I observed that natural gas business revived enough that energy and energy service companies could do well after years in doldrums.

Questions: How did you approach the energy sector recovery?
Answers: I recommended five energy companies in 1993 (two service, three producers) noting excellent risk/reward ratios after thorough cost-cutting and consolidation.

Questions: What auto industry indicator supported your 1993 recommendations?
Answers: I used pent-up demand indicator showing auto industry would sell more cars than predicted, entering only third year of typical 5-6 year up cycle.

Questions: Which auto-related stocks did you recommend in 1993?
Answers: I recommended three automakers plus Harman International (car stereo equipment supplier to automakers).

Questions: What convinced you that steel prices were firming in 1993?
Answers: I learned from analysts and steel industry executives that prices were starting to firm, with expectations of government protection against dumping.

Questions: How many steel and metal companies did you recommend in 1993?
Answers: I recommended three steel companies and two other metal companies, finding biggest bargains in cyclicals.

Questions: What was your approach to cyclical investing in 1993?
Answers: I didn't start intending to buy cyclicals for economic recovery - he simply found biggest bargains and improving earnings were in cyclicals.

Questions: How did you's S&L recommendations perform through 1993?
Answers: I reports all seven 1992 S&L recommendations moved up, leading him to recommend eight new ones in 1993.

Questions: What amazes you about S&L performance since 1991?
Answers: I is amazed by doubles, triples, quadruples in dozens of issues that came public since 1991 with hardly any disappointments.

Questions: Why do you disagree with conventional S&L worries?
Answers: I disagrees that S&L party will end when economy improves and rates rise - believes steady improvement would actually benefit S&Ls.

Questions: How would economic improvement help S&Ls in your investment approach?
Answers: I explain better real estate markets mean faster foreclosure sales at higher prices, fewer defaults, less loan loss reserves needed.

Questions: Why did you begin investing in California companies in 1993?
Answers: I saw California in deep recession with negative press, similar to New England in 1990 - taking optimistic view California would survive like New England.

Questions: Which California companies did you recommend in 1993?
Answers: I recommended Coast Savings Financial, H.F. Ahmanson & Co. (largest thrift), Good Guys (retail electronics), plus Fannie Mae (25% California mortgages).

Questions: How do you conduct his 24-month checkup process?
Answers: I reviews companies by staying in tune with developments, checking quarterly reports, and watching for changes that affect investment thesis.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the disappointing outcome with Allied Capital II?
Answers: Lynch reports what he hoped would happen in 24 months took much longer - company couldn't put equity to work as planned.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why couldn't Allied Capital II deploy its capital as expected?
Answers: Lynch explains other investors and vulture funds were competing for good RTC loans, so Allied sat on cash earning 3% rather than lowering standards.

Questions: What was your mistake with nursery companies?
Answers: I admits his passion for General Host, Sunbelt, and Calloway's was big mistake - he underestimated fierce competition and discount center impact.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did discount centers affect the nursery business?
Answers: Lynch learned that K mart, Home Depot sold huge quantities of fertilizer, mulch, pesticides, and gardening tools, plus moms-and-pops competed by lowering prices.

Questions: What happened to Calloway's stock from your recommendation?
Answers: I note Calloway's fell from $8 when it impressed him to $3 by end of 1993, becoming potential turnaround rather than growth opportunity.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did the Sunbelt acquisition work out?
Answers: Lynch reports Sunbelt was taken over by General Host, but stock was $6.25 when recommended and buyout price was only $5 - a Pyrrhic victory.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what continued to challenge General Host's performance?
Answers: Lynch notes sales at Frank's Nursery outlets disappointing, with 1993 being terrible year due to record heat waves keeping people indoors.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did CMS Energy's rate case resolution affect the stock?
Answers: Lynch reports Michigan PSC ruling in March 1993 wasn't terrific but favorable enough to advance stock to mid-$20s from $18.50.

Questions: What happened to Phelps Dodge after your recommendation?
Answers: I note prosperous 1992 due to cost-cutting and higher copper prices, but softer copper market in 1993 caused company and stock to stall.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Body Shop's fundamentals change despite stock decline?
Answers: Lynch reports company didn't perform well in 1992, but fundamentals improved in 1993 despite stock hitting low of 140 pence in February.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what caused Body Shop's dramatic stock decline?
Answers: Lynch explains British recession hurt home market sales, three of four major markets (Canada, Britain, Australia) in recession, plus new U.S. competitors appeared.

Questions: Why do you remain optimistic about Body Shop long-term?
Answers: I see it as global enterprise in second decade of three-decade story, with most future growth from France, Japan and other countries without competition.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what major development occurred with Sun Distributors ahead of schedule?
Answers: Lynch reports company announced considering sale of divisions in September 1993, four years ahead of expected 1997 timeline.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how had Sun Distributors been preparing for potential sale?
Answers: Lynch notes company worked to maximize Class B share value by reducing debt, cutting costs, and refinancing long-term debt before sale announcement.

Questions: What do you say about Sun Distributors' patience-testing period?
Answers: I explain company did well and earnings increased steadily, but share price went nowhere for two years until September 1993 jump to $4.40.

Questions: How do you view early sales vs. long-term holding?
Answers: I feels same way about Sun Distributors potential sale as Taco Bell acquisition by PepsiCo - shareholders made quick profit but ongoing enterprise had 10x potential.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the current situation with Tenera's recovery?
Answers: Lynch reports Tenera hasn't fully recovered despite debt-free balance sheet, but has new COO, $2 million cash, bought back shares, attracted new clients.

Questions: How do you analyze Tenera's current risk/reward?
Answers: I calculates if company never recovers, liquidation value is $1/share; if it recovers, stock goes to $4.

Questions: What do you recommend about Cedar Fair's continued appeal?
Answers: I see Cedar Fair continuing to thrive after Dorney Park acquisition, with 6% yield, tax advantages until 1997, and potential acquisition target.

Questions: Who might want to acquire Cedar Fair in your investment approach?
Answers: I imagines entertainment giants might want their own amusement parks with themed rides - Disney already bought hockey team, why not amusement park?

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what positive developments occurred with EQK Green Acres?
Answers: Lynch reports refinancing of debt, Home Depot acquisition of property (reducing debt), and CEO purchasing 56,000 additional shares for himself.

Questions: How do you explain delayed market reaction to good news?
Answers: I note EQK stock rose after refinancing announcement but not immediately - investors don't need inside information since Wall Street can be slow to react.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what conversion is EQK Green Acres considering?
Answers: Lynch reports company may convert to REIT, which would strengthen balance sheet, enable lower-rate borrowing, and allow additional shopping center acquisitions.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what startling announcement did Supercuts make?
Answers: Lynch reports Supercuts will open 200 additional New York outlets in joint venture, borrowing money that will penalize 1993-94 earnings short-term.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how will Supercuts' expansion affect long-term growth?
Answers: Lynch explains new stores will accelerate company growth rate, and stock continues trading below market multiple despite being industry leader.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what evidence supports Supercuts' continued success?
Answers: Lynch notes customers continue lining up, same-store sales increased 4-5% without price increases - strong operational performance.

Questions: How has Sun Television performed since your recommendation?
Answers: I reports memorable year with same-store sales up 15.2%, 11 new stores in two years, expanding from Great Lakes to Buffalo and Syracuse.

Questions: What is your view on Sun TV's geographic expansion strategy?
Answers: I see company deploying forces from one end of Great Lakes to other, making it difficult for competitors to establish themselves in between.

Questions: How do you evaluate GM's prospects vs. other automakers?
Answers: I believe GM may be best performer over next few years despite being least-admired, benefiting when Europe recovers and from overseas sales.

Questions: What gives you confidence in GM's turnaround potential?
Answers: I note GM different from IBM turnaround - GM can recover without making money in U.S. auto market thanks to profitable overseas and non-automotive divisions.

Questions: What do you say about Fannie Mae's continued underappreciation?
Answers: I calls Fannie Mae as close to sure winner as you'll find - growing share of booming business with only 3,000 employees making $2 billion profits.

Questions: How do you address concerns about Fannie Mae and interest rates?
Answers: I explain Fannie Mae doesn't care about interest rates - callable debt allows reducing borrowing costs when rates decline, offsetting refinancing losses.

Questions: What do you say about Fannie Mae's California real estate exposure?
Answers: I note 25% of mortgages on California real estate, but average mortgage $100,000 or less, 68% loan-to-value ratio, .6% delinquency rate (historic low).

Questions: How do you differentiate Fannie Mae from Sallie Mae troubles?
Answers: I clarifies Fannie Mae has nothing to do with Sallie Mae - Congress passed bill redefining government-sponsored corporations but left Fannie Mae intact.

Questions: What do you project for Fannie Mae's valuation?
Answers: I believe giving Fannie Mae normal market valuation with 15% earnings growth and strong fundamentals makes it a $120 stock.

Questions: What is your emphasis about mutual savings bank conversions?
Answers: I couldn't be more emphatic about wisdom of investing in mutual savings banks as they convert to public ownership.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many unconverted mutual institutions remain?
Answers: Lynch notes 1,372 mutual savings banks and thrifts may yet convert to public ownership, providing ongoing opportunities.

Questions: What strategy does you suggest for conversion opportunities?
Answers: I recommend opening savings accounts in local mutual institutions, or depositing $1,000 in 50 different unconverted thrifts to improve participation chances.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what regulatory development affected S&L conversions?
Answers: Lynch reports Office of Thrift Supervision imposed moratorium on conversions due to insider profiteering, but expects process to resume after rule changes.

Questions: What do you observe about depositor participation in conversions?
Answers: I note only 2% of depositors nationwide have taken advantage of opportunities to buy shares at favorable initial prices in their local thrifts.

Questions: What was your main reason for retiring from managing the Magellan Fund?
Answers: I retired primarily to spend more time with his family. He realized he was missing his children's school plays, soccer games, and other important moments while being too focused on work.

Questions: How long did you manage the Fidelity Magellan Fund?
Answers: I managed the Magellan Fund for 13 years, from 1977 to 1990.

Questions: What was the performance of $1,000 invested in Magellan in 1977 when you handed over the reins in 1990?
Answers: $1,000 invested in Magellan in 1977 was worth $28,000 when I handed over the reins on May 21, 1990.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #1?
Answers: When the operas outnumber the football games three to zero, you know there is something wrong with your life.

Questions: What was your main investment philosophy described as?
Answers: my main philosophy was 'invest in what you know' - focusing on companies and products that investors could understand and evaluate themselves.

Questions: What were your three main misconceptions he wanted to address in the paperback edition?
Answers: 1) That I was talking down to average investors like a Babe Ruth to Little Leaguers, 2) That I think everyone should be picking individual stocks, 3) That I is against mutual funds.

Questions: In your investment philosophy, what percentage of NAIC investment clubs outperformed the S&P 500 in 1992?
Answers: 69.4 percent of the local investment clubs managed to outperform the S&P 500 in 1992.

Questions: What do you say about people who should NOT be picking individual stocks?
Answers: Millions of Americans should refrain from buying stocks - those who have no interest in investigating companies, cringe at balance sheets, and only look at annual reports for pictures.

Questions: What do you call the harmful practice of buying stocks without research?
Answers: I calls this 'playing the market' - looking for instant gratification without doing any work, seeking excitement from owning different stocks each week.

Questions: What is your view on equity mutual funds?
Answers: I see equity mutual funds as the perfect solution for people who want to own stocks without doing their own research, and believes investors in equity funds have prospered and will continue to prosper.

Questions: What evidence does you provide that individual investors are learning patience?
Answers: I note that individual investors didn't get scared out of stocks during market corrections in 1989 and 1990, showing they're learning that corrections are routine like snowstorms.

Questions: What disappointing discovery did you make about retirement accounts at Fidelity?
Answers: Only a small percentage of money in retirement accounts was invested in pure equity funds, with most going into money-market funds, bond funds, or equity income funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many students were in the St. Agnes seventh-grade portfolio management class?
Answers: The class had multiple teams of four students each, with team names like 'Rags to Riches,' 'the Wizards of Wall Street,' and 'the Lynch Mob.'

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the performance of the St. Agnes model portfolio over two years?
Answers: The St. Agnes portfolio produced a 70 percent gain over two years, outperforming the S&P 500 which gained 26 percent in the same timeframe.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of equity mutual funds did the St. Agnes students outperform?
Answers: The St. Agnes students outperformed 99 percent of all equity mutual funds.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is Peter's Principle #3?
Answers: Never invest in any idea you can't illustrate with a crayon.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the St. Agnes students' investment process?
Answers: Students learned to read Investor's Business Daily, researched companies by checking earnings and relative strength, and had to explain what each company did before being allowed to buy it.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did St. Agnes students discover Pentech International?
Answers: They discovered Pentech through a marker with a highlighter on one end that Ms. Morrissey introduced to class. The pen was very popular, leading students to investigate the company.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what attracted St. Agnes students to Walt Disney Company stock?
Answers: Students were attracted to Disney because 'every kid can explain this one' - it was a company they understood and whose products they used.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why did students choose PepsiCo?
Answers: Students knew PepsiCo four different ways: through Pepsi-Cola, Pizza Hut, Kentucky Fried Chicken, and Frito-Lay.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the students' reasoning for buying Topps?
Answers: Students were 'very much into trading cards within the seventh grade' and felt they were contributing to revenues of one of their companies by actually buying the products.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did students learn about Wal-Mart?
Answers: Through a videotaped segment of 'Lifestyles of the Rich and Famous' featuring Sam Walton talking about how investing benefits the economy.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the only poor performing stock in the St. Agnes model portfolio?
Answers: IBM was the only clunker, which Lynch notes has been a favorite of professional money managers for 20 years but keeps disappointing investors.

Questions: Why do you think the St. Agnes students picked IBM?
Answers: I calls it 'premature adulthood' - the students trying to imitate their elders on Wall Street by picking an 'approved' stock.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the performance of the winning four-person team in 1990?
Answers: The team of Andrew Castiglioni, Greg Bialach, Paul Knisell, and Matt Keating had their portfolio perform as well as or better than the model portfolio.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did Andrew Castiglioni discover National Pizza?
Answers: Castiglioni discovered National Pizza by scanning the NASDAQ list, then followed up with research on the company - the crucial second step many adult investors omit.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what stocks did the 1991 winning team choose?
Answers: Philip Morris, Coca-Cola, Texaco, Raytheon, Nike, Merck, Blockbuster Entertainment, and Playboy Enterprises.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how did students learn about Raytheon during the Gulf War?
Answers: Students sent letters to troops in Saudi Arabia and developed correspondence with Major Robert Swisher, who described how a Scud missile hit near his camp. When they learned Raytheon made the Patriot missile, they researched the stock.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what are some of the key maxims the St. Agnes students learned?
Answers: A good company usually increases its dividend every year; you can lose money quickly but it takes time to make money; the stock market isn't a gamble if you pick good companies; always research before investing.

Questions: What do you say about the relationship between stock performance and company success?
Answers: In the long term, there is 100 percent correlation between company success and stock success, though short-term correlation may not exist.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the NAIC Rule of Five?
Answers: If you pick stocks in five different growth companies, three will perform as expected, one will disappoint, and one will do better than imagined.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how many investment clubs does the NAIC represent?
Answers: The NAIC represents 10,000 stockpicking clubs made up of ordinary men and women.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what percentage of NAIC chapters outperformed the S&P 500 in 1991?
Answers: 61.9 percent of NAIC chapters did as well as or better than the S&P 500 in 1991.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what was the key to success for NAIC investment clubs?
Answers: They invest on a regular timetable, which removes guesswork about market direction and prevents impulse buying and selling.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what would $1,000 invested in the S&P 500 in January 1940 be worth 52 years later?
Answers: $1,000 invested in 1940 would be worth $333,793.30 after 52 years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what if you added $1,000 every January for 52 years to that initial investment?
Answers: Your $52,000 total investment would be worth $3,554,227 after 52 years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what if you added $1,000 every time the market dropped 10% or more?
Answers: Your $83,000 investment (initial plus 31 additional purchases during drops) would be worth $6,295,000.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, how often has the market dropped 10% or more in 52 years?
Answers: The market has dropped 10% or more 31 times in 52 years.

Questions: What do you say about collective decision making in investment clubs?
Answers: Rule by committee helps ensure no foolish proposal to sell everything will be carried out, and members do better with group money than private accounts.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, why do investment club members tend to do better research?
Answers: When you know your recommendations will affect your friends' pocketbooks, you tend to do your homework rather than acting on tips or hunches.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what is the NAIC approach to growth companies?
Answers: The NAIC focuses on well-managed growth companies with a history of prosperity and rising earnings - the land of the many-bagger where 10-30x returns are possible.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what key factors should you look for according to NAIC?
Answers: Sales and earnings per share moving forward at an acceptable rate, reasonable stock price, financial strength and debt structure that can withstand bad years.

Questions: From Peter Lynch's perspective, what should guide your buy/sell decisions according to NAIC?

Questions: What are your six categories of stocks?
Answers: I classifies all stocks into six main categories: (1) Slow Growers (large, aging companies growing slightly faster than GDP, bought mainly for generous dividends), (2) Stalwarts (multi-billion-dollar blue chips like Coca-Cola or Procter & Gamble growing earnings at 10-12% annually), (3) Fast Growers (small, aggressive new enterprises growing at 20-25% a year, which are the land of 10- to 40-baggers), (4) Cyclicals (companies whose sales and profits rise and fall regularly with the business cycle, such as autos, airlines, steel, and chemicals), (5) Turnarounds (battered, depressed, or nearly bankrupt companies recovering from existential trouble, like Chrysler in the early 1980s), and (6) Asset Plays (companies sitting on valuable hidden assets like real estate, timber, oil, or cash that Wall Street has overlooked).

Questions: How do you use the PEG ratio to value stocks?
Answers: I popularized the PEG ratio (Price/Earnings-to-Growth ratio), calculated by dividing a stock's P/E ratio by its annual earnings growth rate (preferably adding the dividend yield into the denominator: P/E divided by [Growth Rate + Dividend Yield]). According to I, a fairly priced company has a P/E ratio equal to its growth rate (PEG = 1.0). A PEG below 1.0 indicates an attractive bargain, a PEG of 0.5 or less is a phenomenal find, while a PEG above 1.5 or 2.0 signals an overpriced, risky stock.

Questions: What is a tenbagger in your investment terminology?
Answers: A 'tenbagger' is a term coined by I (borrowed from baseball) for an investment that appreciates to ten times its original purchase price. I note that in a diversified portfolio, just one or two tenbaggers can turn an average portfolio into an extraordinary outperformer because the most you can lose on any stock is 100% of what you invest, while the upside on a fast grower or turnaround is 1,000% or more.

Questions: What is your Cocktail Party Theory of market cycles?
Answers: I's Cocktail Party Theory gauges market sentiment across four stages based on how guests react when he says he manages a mutual fund: Stage 1 (Bottom): People nod politely and walk away to talk to a dentist about plaque; the market is beaten down and ready to rise. Stage 2: Guests linger a bit longer to complain that the stock market is too risky, even though it's already up 15%. Stage 3: Everyone crowds around Peter asking what stocks to buy, and even the dentist has stock tips; the market is up 30%. Stage 4 (Top): Guests crowd around Peter to tell HIM which stocks he should buy, and when he checks those tickers later, they're all up immediately--a classic sign of a market top about to correct.

Questions: What is your Two-Minute Drill?
Answers: Before buying any stock, I requires investors to deliver a concise 'two-minute monologue' aloud explaining: (1) What category the stock belongs to (Slow Grower, Stalwart, Fast Grower, Cyclical, Turnaround, or Asset Play), (2) What has to happen for the company to succeed and grow earnings, and (3) What the specific pitfalls and obstacles are that could derail the story. If you cannot explain why you own a stock in two minutes so that a fifth-grader can understand it, you shouldn't own it.

Questions: What does you mean by 'diworsification'?
Answers: I coined the word 'diworsification' to describe what happens when a profitable, cash-rich company blows its excess cash on overpriced, unrelated acquisitions outside its core competence instead of buying back shares, raising dividends, or expanding its proven business. Classic examples include Mobil buying Marcor (Montgomery Ward) or Gillette buying unrelated businesses before returning to razors and blades.

Questions: How do you analyze a company's balance sheet and debt-to-equity ratio?
Answers: I emphasize that it is almost impossible for a company with no debt to go bankrupt. He looks at the balance sheet comparing cash and marketable securities against short-term and long-term debt. For normal corporate balance sheets, I prefers about 75% equity and 25% debt (a debt-to-equity ratio around 0.33 or less). In turnarounds and small companies, high short-term bank debt callable on demand is the biggest red flag, whereas funded long-term bond debt gives a company breathing room.

Questions: How do you calculate and use net cash per share?
Answers: To find net cash per share, I adds a company's cash and cash equivalents, subtracts all long-term debt, and divides by the total number of shares outstanding. He then subtracts this net cash per share from the current stock price to compute the 'effective P/E ratio.' For example, if a stock trades at $20 with $5 per share in net cash and $2 in earnings, you are really paying $15 for the business, making the effective P/E 7.5 instead of 10.

Questions: What is your view on free cash flow?
Answers: I prizes free cash flow--the cash left over from operating cash flow after normal capital expenditures required to maintain the business. A company that doesn't have to spend heavily on capital equipment to grow (like software, consumer brands, or asset-light franchises) generates abundant free cash flow that can be used to retire debt, repurchase shares, raise dividends, or fund organic expansion.

Questions: Why do you closely watch inventory growth relative to sales growth?
Answers: For manufacturers and retailers, I checks whether inventories are piling up faster than sales. When inventory grows faster than sales, it is a major warning sign that demand is slowing down and the company will soon have to mark down merchandise, hurting gross margins and future earnings. Conversely, if a depressed company's inventories begin shrinking while sales stabilize, it is an early sign of a turnaround.

Questions: When does you say you should sell a Stalwart stock?
Answers: I treats Stalwarts as 30% to 50% gainers rather than lifetime holds. He recommends selling a Stalwart when: (1) the stock has risen 30-50% ahead of fundamentals and its P/E ratio has strayed far above its normal historical range, (2) its P/E has climbed well above its growth rate (PEG > 1.5), (3) new products introduced over the past two years have had mixed results and nothing exciting is in the pipeline, or (4) you find a similarly safe Stalwart whose stock price has lagged and offers better value.

Questions: When does you say you should sell a Fast Grower?
Answers: With Fast Growers, the key is not to sell too early while the expansion story is intact, nor too late when growth saturates. I sells a Fast Grower when: (1) same-store sales are falling or new store openings are disappointing, (2) the company has expanded into almost every geographic region and has nowhere left to replicate its concept, (3) top executives and key personnel are leaving to join competitors, or (4) the stock trades at an absurd P/E (such as 40-50x earnings) that prices in perfection for the next decade.

Questions: When does you say you should buy and sell a Cyclical stock?
Answers: Timing is everything in Cyclicals, and P/E ratios work backwards compared to growth stocks. For Cyclicals (autos, steel, paper, chemicals), a low P/E ratio usually happens at the peak of the cycle when record earnings are unsustainable--making a low P/E a warning sign to SELL, not buy! Conversely, at the bottom of a recession when earnings are depressed, the P/E looks sky-high, which is often the best time to buy. Sell a cyclical when inventories build up, commodity prices start falling, union wage contracts expire, or capital spending across the industry creates overcapacity.

Questions: When does you say you should sell a Turnaround stock?
Answers: According to I, the best time to sell a Turnaround is right after it has turned around! Once the crisis is over, debt is back under control, earnings have rebounded, and everyone on Wall Street knows the company survived and starts treating it as a normal growth or cyclical stock again, the easy recovery gains have been made. You must re-classify the company and evaluate whether it still merits holding at its new valuation.

Questions: When does you say you should sell an Asset Play?
Answers: With an Asset Play, patience is required until a catalyst unlocks the hidden value. I advise holding until a corporate raider, private equity buyer, or management restructuring monetizes the undervalued real estate, natural resources, or tax-loss carryforwards. Sell if management starts issuing new shares that dilute your claim on the assets, takes on heavy new debt to fund 'diworsification,' or if the asset sells for much less than expected.

Questions: What are the 13 qualities of your 'perfect company'?
Answers: In 'One Up On Wall Street', I lists 13 attributes of the ideal tenbagger stock: (1) It sounds dull--or even better, ridiculous, (2) It does something dull, (3) It does something disagreeable or depressing (like funeral homes or waste management), (4) It's a spinoff, (5) Institutions don't own it and analysts don't follow it, (6) Rumors abound that it's involved with toxic waste or the mafia, (7) There's something depressing about it, (8) It's in a no-growth industry, (9) It's got a niche, (10) People have to keep buying its product repeatedly, (11) It's a user of technology rather than a cutthroat maker of technology, (12) The insiders are buyers, and (13) The company is buying back its own shares.

Questions: Why do you love corporate spinoffs?
Answers: I loves spinoffs because parent corporations rarely spin off a subsidiary planning for it to go bankrupt--that would embarrass the parent's board. Spun-off companies usually receive strong balance sheets, freed-up management incentives (since executives now own stock directly in their division), and ability to cut bloated corporate overhead. Even better, institutional investors who receive spinoff shares automatically often dump them blindly because the spinoff is too small for their charters, creating temporary bargain prices.

Questions: What does insider buying vs. insider selling mean to you?
Answers: I famously notes: 'Insiders might sell their shares for any number of reasons, but they buy them for only one: they think the price will rise.' When corporate officers and mid-level managers spend their own salaries buying shares on the open market--especially after a price drop--it is one of the strongest signals of confidence. Routine insider selling (to pay taxes, buy a house, or pay college tuition) is usually meaningless unless multiple executives dump huge portions of their holdings simultaneously.

Questions: Why do you favor share buybacks over acquisitions?
Answers: When a company buys back its own shares, those shares are retired from circulation, shrinking the denominator in Earnings Per Share (EPS). Even if total company net income stays flat, cutting the share count by 20% automatically boosts EPS by 25%! I view consistent share repurchases as the purest sign that management believes in its own company and cares about shareholder returns.

Questions: What type of stocks does you urge investors to avoid at all costs?
Answers: I warn investors to avoid: (1) the hottest stock in the hottest industry (which draws relentless competition and overpriced valuations), (2) any company touted as 'the next IBM, the next McDonald's, or the next Intel' (because the 'next' something almost never is), (3) companies engaging in 'diworsification', (4) 'whisper stocks' with exciting stories about miracle cures or futuristic tech but zero current revenues or earnings, (5) middleman suppliers dependent on a single customer for 25-50% of sales, and (6) companies with silly or grandiose names designed to sound trendy.
